82149025.extract:
# Skiddaw Group SSSI

**Skiddaw Group SSSI** is a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) located in the Lake District High Fells in Cumbria, England. Designated in 1995, the site covers an area of approximately 10,256 hectares (39.60 square miles), making it one of the largest designated sites in the county . The SSSI is notified for both its geological and biological importance, encompassing the Skiddaw massif and the Caldbeck Fells.

The site contains the oldest rocks in the Lake District, the Ordovician Skiddaw Group, and is a key location for the study of stratigraphy, igneous petrology, and mineralogy . Biologically, the area supports extensive upland habitats including blanket bog, heathland, and montane grassland, which provide breeding grounds for a diverse assemblage of upland birds and invertebrates . The site includes Skiddaw Forest, a large area of upland terrain that was the subject of a major acquisition and restoration project by the Cumbria Wildlife Trust in 2024 .

## Geography and Topography

The Skiddaw Group SSSI is situated in the northern part of the Lake District National Park. The site forms an irregular circle centred near Great Calva and includes several major summits exceeding 610 metres (2,000 ft) in elevation . Prominent peaks within the SSSI include Skiddaw (931 m), Blencathra, Skiddaw Little Man, Lonscale Fell, Carl Side, and Long Side in the south, and High Pike, Carrock Fell, Knott, Great Calva, and Bowscale Fell in the north and east .

The topography is characterized by smooth-sided mountains typical of the Skiddaw Slate geology, contrasting with the more rugged volcanic fells found further south in the Lake District . The high ground serves as a major watershed, dividing water flow between three operational catchments: the River Caldew flowing north towards Carlisle; the River Ellen flowing west; and the River Derwent flowing towards the west coast at Workington and Maryport .

The site contains two glacial tarns: Bowscale Tarn and Scales Tarn . These water bodies and the associated headwaters of streams such as Dash Beck, Glenderaterra Beck, and the River Caldew are integral to the site's hydrological and ecological systems .

## Geology

The geological significance of the Skiddaw Group SSSI is a primary reason for its designation. The site provides the type locality for the Skiddaw Group of sedimentary rocks and contains the Caldbeck Fells, an area renowned for its mineral diversity and mining history .

### Skiddaw Group
The dominant rock formation is the Skiddaw Group, consisting of metamorphosed mudstones, siltstones, and wacke-type sandstones of marine origin . These rocks are the oldest in the Lake District, dating to the Ordovician period (Tremadoc to Llanvirn epochs, approximately 485–460 million years ago) . The sedimentary sequence is estimated to be over 5,000 metres thick, although the base is not exposed .

The stratigraphy includes several formations, such as the Bitter Beck, Watch Hill, Hope Beck, Loweswater, and Kirk Stile Formations . The rocks exhibit complex polyphase folding resulting from the Caledonian Orogeny, with classic exposures of fold structures visible in areas such as Mosedale .

### Igneous and Metamorphic Features
The SSSI contains significant igneous features, most notably the Skiddaw Granite and the Carrock Fell Complex. The Skiddaw Granite is a Devonian pluton (intruded approximately 390 million years ago) that lies beneath the Skiddaw massif . Although the granite itself has limited surface exposure (e.g., in the valley of the River Caldew and Sinen Gill), its thermal metamorphism has created a distinct aureole in the surrounding sedimentary rocks . This aureole displays a progression of metamorphic zones, from outer andalusite slates to inner cordierite-rich hornfels .

### Mineralogy
The Caldbeck Fells, located in the northern sector of the SSSI, are considered one of the most mineralogically diverse sites in the United Kingdom . The area is crisscrossed by mineral veins containing ores of copper, lead, zinc, iron, and tungsten . Over 175 valid mineral species have been identified in the area, with some sources suggesting the count is significantly higher .

Notable locations include Roughton Gill, Red Gill, and Dry Gill . The site is the type locality for several minerals and has produced world-class specimens of pyromorphite, hemimorphite, and plumbogummite . Due to the scientific importance and finite nature of these mineral resources, collecting is strictly regulated, and the area is monitored to prevent unauthorized extraction .

## Ecology and Habitats

The Skiddaw Group SSSI is a component of the Lake District High Fells Special Area of Conservation (SAC), recognized for its extensive upland habitats .

### Flora
The vegetation is dominated by upland heath and blanket bog communities. Key habitats identified under the SAC designation include:
* **Northern Atlantic wet heaths** with cross-leaved heath (*Erica tetralix*) .
* **European dry heaths** dominated by heather (*Calluna vulgaris*) and bilberry (*Vaccinium myrtillus*) .
* **Alpine and Boreal heaths** found at higher altitudes .
* **Blanket bogs**, particularly in areas around Bannerdale Beck and Skiddaw Forest .
* **Siliceous scree** communities containing parsley fern (*Cryptogramma crispa*) .

A notable botanical feature is **Young Wood** on Bowscale Fell. Situated between 465 and 485 metres above sea level, it is considered the highest Atlantic oakwood in England . This fragment of ancient semi-natural woodland consists of sessile oak (*Quercus petraea*) and is a remnant of high-altitude woodland that was once more widespread . Other significant woodland features include stands of juniper (*Juniperus communis*) scrub, particularly in the Swinside Valley .

The glacial tarns within the SSSI support aquatic flora such as quillwort (*Isoetes lacustris*), shoreweed (*Littorella uniflora*), and water lobelia (*Lobelia dortmanna*) .

### Fauna
The site supports a diverse assemblage of upland birds. It is a key breeding site for the Ring Ouzel (*Turdus torquatus*), a species that has suffered significant national declines . Other breeding birds recorded in the area include the Merlin (*Falco columbarius*), Peregrine Falcon (*Falco peregrinus*), Buzzard (*Buteo buteo*), Raven (*Corvus corax*), Golden Plover (*Pluvialis apricaria*), and Dotterel (*Charadrius morinellus*) .

Invertebrate populations include the rare montane ground beetle *Leistus montanus*, which has been recorded on the summit of Skiddaw . The area also supports the Northern Dart moth (*Xestia alpicola*) and the beetle *Carabus nitens* .

## History and Land Use

### Mining History
The Caldbeck Fells have a long history of mineral extraction, dating back potentially to the 14th century or earlier . The most significant period of mining began in the 16th century with the arrival of German miners from Austria and Bavaria, brought to the area by the Company of Mines Royal . Operations at Caldbeck were among the first large-scale copper mining and smelting enterprises in the British Isles .

Mining continued intermittently through the centuries, exploiting lead, copper, and barytes. The Roughton Gill mine was one of the largest operations, producing significant quantities of lead and copper ores before closing in the late 19th century . The spoil heaps and adits remaining from these activities are now protected as part of the SSSI for their lichen communities and industrial archaeology, as well as their mineralogical value .

### Agriculture and Forestry
Much of the land within the SSSI is common land used for sheep grazing, which has historically influenced the vegetation composition, particularly the extent of heath and woodland . Overgrazing has been identified as a pressure on the condition of upland habitats .

Commercial forestry has occurred on the periphery of the SSSI, such as at Dodd Wood. Management plans in the 21st century have focused on removing non-native conifer regeneration from the SSSI and restoring transitional habitats .

## Conservation and Management

The Skiddaw Group SSSI is managed to maintain and enhance its geological and biological features. It falls under the regulatory purview of Natural England.

### Condition and Restoration
Assessments by Natural England have classified various units of the SSSI. While some areas, such as invertebrate habitats, have been assessed as "favourable," other habitats like blanket bog and dwarf shrub heath have historically been classified as "unfavourable – recovering" due to pressures such as grazing .

Restoration projects have included fencing initiatives on Mungrisdale Common and Caldbeck Common to exclude livestock and allow the regeneration of heather, bilberry, and scrub habitats .

### Skiddaw Forest Acquisition
In 2024, the Cumbria Wildlife Trust completed the purchase of the Skiddaw Forest, a 1,200-hectare (3,000-acre) area including the summit of Skiddaw . The acquisition was funded by a public appeal and a partnership with Aviva . The Trust announced a 100-year vision to restore the area, which includes the re-establishment of temperate rainforest (Atlantic oakwood) on lower slopes, the restoration of 992 acres of peatbog, and the enhancement of montane scrub and wildflower grasslands . This project aims to create England's highest nature reserve .

The **Skiddaw Group** is a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_/(stratigraphy/) "Group (stratigraphy)") of [sedimentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedimentary "Sedimentary") rock formations named after the mountain [Skiddaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw "Skiddaw") in the [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") [Lake District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_District "Lake District"). The rocks are almost wholly [Ordovician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordovician "Ordovician") in age ([Tremadoc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tremadocian "Tremadocian") through [Arenig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arenig "Arenig") to [Llanvirn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordovician#Subdivisions "Ordovician") [epochs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epoch_/(geology/) "Epoch (geology)")) though the lowermost beds are possibly of [Cambrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambrian "Cambrian") age.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group#cite_note-1) This rock sequence has previously been known as the **Skiddaw Slates**, the **Skiddaw Slates Group** and the Skiddavian Series. Its base is not exposed but in its main outcrop area, it is considered to be in excess of 5,000 metres (16,000 ft) thick though less elsewhere.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group#cite_note-BGS_lexicon-2) It consists largely of [mudstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudstone "Mudstone") and [siltstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siltstone "Siltstone") with subordinate [wacke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wacke "Wacke")\-type [sandstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone"). Their main occurrence is within the northern and central fells of the Lake District, either side of the major ENE-WSW aligned [Causey Pike Fault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causey_Pike_Fault "Causey Pike Fault"), but [inliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inliers_and_outliers_/(geology/) "Inliers and outliers (geology)") are found at [Black Combe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Combe "Black Combe") in the south of the Lake District and at [Cross Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_Fell "Cross Fell") in the [North Pennines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pennines "North Pennines").

In the [Northern Fells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Fells "Northern Fells") of the Lake District, the Skiddaw Group comprises five formations of which the earliest/lowest is the Bitter Beck Formation. This is succeeded by the Watch Hill Formation, then the Hope Beck, Loweswater and Kirk Stile Formations in ascending order. The inlier at Cross Fell comprises just the Catterpallot Formation, a wacke sandstone which is the rough equivalent of the Watch Hill Formation, itself a wacke sandstone as is the Loweswater Formation.

Within the [Central Fells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Fells "Central Fells") are the Buttermere Formation and the overlying Tarn Moor Formation. These are matched by the Murton Formation (grey slates and thin sandstones) and the Kirkland Formation (mudstones with [tuffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuff "Tuff") and lavas) at Cross Fell. The Buttermere Formation is interpreted as an [olistostrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olistostrome "Olistostrome"). The Tarn Moor and Kirkland Formations contain some [volcaniclastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyroclastic_rock "Pyroclastic rock") rocks. The inlier to the south at Black Combe contains the wackes of the Knott Hill Formation.

The group underlies the [Borrowdale Volcanic Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borrowdale_Volcanic_Group "Borrowdale Volcanic Group") in the southern and central Lake District and the [Eycott Volcanic Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eycott_Volcanic_Group "Eycott Volcanic Group") in the northern part of the district.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group#cite_note-3)

The Kirkland Formation has provided fossils of _[Dichograptus octobrachiatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dichograptus "Dichograptus")_ and _[Heminectere rushtoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Heminectere&action=edit&redlink=1 "Heminectere (page does not exist)")_.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group#cite_note-4)

The sequence was affected by low-grade regional [metamorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metamorphism "Metamorphism") and deformation associated with the [Acadian Orogeny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acadian_Orogeny "Acadian Orogeny"), causing the dominant fine-grained parts of the sequence to become [slates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slate "Slate"). The resulting slaty [cleavage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleavage_/(geology/) "Cleavage (geology)") is parallel to the axial plane of regional [folds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fold_/(geology/) "Fold (geology)").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group#cite_note-Stone_et_al_1999-5)

### Description

This contract covers Five SSSI Lake Sites in Cumbria, assessing the 'Lake Habitat' feature:

1\. Armboth Fells SSSI (2 Lakes: Blea Tarn & Dock Tarn)  
2\. Skiddaw Group SSSI (2 Lakes: Scales & Bowscale Tarn)  
3\. Helvellyn & Fairfield SSSI (2 Lakes included in contract: Red Tarn & Grisedale Tarn)  
4\. Scafell Pikes SSSI (2 Lakes: Styhead Tarn & Sprinkling Tarn)  
5\. Claife Tarns and Mires SSSI (3 Lakes: Three Dubs Tarn, Moss Eccles Tarn & Hodson's Tarn)

Aims

The purpose of the contract is listed below:

1\. Undertake a whole site assessment of the Lake Habitat using the standardised methods outlined in Common Standards Monitoring Guidance & provide a recommended condition of the Lake Habitat at each of the five sites.    
2\. Provide a unit-by-unit description of the designated lake habitat, including an assessment of each unit/lake.    
3\. Record details of any 'pressures' observed which may impact on the condition of the lake habitat.    
4\. Suggest where current management is supporting favourable condition, where it is not and why might that be.      
5\. Undertake a climate change risk assessment of the lake feature at each site.  
6\. Comment, where relevant, on the targets in the monitoring specification

Further information about the sites can be located on Natural England's Designated Sites View: [https://designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk/](https://designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk/%E2%80%AF%E2%80%AF)

The results will allow Natural England to undertake a Commons Standards Monitoring assessment of the condition of the lake feature at each site and help with advising future management.

Skiddaw Group SSSI

Cumbria



 |
| Nearest town | [Keswick, Cumbria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keswick,_Cumbria "Keswick, Cumbria") |
| Coordinates | [54°40′08″N 3°06′07″W / 54.669°N 3.102°W](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.669_N_3.102_W_type:landmark_dim:11km) |
| Area | 10,256 ha (39.60 sq mi) |
| Average elevation | 490 m (1,610 ft) |
| Max. elevation | 930 m (3,050 ft) |
| Min. elevation | 126 m (413 ft) |
| Designation | SSSI |

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI.svg/250px-Skiddaw_Group_SSSI.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Skiddaw_Group_SSSI.svg)

Relief map of Skiddaw Group SSSI including unit numbers

**Skiddaw Group SSSI** is a [site of special scientific interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site_of_special_scientific_interest "Site of special scientific interest") in the [Lake District High Fells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_District_High_Fells "Lake District High Fells"), England. Its shape is approximately an irregular circle centred near [Great Calva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Calva "Great Calva"), with an area of 10,256.3 hectares (39.600 sq mi).[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4) The high ground creates a [watershed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_divide "Drainage divide") between the _Caldew Operational Catchment_ with water flowing north towards [Carlisle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlisle "Carlisle"), and the _Ellen and West Coast_ and _Derwent Operational Catchments_ flowing towards the west coast at [Workington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workington "Workington") and [Maryport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryport "Maryport").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-derwent_man_catchment-5)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-caldew_op_catchment-6) The area includes the **Skiddaw Forest** nature reserve.

The SSSI is designated for its flora and fauna, and for its geology.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4) The geology includes the [Skiddaw Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group "Skiddaw Group") of [sedimentary rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedimentary_rock "Sedimentary rock") formations, and the **Caldbeck Fells** former mining area. [Fells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fell "Fell") above 2,000 feet (610 m) include [High Pike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Pike "High Pike"), [Carrock Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrock_Fell "Carrock Fell"), [Knott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knott,_Caldbeck "Knott, Caldbeck"), [Great Calva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Calva "Great Calva"), and [Bowscale Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowscale_Fell "Bowscale Fell"). The highest peaks are in the [Skiddaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw "Skiddaw") area, including Skiddaw itself, [Long Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Side "Long Side"), [Carl Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Side "Carl Side"), [Little Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Little_Man "Skiddaw Little Man"), [Lonscale Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonscale_Fell "Lonscale Fell") and, further east, [Blencathra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blencathra "Blencathra").

The SSSI is divided into a patchwork of "units" which are used as the level of geographic detail for reporting overall features and conditions.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-7) Each unit is identified by the Ordnance Survey grid reference at the centre of the unit, its area in hectares, the date it was last surveyed, and the [drainage catchment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_basin "Drainage basin") it is located in.[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-8) For example _Bassenthwaite Common_, which is unit 27, is nearly 700 ha (2.7 sq mi) centred at [NY252299](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.658615_N_3.161010_W_region:GB_dim:4083m) in the _Dash beck_ catchment. The habitat is there is _dwarf shrub heath_ which, when surveyed in November 2010, was in an "unfavourable – recovering" condition.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4)

Skiddaw Forest is the ancient name of an expanse of land to the east of Skiddaw summit, with the word "[forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chase_/(land/) "Chase (land)")" referring here to a medieval pattern of land ownership.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-9)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-10) In 2024 the forest area within the [Underskiddaw civil parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underskiddaw "Underskiddaw") area,[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-11) essentially SSSI units 30 and 31 together with the summits of Skiddaw (unit 16) and Great Calva (unit 17), was purchased by [Cumbria Wildlife Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumbria_Wildlife_Trust "Cumbria Wildlife Trust") as a 1,200 ha (4.6 sq mi) nature reserve.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-barkham-12)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-13) The long term [biodiversity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biodiversity "Biodiversity") and [rewilding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rewilding "Rewilding") goals include encouraging tree growth to create tracts of [temperate rainforest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperate_rainforest "Temperate rainforest"), and restoring [peatlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peatland "Peatland").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-14)

Unit 30, _Skiddaw Forest West_, was assessed in 2021 as having "favourable" conditions for invertebrate and breeding bird features, but "unfavourable – recovering" blanket bog and upland dry heath habitats.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-15) Conditions in unit 31, _Skiddaw Forest East_ were assessed as "favourable" in 2021.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-16)

Caldbeck Fells mines
--------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Caldbeck Fells mines")\]

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/Disused_mine_workings_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1506663.jpg/250px-Disused_mine_workings_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1506663.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Disused_mine_workings_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1506663.jpg)

Disused mine workings on Caldbeck Fells

The northern part of the SSSI includes several sites of former mines, noted today for the presence of minerals in spoil heaps and erosion sites.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-jecock-17)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-othermines-18)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-tylercarrock-19)

Spoil heaps at Red Gill Mine ([NY295347](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.702364_N_3.095530_W_region:GB_dim:4083m), unit 26) include rare, crystallised lead sulphates, carbonates and phosphates. An adjacent mine at Roughtongill ([NY302344](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.699766_N_3.084598_W_region:GB_dim:4083m), unit 23) reveals [supergene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supergene_/(geology/) "Supergene (geology)") minerals including copper and zinc varieties.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4) English Heritage undertook a detailed survey of Roughtongill in 2001 and reported on its history and archaeology.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-jecock-17)

Dry Gill Lead Mine ([NY324345](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.700966_N_3.050490_W_region:GB_dim:4083m), unit 24) has a unique form of [mimetite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mimetite "Mimetite"), known as '[campylite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campylite "Campylite")'. Natural England surveyed the site in 2022 and found the exposed mineral veins had been damaged by collectors in the past but not recently. Burdell Gill ([NY307324](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.681866_N_3.076365_W_region:GB_dim:4083m), unit 20) "is of national importance as the only relatively abundant source of the rare arsenic mineral, [pharmacosiderite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmacosiderite "Pharmacosiderite"), in Britain."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4) A vein at Wet Swine Gill ([NY314321](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.679266_N_3.065439_W_region:GB_dim:4083m)) includes [stibnite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stibnite "Stibnite") and [fuloppite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuloppite "Fuloppite") but the 2022 survey (SSSI Unit 2) found that geological specimen collecting continued to cause damage. In the Carrock Mine – Brandy Gill spoil heaps ([NY322338](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.694649_N_3.053430_W_region:GB_dim:4083m)) the mineralisation is [tungsten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tungsten "Tungsten")\-rich.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4) The Carrock Tungsten Mine ([NY323329](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.686576_N_3.051670_W_region:GB_dim:4083m))[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-20) and Carrock End Copper Mine[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-tylercarrock-19) are Scheduled Monuments.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-21)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-22)

There are other mine sites not mentioned in the SSSI designation, such as in the wider Grainsgill area ([NY327327](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.684833_N_3.045420_W_region:GB_dim:4083m)),[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-Loughlin-23) near to Carrock mine. A 2021 survey in that area (SSSI unit 8) observed "[Ordovician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordovician "Ordovician") igneous geological features".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4) Breafell lead mine ([NY299357](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.711405_N_3.089565_W_region:GB_dim:4083m), unit 26) was downstream from Redgill and Roughtongill on the Dale Beck, a tributary of the Whelpo. Driggith lead mine[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-24) was downstream from Drygill mine. Sandbeck lead and copper mine ([NY332362](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.716347_N_3.038469_W_region:GB_dim:4083m), unit 24/25) was 1,800 metres (1.1 mi) north east of High Pike.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-othermines-18)

Caldew operational catchment
----------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Caldew operational catchment")\]

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/House_at_the_foot_of_Carrock_Fell_-_geograph.org.uk_-_5163753.jpg/250px-House_at_the_foot_of_Carrock_Fell_-_geograph.org.uk_-_5163753.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:House_at_the_foot_of_Carrock_Fell_-_geograph.org.uk_-_5163753.jpg)

House at the foot of Carrock Fell

The Skiddaw Group SSSI includes the headwaters of the _Whelpo (Cald) Beck_ and _Caldew (upper)_ 'water bodies' (catchments).[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-caldew_op_catchment-6) These are part of the _Caldew operational catchment_.[\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-jargon-25)

The _[Whelpo Beck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whelpo_Beck "Whelpo Beck")_ catchment includes [Brae Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brae_Fell "Brae Fell") (586 m (1,923 ft), unit 26), and the former mine sites at Red Gill and Roughtongill (units 26 and 23).[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4) When surveyed by Natural England in 2010, both mine sites (SSSI Units 3 and 11) were showing some signs of collector activity and erosion but were not considered to be under threat. The "dwarf shrub heath" habitats were surveyed in 2022 (SSSI units 23 – Roughton Gill; 25 – Caldbeck North; and 26 – Brae Fell). They were all depleted by heavy grazing. Patches of bilberry (_[Vaccinium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaccinium "Vaccinium") spp._) were observed on Brae Fell.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4)

The _Caldew (upper)_ catchment accounts for 40% of the total area of the SSSI and the majority of its assessment units.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-caldew_op_catchment-6)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-unitmap-26) The [River Caldew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Caldew "River Caldew") flows there between the Blencathra uplands in the south-east of the SSSI, and the Skiddaw and Caldbeck Fells uplands to the west and north. The catchment includes [Great Calva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Calva "Great Calva") (690 m (2,260 ft), unit 17) and [Carrock Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrock_Fell "Carrock Fell") (661 m (2,169 ft), units 22 and 24). Around the edge of the catchment, [Lonscale Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonscale_Fell "Lonscale Fell"), [Skiddaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw "Skiddaw"), [Skiddaw Little Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Little_Man "Skiddaw Little Man"), and [Bowscale Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowscale_Fell "Bowscale Fell") form watersheds with the catchments in the _Derwent Operational Catchment_ area.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-derwent_man_catchment-5) It includes the former mine sites at Dry Gill Mine, Carrock Mine-Brandy Gill, Burdell Gill and Wet Swine Gill.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4) It also includes Bowscale Tarn ([NY336313](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.672373_N_3.031143_W_region:GB_dim:4083m), unit 13), one of two [glacial tarns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarn_/(lake/) "Tarn (lake)") in the SSSI,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4) where quillwort (_[Isoetes lacustris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isoetes_lacustris "Isoetes lacustris")_), shoreweed (_[Littorella uniflora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Littorella_uniflora "Littorella uniflora")_) and water lobelia (_[Lobelia dortmanna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lobelia_dortmanna "Lobelia dortmanna")_) have been found.

[Heather moor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorland "Moorland") predominates on sloping ground north and west of the River Caldew across several catchments. The east-facing slopes of Skiddaw, Little Man and Jenkin Hill exhibit degraded [moss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moss "Moss") heath. Common juniper (_[Juniperus communis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juniperus_communis "Juniperus communis")_) scrub, which is a nationally rare habitat, is most extensive on the steep, rocky south-facing slopes of Carrock Fell ([NY342336](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.693118_N_3.022361_W_region:GB_dim:4083m)).[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4)

*   [![Image 7: Shoreweed](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Littorella_uniflora_kz01.jpg/250px-Littorella_uniflora_kz01.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Littorella_uniflora_kz01.jpg "Shoreweed")
    
    Shoreweed
    
*   [![Image 8: Water lobelia](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Lobelia_dortmanna_kz06.jpg/250px-Lobelia_dortmanna_kz06.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lobelia_dortmanna_kz06.jpg "Water lobelia")
    
    Water lobelia
    
*   [![Image 9: Common juniper](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Einebusk_Juniperus_communis.jpg/120px-Einebusk_Juniperus_communis.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Einebusk_Juniperus_communis.jpg "Common juniper")
    
    Common juniper
    

Derwent management catchment
----------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Derwent management catchment")\]

The Skiddaw Group SSSI includes headwaters of the _Derwent management catchment_,[\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-jargon-25) consisting of the _Ellen (upper)_ catchment, which flows towards [Maryport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryport "Maryport"), and four catchments flowing towards [Workington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workington "Workington"):[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-derwent_man_catchment-5)

*   _Dash Beck_
*   _Derwent US Bassenthwaite Lake_ and _Derwent DS Bassenthwaite_[\[e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-usds-27)
*   _Glenderaterra Beck_
*   _Glenderamackin u/s Troutbeck_ and _Glenderamackin (Greta)_[\[e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-usds-27)

The _Ellen (upper)_ catchment is at the north of the SSSI in the Uldale Fells. It is bounded by Longlands Fell, Lowthwaite Fell, Little and Great Sca Fells, Meal Fell and Great Cockup. Great Cockup ([NY270334](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.690327_N_3.133990_W_region:GB_dim:4083m), unit 18) is known for fossils of [dendroid graptolites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dictyonema_/(graptolite/) "Dictyonema (graptolite)"). [Tremadoc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tremadocian "Tremadocian")–[Llanvirn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llanvirn "Llanvirn") geology[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-GCR36-28) is visible in the crags around Great Cockup. The heathland lacks species diversity and shows signs of [heavy grazing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overgrazing "Overgrazing").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4) For catchment management purposes, the main water body is the Dale Gill which rises between Great and Little Cockup. The River Ellen's headwaters, with numerous small tributaries, drain the Uldale Fells and join Dale Gill beyond the SSSI boundary.

[![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/Whitewater_Dash_-_geograph.org.uk_-_2137126.jpg/250px-Whitewater_Dash_-_geograph.org.uk_-_2137126.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Whitewater_Dash_-_geograph.org.uk_-_2137126.jpg)

Whitewater Dash

The SSSI includes the headwaters of the _Dash Beck_ catchment, including short lengths of [Dash Beck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dash_Beck "Dash Beck") itself, and of several of its tributaries. The part of the catchment within the SSSI stretches from [Great Sca Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Sca_Fell "Great Sca Fell") in the north-east to [Ullock Pike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ullock_Pike "Ullock Pike") 7 km (4.3 miles) away in the south-west, with the Whitewater Dash waterfall ([NY272313](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.671488_N_3.130364_W_region:GB_dim:4083m)) where the [beck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beck_/(stream/) "Beck (stream)") crosses the catchment midway between the two.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-dashbeck_catchment-29) The area includes [Bakestall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakestall "Bakestall") where crowberry (_[Empetrum nigrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empetrum_nigrum "Empetrum nigrum")_) is the dominant dwarf-shrub. It also includes Broad End which has "the best developed example \[of montane moss-grass heath in West Cumbria\] at about 700 m (2,300 ft)" elevation. There are two monitoring units in the _Dash beck_ catchment: _Uldale South_ (SSSI Unit 19, [NY282322](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.679718_N_3.115083_W_region:GB_dim:4083m)) has low species diversity with some areas recovering; _Uldale North_ (SSSI Unit 18, [NY272342](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.697544_N_3.131088_W_region:GB_dim:4083m)) includes heather (_[Calluna vulgaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calluna_vulgaris "Calluna vulgaris")_), bilberry (_[Vaccinium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaccinium "Vaccinium") spp_), crowberry (_[Empetrum nigrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empetrum_nigrum "Empetrum nigrum")_) and cross-leaved heath (_[Erica tetralix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erica_tetralix "Erica tetralix")_) but the sites are fragmented where they should be continuous.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4) In the north-east of the catchment, the watershed is marked by [Knott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knott,_Caldbeck "Knott, Caldbeck"), Great Sca Fell, [Meal Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meal_Fell "Meal Fell"), and [Great Cockup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Cockup "Great Cockup").

The _Glenderaterra Beck_ catchment includes _Lonscale Fell_ (SSSI Unit 29, [NY289269](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.632197_N_3.102938_W_region:GB_dim:4083m), surveyed 2024) and _Blencathra North West_ (SSSI Unit 32, [NY311274](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.636995_N_3.068982_W_region:GB_dim:4083m), surveyed 2019). Lonscale Fell ecology included some bracken and limited cover of ericoid shrubs in its "acidic grassland with bilberry" habitats. Blencathra North West had "blanket bog with abundant hare's-tail cottongrass (_[Eriophorum vaginatum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eriophorum_vaginatum "Eriophorum vaginatum")_) and deergrass (_[Trichophorum cespitosum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichophorum_cespitosum "Trichophorum cespitosum")_) over locally abundant bog mosses".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4)

There is a small area of common juniper (_[Juniperus communis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juniperus_communis "Juniperus communis")_) scrub in _Glenderamackin u/s Troutbeck_[\[e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-usds-27) on The Tongue ([NY347302](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.662634_N_3.013843_W_region:GB_dim:4083m)). The same catchment includes Scales Tarn (Blencathra), one of the two glacial tarns in the SSSI. The tarn has "low nutrient levels and \[is\] inherently species-poor." The area around the tarn has in the past been subject to heavy grazing. Mungrisdale East (SSSI Unit 35, [NY343297](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.658089_N_3.019931_W_region:GB_dim:4083m)) includes hare's-tail cottongrass (_[Eriophorum vaginatum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eriophorum_vaginatum "Eriophorum vaginatum")_), abundant sphagnum moss (_[Sphagnum spp.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphagnum_spp. "Sphagnum spp.")_) and a good population of serrated wintergreen (_[Orthilia secunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthilia_secunda "Orthilia secunda")_). Young Wood (SSSI Unit 38, [NY350307](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&params=54.667165_N_3.009305_W_region:GB_dim:4083m)) is protected by fencing to keep grazing animals away and the oak woodland is recovering.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-designation-4)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-30)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-31)

### Special Area of Conservation

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Special Area of Conservation")\]

Skiddaw Group SSSI is a component of the [Lake District High Fells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_District_High_Fells "Lake District High Fells"), a [Special Area of Conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Area_of_Conservation "Special Area of Conservation").[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-jncc-32) The SAC covers ten SSSIs but, within the Skiddaw Group, the SAC documentation identifies a range of habitats:

*   4010 Northern Atlantic wet heaths with cross-leaved heath (_[Erica tetralix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erica_tetralix "Erica tetralix")_)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-33)
*   4030 European dry heaths[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-34)
*   4060 Alpine and Boreal heaths[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-35)
*   5130 Common juniper (_[Juniperus communis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juniperus_communis "Juniperus communis")_) formations on heaths or calcareous grasslands[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-36)
*   7130 Blanket bogs[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-37)
*   8110 Siliceous scree of the montane to snow levels (alpine rock-jasmine (_[Androsace alpina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Androsace_alpina "Androsace alpina")_) and red hemp-nettle (_[Galeopsis ladanum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galeopsis_ladanum "Galeopsis ladanum")_))[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-38)

### Cumbria Local Nature Recovery Strategy

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Cumbria Local Nature Recovery Strategy")\]

[Local Nature Recovery Strategies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Nature_Recovery_Strategy "Local Nature Recovery Strategy") (LNRS) are a UK government response to declining biodiversity.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-39) The local strategies are established to agree priorities and propose actions to reverse the decline. The Cumbria Local Nature Recovery Strategy was developed following initial "Vision and Priority" workshops held in March 2024,[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-40) with further consultation during 2025. The strategy includes the development of an interactive habitat map.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-LNRSmap-41) The map shows where habitats need enhancing or, in worse cases, restoring. For example SSSI Unit 22 "Carrock Fell" includes an area of "moorland, heathland and montaine" habitat which would benefit from enhancement. However the south west edge of the unit is in worse condition so would need restoration.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-LNRSmap-41)

### United Kingdom Biodiversity Action Plan

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Skiddaw_Group_SSSI&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: United Kingdom Biodiversity Action Plan")\]

[![Image 14](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/On_Mungrisdale_Common_-_geograph.org.uk_-_3840350.jpg/250px-On_Mungrisdale_Common_-_geograph.org.uk_-_3840350.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:On_Mungrisdale_Common_-_geograph.org.uk_-_3840350.jpg)

Blanket bog on Mungrisdale Common

The [United Kingdom Biodiversity Action Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_Biodiversity_Action_Plan "United Kingdom Biodiversity Action Plan") identified a range of priority habitats which occur across the UK. The Skiddaw Group SSSI has large areas of _grass moorland_ and _upland heath_, together with more fragmented areas of _[blanket bog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanket_bog "Blanket bog")_.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-42)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-43) For example, the upland areas around [Bannerdale Beck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bannerdale_Crags "Bannerdale Crags") (SSSI Unit 35) contain 69 hectares (0.27 sq mi) of blanket bog, split across several smaller sites. More detailed mapping from DEFRA[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-44) and the UK government open data resource[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-45) shows the same areas of blanket bog but additionally shows areas where the habitat could be restored, where it could potentially be created, and where smaller areas could be used to re-join existing fragmented ones.[\[f\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI#cite_note-46)

11.content:
An Overview
-----------

For its size, Cumbria is one of the most geologically diverse areas in Europe, including as it does, an exceptionally wide range of rock types and landforms.

In broad terms, as can be seen from the geological map (Figure 1), the central part of the county is occupied by a roughly circular inlier of Ordovician and Silurian marine metasediments, volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks, and granites. Together these form the rugged landscapes of the Lake District National Park, the boundary of which roughly follows the borders of the inlier.

Surrounding the Lower Palaeozoic inlier are the Carboniferous limestones and sandstones of the Pennines, West Cumbria and South Cumbria, and the Permo-Triassic sediments (mainly red sandstones and mudstones) of West Cumbria, Carlisle and the Eden Valley.

[![Image 1](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Lake-District-Geology-courtesy-Yorkshire-Geological-Society.jpg)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Lake-District-Geology-courtesy-Yorkshire-Geological-Society.jpg)

**Figure 1** Geological map of Cumbria (Image courtesy Yorkshire Geological Society)

All these rocks have been subjected to tectonic disturbance to varying degrees over the region’s 480-million-year history. Uplift, folding and faulting, have imposed structural controls on landscape development, influencing large-scale drainage patterns, the distribution of river valleys and lakes, as well as the boundaries of the Pennine and Lake District uplands.

The contrasting landscape character of the different parts of county owes a great deal to the underlying rock-types. The rugged mountainous scenery of the Lake District is formed from erosion-resistant granites, metamorphosed sediments and volcanic rocks (Figure 2). Outside this core of older rocks, Carboniferous limestones form a belt of hill country on the southern, eastern and northern edges of the Lake District (Figure 3) as well as the high moorland plateaus of the Pennines in the east.

[![Image 2](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-1.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-1.png)

**Figure 2**  Lower Palaeozoic metasediments, granites, and volcanic rocks produce the mountainous landscape of the Lake District fells. Here looking northwards from Great End towards Great Gable (middle distance) composed of Ordovician (Caradoc) volcanics rocks of the Borrowdale Volcanic Group. On the distant horizon are the outlines of Skiddaw (right) and the Lorton Fells (centre) composed of older Ordovican (Tremadoc – Llanvirn) marine mudstones and sandstones known as the Skiddaw Group. (Photo: Stuart Holmes)

[![Image 3](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-2.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-2.png)

**Figure 3** At Moota, near Cockermouth, Carboniferous Limestone (foreground) forms a series of low hills around the eastern margin of the Lower Palaeozoic inlier seen in the distance. Skiddaw dominates the skyline. (Photo: Ian Francis)

Succeeding these rocks in the stratigraphic succession are red Permo-Triassic sandstones which – as well underlying the low pasturelands of the northern Cumbrian plain, West Cumbria, and the Eden Valley –   produce the dramatic coastal scenery around St Bees and Whitehaven.

[![Image 4](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-3.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-3.png)

**Figure 4** Red Triassic sandstones (St Bees Sandstone) forms the cliffs on the St Bees Heritage Coast south of Whitehaven.  The Isle of Man can be seen on the horizon. (Photo: Stuart Homes)

The different rocks have weathered to give diverse soil types (which in turn affect natural ecosystems, as well as agriculture). The region’s rich mineral resources, such as roofing slates, building stones, metal ores, and coal, have strongly influenced local settlement patterns and architectural styles. Over the millennia, ice, wind and water have worked on the geology to produce a stunning variety of different landforms. Particularly noteworthy are the karst terrains of the Pennines and southern Cumbria, the dune fields of the Cumbrian coast, and – best-known of all – the glacially eroded U-shaped valleys, cirques, tarns, ribbon lakes and hanging valleys of the Lake District (Figure 5)

[![Image 5](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-4.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-4.png)

**Figure 5** The landforms of the Lake District show many classic features of glacial erosion. This aerial photograph shows Blea Water Tarn, occupying a pronounced cirque on the east side of the High Street Ridge. The U-shaped valley of Riggindale lies to left. Haweswater reservoir can be seen left middle distance. (Photo: Stuart Holmes)

Some Classic Cumbrian Geological Localities
-------------------------------------------

Cumbria contains more than its fair share of geological localities valued either for their significance in the history of geological science, as exemplars of geological or geomorphological phenomena, or as localities where generations of geology students learn their craft.  The county has 70 SSSIs listed purely for their geological significance, and a further 38 for combined geological/biological interest. Taken together this is the largest number of geological SSSIs of any county in England. Some classic localities are described below, with a suggested further reading list, and some selected references for those who wish to explore more advanced information on the localities listed.

The Skiddaw Granite and its Metamorphic Aureole
-----------------------------------------------

The Devonian Skiddaw granite pluton was intruded into folded Skiddaw Group mudstones around 390 million years ago, during the final phase of the Acadian Orogeny. A walk from Threlkeld to Sinen Gill provides a classic cross-section through the southern part of the c. 10 km diameter metamorphic aureole, with an outer zone of andalusite slates (Figure 6), and an inner zone of cordierite-rich hornfels, and the country-rock contact with the granite itself (Figure 7), all well exposed at numerous locations. The cleavage and folding in the slates has been overprinted by the effects of thermal metamorphism, indicating that the intrusion post-dates the main period of Acadian tectonic compression (Woodcock _et al_ 2019).

[![Image 6](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-5.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-5.png)

**Figure 6** A cleavage surface of andalusite slate from the metamorphic aureole of the Skiddaw granite. Some crystals are seen as white squares, rather than needles. This is because we are seeing them in cross-section – they have grown at right-angles _through_ the cleavage, indicating that they formed _after_ it. (Photo: Ian Francis)

[![Image 7](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-6.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-6.png)

**Figure 7**  The exposure of the Skiddaw granite forms a prominent waterfall in Sinen Gill.  (Photo: Ian Francis)

[![Image 8](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-7.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-7.png)

**Figure 8** Tight folding in Skiddaw Group hornfels, Sinen Gill. (Photo: Ian Francis)

Polyphase Folding in the Skiddaw Group, Mosedale
------------------------------------------------

The complex polyphase folding in Skiddaw Group hornfels, beautifully exposed along the banks of the River Caldew in Mosedale, is described by Roberts (1992)  as “as one of the finest sets of fold structures in the country”. The pattern of folding in the area may indicate that early (pre-Caledonian)  soft-sediment gravity folds have been re-folded during the later stages of the Caledonian Orogeny.

[![Image 9](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-8-1024x768.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-8.png)

**Figure 9** Polyphase folding in Skiddaw Group hornfels exposed on the banks of the River Caldew, Mosedale. (Photo: Ian Francis)

The Porphyritic Andesites of Eycott Hill
----------------------------------------

This is the type locality of the Eycott Volcanic Group, approximately coeval with the Birker Fell Formation of the Borrowdale Volcanic Group in central Lakeland (Millward _et al_ 2000) .  A series of andesite and basaltic andesite lava flows, dipping to the east, display particularly well-developed trap topography (Figure 10). Some of the lower andesite flows display spectacular porphyritic texture, with grey or blue-grey feldspar crystals in a in a dark grey groundmass (Figure 11).

[![Image 10](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-9.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-9.png)

**Figure 10** Aerial view of Eycott Hill, looking southeast, showing trap topography. Each line of ridges marks a separate lava flow. Above the lavas are Carboniferous limestone beds, which lie beneath the flat green fields (top left). In the top right of the image are Great Mel Fell (in shadow), with the Ullswater fells in the far distance. (Photo: Stuart Holmes)

[![Image 11](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-10.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-10.png)

**Figure 11** Polished section of the Eycott-type porphyritic andesite. The largest feldspar crystals have long axes of about 2cm. (Photo: Peter del Strother)

Peperites on Fleetwith Pike
---------------------------

Around Honister Crag (Buttermere), a series of southeast-dipping andesite sheets, most of which are thought to be sills, were intruded into a thick sequence of unlithified volcaniclastic lake-bottom muds (Figure 12).  Several locations, including Hopper Quarry (pictured) show exceptionally fine examples of peperitic texture (Figure 13), caused when molten andesite lava came into contact with water-saturated sediment, resulting in explosive generation of steam and fragmentation of the magma margins (Tuffen, 2008).

[![Image 12](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-11.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-11.png)

**Figure 12** A series of thick andesite sills, separated by thinner beds of volcaniclastic sandstone (the famous Honister Slate), give rise to the distinct layering seen on Honister Crag, viewed from Dale Head.  The beds were originally horizontal but have since been tilted to the south by Earth movements. (Photo: Ian Francis)

[![Image 13](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-12.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-12.png)

**Figure 12** Peperite at Hopper Quarry, Honister.  Andesite magma forced its way into waterlogged sediment , causing the water to boil explosively. This shattered the top of the sill to produce a peperite –  a mixture of dark andesite fragments surrounded by light-blue fine-grained sediment.  (Photo: Ian Francis)

Volcanic Rocks on Crinkle Crags
-------------------------------

Late Caradoc volcanism produced a 6 km thick series of pyroclastic and volcaniclastic deposits, well exposed in the craggy central fells of the Lake District. Parts of the volcanic succession are associated with the collapse of several calderas, the largest of which is known as the Scafell caldera.  The collapse was accompanied by a series of violent eruptions (Branney, 1991), the largest of which involved the ejection of at least 100 km3 of andesitic pyroclastics. These rocks are particularly well exposed on the slopes of Crinkle Crags and Pike O’Blisco in the form of thick air-fall tuffs and ignimbrites.

[![Image 14](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-13.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-13.png)

**Figure 13** Air-fall tuff in the Borrowdale Volcanic Group Whorneyside Formation, Crinkle Crags. (Photo: Ian Francis)

[![Image 15](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-14.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-14.png)

**Figure 14** Ignimbrite tuff in the Borrowdale Volcanic Group Whorneyside Formation, Crinkle Crags. (Photo: Ian Francis)

Silurian Turbidites at Eccle Riggs Bank Quarry
----------------------------------------------

Sole marks on the base of a vertically inclined turbidite bed in the Silurian Gawthwaite Formation (Coniston Group) is superbly exposed in this quarry (also known as the ‘Donkey Rock’ quarry). See Stone et al (2010).

[![Image 16](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-15.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-15.png)

**Figure 15** Turbidite sole structures on the base of a Windermere Supergroup (Coniston Grit Formation)  sandstone bed (originally horizontal but tilted into a vertical position by Earth movements). The sandstone was deposited by a turbidity current which scoured grooves as it flowed over the muddy sea floor. As the current slackened it deposited its load of suspended sand, filling the grooves. In this quarry face, the mud layer into which the grooves were cut (in effect the mould) has broken away and we see the base of the sandstone bed as the groove fillings (the cast).  Eccle Riggs Bank (or ‘Donkey Rock’) quarry, Broughton-in-Furness. (Photo: Ian Francis)

The Karst Landscapes of Orton Scar
----------------------------------

Cumbria has several nationally important areas of karst landscape, of which perhaps the most important is found at Asby Scar, northeast of Tebay. Here the Carboniferous Great Scar limestone forms some of the finest limestone pavement found in Britain.

[![Image 17](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-16.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-16.png)

**Figure 16** Aerial view of limestone pavement on Orton Scar. The rectilinear pattern of clints and grikes comes about as a result of preferential weathering along pre-existing joints in the Carboniferous  Limestone.

The Basal Permian Unconformity at Saltom Bay, and the Triassic Sandstones of the St Bees Heritage Coast
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

At Saltom Bay, south of Whitehaven, a wave-cut platform displays a superb exposure of the Carboniferous/ Permian unconformity. Cross-bedded grey-brown sandstones of the Upper Carboniferous Westphalian C show an abrupt erosive surface upon which lies the basal breccia of the Permian (known in Cumbria as Brockram).  Above the wave-cut platform, low cliffs give a good exposure of the overlying Permian Saltom Dolomite member of the Permian St Bees Evaporite Formation (Jones & Guion, 1990)

[![Image 18](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-17-768x1024.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-17.png)

**Figure 16** At Saltom Bay,Carboniferous sandstones (Westphalian) form the wave-cut platform in the foreground, and are overlain unconformably by a reddish brown Permian conglomerate, known locally as Brockram.  The low cliff in the background is formed from beds of the fossiliferous Saltom Dolomite. (Photo: Ian Francis)

South of Saltom Bay the Triassic St Bees Sandstone forms impressive cliffs, with extensive exposure of massive cross-bedded red sandstone, with thinner intervening shale horizons.  The sandstones are also seen Birkham’s Quarry, next to the coastal path on the cliff tops, where cross-bedding, clay rip-up clasts , and ripples are all well exposed on sandstone blocks around the quarry entrance, where there are also informative interpretation boards.

[![Image 19](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-18.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-18.png)

**Figure 17** Ripple marks on a bedding surface of the Triassic St Bees Sandstone at Birkham’s Quarry on the cliff-tops south of Whitehaven (Photo: Ian Francis)

High Cup Nick, and the Whin Sill
--------------------------------

One of Cumbria’s most famous geological localities is the Pennine valley of High Cup Nick, between Dufton and Murton Fells.  Here the Whin Sill dolerite (of late Carboniferous/early Permian age)  forms an impressive palisade of columnar-jointed crags around a deep U-shaped glaciated valley, with views westwards towards the Eden valley and the Lakeland Fells beyond.

[![Image 20](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-19.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-19.png)

**Figure 18.** The eastern extremity of the glacial trough of High Cup Nick, with the columnar jointed Whin Sill dolerite forming the prominent line of crags (Creative Commons: photo by Robert J. Heath)

Moraines in Ennerdale
---------------------

Many Lakeland valleys contain examples of  moraines, presumed to be of Younger Dryas age. Those at the head of Ennerdale valley have long been regarded as ‘one of the finest moraine-mound (‘hummocky moraine’) complexes in England (Graham & Hambury , 2007).

[![Image 21](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-20.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-20.png)

**Figure 19** Hummocky moraines at the head of Ennerdale valley. Black Sale YHA (middle top) gives scale. (Photo: Stuart Holmes)

Classic Features of Glacial Erosion on Helvellyn
------------------------------------------------

The Lake District is one of the best places in Britan to appreciate the geomorphological effects of upland glacial erosion (Wilson, 2010).  Cirques, arrêtes, hanging valleys and ribbon lakes abound  throughout the region, but one of the finest collection of such features can be seen on the Helvellyn massif, where a series of cirques and intervening arrêtes occupy the eastern slopes of the range.

[![Image 22](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-21.png)](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image-21.png)

**Figure 20** Ice has sculpted a series of pronounced cirques with intervening arrêtes on the east flank of the Helvellyn range. Red Tarn is just visible beyond the arrête known as Striding Edge. (Photo: Stuart Holmes)

References
----------

Branney, M J, 1991. _Eruption and depositional facies of the Whorneyside Tuff Formation, English Lake District: An exceptionally large-magnitude phreatoplinian eruption._ Bulletin of the Geological Society of America, **103**, p.886-897.

Goldie, H. 1996 _The limestone pavements of Great Asby Scar, Cumbria, UK._ Environmental Geology **28**, 128–136

Jones, N.S., and Guion, P.DF., 1990. The Westphalian and Permian Geology of the Whitehaven Area. In Moseley, F. (Ed)  _Geology of the Lake District_ Geologists’ Association Guide pp.178-185

Millward, D,   Marriner, G. F., and Beddoe-Stephens, B. 2000 _The Eycott Volcanic Group, an Ordovician continental margin andesite suite in the English Lake District_. Proc Yorks Geol Soc **53.**

Roberts, D.E. 1992 in Treagus, J.E. (Ed) Caledonian Structures in Britain. _Geological Conservation Review Series_. Chapman & Hall

Stone, P, Millward, D, Young, B, Merritt, J W, Clarke, S M, McCormac, M and Lawrence, D J D. 2010. [_British regional geology: Northern England_](https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/British_regional_geology:_Northern_England)_._ Fifth edition. Keyworth, Nottingham: British Geological Survey.

Tuffen, H. 2008. Honister and Haystacks. _Exploring Lakeland Rocks and Landscapes_, Beale & Dodd, (Eds) pp 126-134 The Cumberland Geological Society.

Woodcock, N.H., Soper, N. J, and Miles, A. J. 2019 _Age of the Acadian deformation and Devonian granites in northern England: a review_. Proc Yorks Geol Soc **62**

Resources
---------

Web Resources
-------------

The late Clive Boulter produced an excellent, up-to-date, overview of [Lake District geology](http://englishlakedistrictgeology.org.uk/) for those with a geological background, with particular emphasis on the Borrowdale Volcanic Group.

The Cumbria GeoConservation Group has a [useful website](https://www.cbdc.org.uk/cumbria_geoconservation_home/), including a map of Cumbria with placemarks for Local Geological Sites, and other Sites of Special Scientific Interest, as well as summaries of the features of each site. They have also published a variety of useful [Geotrails.](https://www.cbdc.org.uk/cumbrialgs_home-new-test/cumbria-geology-geotrails/)

​The Lake District National Park website has some useful geological information [here](https://www.lakedistrict.gov.uk/learning/geology).

​Chris Wilson has produced a nicely illustrated set of .ppt slides dealing with the [geology of the Keswick area](https://www.keswick.org/usercontent/doc/50941/an%20introduction%20to%20geological%20features%20in%20and%20around%20keswick.pdf) , including a useful guide to the town’s building stones.

​For those with a geological background, the British Geological Survey hosts plentiful on-line resources, such this general introduction to the [geology of Northern England.](http://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Northern_England_%E2%80%93_introduction_to_geology)

​Michael Hambrey’s brief introduction to the [glacial history of the Lake District](https://www.cumberland-geol-soc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/Glacial-history-of-the-Lake-District-CGS.pdf) written for the Cumberland Geological Society (see also Societies).

​The Lake District National Park’s latest [landscape character assessment document.](https://www.lakedistrict.gov.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0041/388985/Final-LDNP-LCA-for-Adoption-May-2021-compressed.pdf)

UNESCO’s web pages for the [Lake District World Heritage Site](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/422/)

Ian Francis has produced a [website](http://www.lakedistrictgeology.co.uk/) which  includes an illustrated glossary, excursions, a list of Norse landscape words, and a link to a Google Earth Lakeland Geology project.

Further Reading
---------------

General Lakeland Geology
------------------------

_The Lake District: Landscape and Geology_ by Francis, Holmes & Yardley,  Crowood Press 2022

A highly illustrated non-specialist introduction to the geology and scenery of Lakeland.

_Lakeland Rocks_ by Alan Smith, Crowood Press, 2019

Excellent illustrated descriptions of the region’s different rock types.

_Geology in the Lake District National Park_ by Phil Davies, Otley’s Steps 2018

A guide to 32 key geological location in the National Park.

_British Regional Geology_: Northern England. Fifth edition by Stone, P, Millward, D, Young, B, Merritt, J W, Clarke, S M, McCormac, M and Lawrence, D J D, British Geological Survey, 2010

Detailed geology of the region for more advanced readers.

_Earth, Water, Ice and Fire: Two Hundred Years of Geological Research in the Lake District_ by

David Oldroyd. Geological Society Memoir No. 25. The Geological Society, 2002.

A scholarly account of the history and development of Lake District geology.

_The Geology of the Lake District_, by F. Mosely (editor), Yorkshire Geological Society, 1978

A detailed overview of key aspects of Lake District geology aimed at relatively advanced readers. Some details now rather dated.

Geology Guidebooks
------------------

_Cumbria Vols 1 (Cumberland) and 2 (Westmorland and Furness)_  Richard Wigley (Ed) Geologists Association Guide No 77 2023

The most up-to-date and comprehensive guide currently available.

_The Coast-to-Coast walk: Rocks and Scenery_, by Butler & Gunner, 2qt Publishing, 2017.

The first chapter (Cleator to Shap) covers much interesting Lakeland geology along C2C route.

_Rock Trails Lakeland_ by Paul Gannon, Pesda Press, 2009.  Useful general geological introduction, with geological trails for the experienced fell-walker.

_Exploring Lakeland Rocks and Landscape_ by Susan Beale & Mervyn Dodd (editors), The Cumberland Geological Society, 2008

A successor to the 1992 volume (see below), this time in colour, with seventeen new geological excursions.

_Lakeland Rocky Rambles_ by Bryan Lynas, Sigma Leisure, 1994

Lake District rocks and how they formed introduced in 10 well-chosen ‘rambles’.

_Lakeland Rocks and Landscape: A Field Guide_ by Mervyn Dodd (editor), The Cumberland Geological Society,  Ellenbank Press, 1992

Eighteen field excursions to key geological localities, still relevant today.

_Geology of the Lake District_ by Frank Moseley (editor) The Geologist’s Association, 1990

Geological excursions to 25 key localities for more advanced readers.

_Lakeland Geology: Where to Go and What to See_ by E.H. Shakleton, Dalesman Publishing 1987

A beautifully written introduction to the region’s geology, with 13 excursions.

Mines, Minerals, and Quarries
-----------------------------

_The Red Earth Revisited: An Introduction to the Iron Mines and Iron Industry of Furness_ by Cubbon, Sanbach and Woollard, CATMAS, 2021

Industrial history rather than geology, but very well researched.

_Slate Mining in the Lake District_ by Alastair Cameron, Amberley Publishing, 2016

_Ore Mining in the Lake District_ by Alastair Cameron & Liz Withey, Amberley, 2017

Companion volumes giving brief histories of mining and quarrying in Lakeland with excellent location photos.

_The Lakes and Mines Guide_ by Ian Tyler, Blue Rock Publication, 2006

A brief but comprehensive catalogue of Lakeland mine locations.

_Goldscope and the Mines of Derwent Fells_ by Ian Tyler Blue, Rock Publications, 2005

_Carrock and the Mines of Skiddaw and Blencathra_ by Ian Tyler, Blue Rock Publications, 2003

The above two books provide the most detailed and comprehensive accounts of the history of these important mining regions of northern Lakeland.

_Mines of the Lake District_ by John Adams, Dalesman Books, 1998

Probably the best non-specialist guide to the region’s mines and their history.

_Minerals of the English Lake District: Caldbeck Fells_ by Cooper & Staley, British Museum (Natural History), 1990.

A beautifully illustrated catalogue of minerals from the world-famous Caldbeck mines.

_Coniston Copper Mines: A Field Guide_ by Eric Holland, Cicerone Press, 1981

A brief guide with hand-drawn sketch maps to the mines of Tilberthwaite and Coniston

_Industrial Archaeology of the Lake Counties_ by Marshall & Davies-Shiel, Michael Moon, 1979.

Has an excellent overview chapter on mining and quarrying.

_Mining in the Lake Counties_ by W.T. Shaw, Dalesman Publishing, 1970

An account of Lakeland mining history, with details of some the region’s key mines written by a local mining engineer living when some of the mines were still active.

_Burlington Blue-Grey_ by Stanley Geddes, Published by the author, 1975.

The definitive history of Burlington’s Kirkby-in-Furness quarries.

_Mines and Mining in the Lake District_ by John Postlethwaite 3ed 1913, Moss & Sons, Whitehaven.

Perhaps the most celebrated account of the region’s mines and quarries in their heyday. Copies can still be found on ebay, including the 1976 re-issue by Michael Moon’s bookshop.

Glacial Geology and Geomorphology
---------------------------------

_The Quaternary of the Lake District Field Guide_ Edited by McDougall & Evans, Quaternary Research Association 2015

Good (but advanced) guide to Quaternary processes and landforms in some key Lake District localities.

_Lake District Mountain Landforms_ by Pete Wilson, Scotforth Books, 2010

An excellent, well-illustrated,  general introduction to Lakeland geomorphology with an emphasis on glacial features.

_Classic Landforms of the Lake District_ by John Boardman, The Geographical Association 1996

Brief but well-illustrated introduction to Quaternary landforms and processes, suitable for A-level geography students.

_The Ice Age in Cumbria_ by Alan Smith, Rigg Side Publications 2008

An excellent introduction to how the Ice Age helped created Lakeland’s landscape features.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The **German mines at Caldbeck** were part of the operations of the [Company of Mines Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Mines_Royal "Society of Mines Royal") in [Caldbeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caldbeck "Caldbeck"), which introduced German miners from modern day [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria") and [Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavaria "Bavaria") into the [Lake District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_District "Lake District") in 1563, though earlier works in the area are thought to have been begun in the 1300s.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_mines_at_Caldbeck#cite_note-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_mines_at_Caldbeck#cite_note-2) The importance of the operation lies in its historical significance as the first large-scale [copper mining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper_mining "Copper mining") and smelting operation in the British Islands which was well-documented. New smelting techniques were introduced which were allowed the treatment of [argentiferous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentiferous "Argentiferous") [copper sulphide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper_sulphide "Copper sulphide") ores and the more complex lead-copper-silver ores from Caldbeck.

Mining started at Caldbeck in June 1566 but was soon discontinued and was not resumed until 1568, when work continued under the supervision of the [Hochstetter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hochstetter "Hochstetter") family until around 1630, and then was not resumed until around 1695. One of the German miners [Cornelius de Vos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_de_Vos "Cornelius de Vos") left to set up gold mines in Scotland.

In July 1594 Emanuel Hochstetter sent Steffan Mur, who managed stamping mills to process the ore at Caldbeck and [Newlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newlands_Valley "Newlands Valley"), to [Nicholas Williamson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Williamson "Nicholas Williamson") at Sheffield, a steward of the [Earl of Shrewsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Talbot,_7th_Earl_of_Shrewsbury "Gilbert Talbot, 7th Earl of Shrewsbury"). Williamson had relations at Millbeck in [Underskiddaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underskiddaw "Underskiddaw").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_mines_at_Caldbeck#cite_note-3) Steffan Mur married a woman from Keswick, Isobel Wood, and their family is documented.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_mines_at_Caldbeck#cite_note-4)

[George Bowes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Bowes_/(prospector/) "George Bowes (prospector)") and Francis Nedham (a son of [George Nedham or Needham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Nedham_/(miner/) "George Nedham (miner)")) reported on the state of the mines in 1602.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_mines_at_Caldbeck#cite_note-smith-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_mines_at_Caldbeck#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_mines_at_Caldbeck#cite_note-7) Robert Bowes was killed in an accident in the mines in 1610.

The identity of the principal copper mines near [Keswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keswick,_Cumbria "Keswick, Cumbria") and [Coniston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coniston,_Cumbria "Coniston, Cumbria") has long been known, but the locations of the Caldbeck mines have not. The lead-copper mines at [Roughtengill](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Roughtengill&action=edit&redlink=1 "Roughtengill (page does not exist)") have been considered to be the most probable candidates. However, recent fieldwork combined with records from archives has allowed identification of the principal mines.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_mines_at_Caldbeck#cite_note-smith-5)

The area falls within the [Skiddaw Group SSSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI "Skiddaw Group SSSI"), is a [site of special scientific interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site_of_special_scientific_interest "Site of special scientific interest").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_mines_at_Caldbeck#cite_note-designation-8)
