**Skiddaw** is a [mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain "Mountain") in the [Lake District National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_District_National_Park "Lake District National Park") in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"). Its 931-metre (3,054 ft) summit is traditionally considered to be the [fourth-highest peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Wainwrights "List of Wainwrights") but depending on what [topographic prominence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographic_prominence "Topographic prominence") is thought to be significant is also variously ranked as the [third-](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Marilyns_in_the_British_Isles "List of Marilyns in the British Isles") and the [sixth-highest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Furths#England "List of Furths") in England. It lies just north of the town of [Keswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keswick,_Cumbria "Keswick, Cumbria"), [Cumbria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumbria "Cumbria"), in the [historic county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historic_counties_of_England "Historic counties of England") of [Cumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland "Cumberland") and dominates the skyline in this part of the northern lakes. It is the simplest of the Lake District mountains of this height to ascend (as there is a well-trodden tourist track from a car park to the north-east of Keswick, near the summit of [Latrigg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latrigg "Latrigg")) and, as such, many walking guides recommend it to the occasional walker wishing to climb a mountain. This is the first summit of the [fell running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fell_running "Fell running") challenge known as the [Bob Graham Round](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Graham_Round "Bob Graham Round") when undertaken in a clockwise direction. The mountain lends its name to the surrounding areas of Skiddaw Forest and Back o' Skidda, and to the isolated Skiddaw House, situated to the east, formerly a shooting lodge and subsequently a [youth hostel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth_hostel "Youth hostel"). It also provides the name for the slate derived from that region: [Skiddaw slate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_slate "Skiddaw slate"). Skiddaw slate has been used to make tuned percussion musical instruments or [lithophones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithophone "Lithophone"), such as the [Musical Stones of Skiddaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_Stones_of_Skiddaw "Musical Stones of Skiddaw") held at the [Keswick Museum and Art Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keswick_Museum_and_Art_Gallery "Keswick Museum and Art Gallery"). [![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Skiddaw_sketch_map.JPG/330px-Skiddaw_sketch_map.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Skiddaw_sketch_map.JPG) Sketch map of the Skiddaw locality The [Northern Fells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Fells "Northern Fells") make up a roughly circular upland area approaching 10 miles (16 kilometres) in width. At the centre is the marshy depression of Skiddaw Forest, a treeless plateau, or valley, at an elevation of about 400 metres (1,300 feet); flowing outwards from here are the rivers that divide the area into three sectors. "Forest" is used here in its original sense, meaning land used for hunting, rather than a woodland. The south-western sector, between the [Glenderaterra Beck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenderaterra_Beck "Glenderaterra Beck") and Dash Beck, contains Skiddaw and its satellites.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-wainwright-1) Skiddaw itself takes the form of a north–south ridge about 1⁄2 mile (800 metres) long, with steep slopes to east and west. The ridge continues northwards over Broad End to [Bakestall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakestall "Bakestall"), a fell overlooking the Whitewater Dash waterfall. Further ridges fan out east and west from the southern end of Skiddaw. To the south-east are [Skiddaw Little Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Little_Man "Skiddaw Little Man"), [Lonscale Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonscale_Fell "Lonscale Fell") and [Latrigg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latrigg "Latrigg"), an easily accessible viewpoint for Keswick and [Derwentwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derwentwater "Derwentwater"). Beyond these fells are the [Glenderaterra Beck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenderaterra_Beck "Glenderaterra Beck") and the [Blencathra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blencathra "Blencathra") group. The south-western ridge curves round through 180 degrees to run north above the shore of [Bassenthwaite Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bassenthwaite_Lake "Bassenthwaite Lake"). This gives Skiddaw an 'outer wall', comprising [Carl Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Side "Carl Side"), [Long Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Side "Long Side") and [Ullock Pike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ullock_Pike "Ullock Pike"), collectively referred to as Longside Edge. The final member of the Skiddaw Group is [Dodd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dodd_/(Lake_District/) "Dodd (Lake District)"), a satellite of Carl Side. Between Skiddaw and Longside Edge are the quiet valleys of Southerndale and Barkbethdale, separated by the spur of Buzzard Knott. These drain the western flanks of the fell to Bassenthwaite Lake. The eastern side of Skiddaw drains into Skiddaw Forest, much of the water reaching Candleseaves Bog. This marsh is the source of both the Dash Beck flowing north west to Bassenthwaite and the [River Caldew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Caldew "River Caldew"), beginning its long journey north-eastward to the [Solway Firth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solway_Firth "Solway Firth") via [Carlisle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlisle,_Cumbria "Carlisle, Cumbria"). Two smooth spurs on this eastern flank of Skiddaw, Sale How and Hare Crag, are listed as separate tops in some guidebooks.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-birkett-2) Sale How is also a [Nuttall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuttall_/(hill/) "Nuttall (hill)"). Skiddaw's slopes are generally rounded and convex, looking from a distance as though a thick velvet blanket has been draped over a supporting frame. On the ridges the general terrain is of loose stones, but elsewhere all is grass and heather. [Wainwright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Wainwright "Alfred Wainwright") noted that "Its lines are smooth, its curves graceful; but because the slopes are steep everywhere, the quick build-up of the “massif” from valley levels to central summit is appreciated at a glance — and it should be an appreciative glance, for such massive strength and such beauty of outline rarely go together."[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-wainwright-1) The bedrock of Skiddaw, commonly known as [Skiddaw Slate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Slate "Skiddaw Slate"), is the Kirkstile Formation. This [Ordovician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordovician "Ordovician") rock is composed of laminated [mudstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudstone "Mudstone") and [siltstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siltstone "Siltstone") with [greywacke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greywacke "Greywacke") sandstone. At the summit this is overlain by [scree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scree "Scree") and to the south are areas where the underlying Loweswater Formation surfaces. [![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Skiddaw_from_derwentwater_by_Richard_Corbould.jpg/330px-Skiddaw_from_derwentwater_by_Richard_Corbould.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Skiddaw_from_derwentwater_by_Richard_Corbould.jpg) Skiddaw from Derwentwater, by [Richard Corbould](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Corbould "Richard Corbould") (1757–1831) [![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Skiddaw_engraving_by_William_Miller_after_Turner_R513.jpg/330px-Skiddaw_engraving_by_William_Miller_after_Turner_R513.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Skiddaw_engraving_by_William_Miller_after_Turner_R513.jpg) Skiddaw after [J. M. W. Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._M._W._Turner "J. M. W. Turner") (1833) [![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Skiddaw_Massif3.jpg/330px-Skiddaw_Massif3.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Skiddaw_Massif3.jpg) Skiddaw Massif as seen from [Outerside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outerside "Outerside") [Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fell "Fell") The summit ridge bears a number of tops, which from north to south are known[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-wainwright-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-birkett-2) as North Top, High Man (the summit), Middle Top and South Top. All now bear [cairns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairn "Cairn") and a number of stone windshelters have been erected. Skiddaw has a subsidiary summit, [Little Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Little_Man "Skiddaw Little Man"), which lies about 1.5 kilometres (1 mile) south-south-east of the main peak. Despite its limited independence, Wainwright listed it as a separate fell in his influential _[Pictorial Guide to the Lakeland Fells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pictorial_Guide_to_the_Lakeland_Fells "Pictorial Guide to the Lakeland Fells")_, a convention which is often followed. Skiddaw Little Man has its own subsidiary summit, known as Lesser Man. The view is as panoramic as might be expected, given Skiddaw's [topographic prominence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographic_prominence "Topographic prominence"). From High Man the north east quadrant is filled by the quiet fells of Back o'Skiddaw, with the Border hills, the [Cheviots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cheviot "The Cheviot") and the North [Pennines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennines "Pennines") behind them. To the south east are Blencathra, the [Far Eastern Fells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_Eastern_Fells "Far Eastern Fells") and the [Helvellyn range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helvellyn_range "Helvellyn range"); behind these are vistas of the [Yorkshire Dales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales "Yorkshire Dales") and [Forest of Bowland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_of_Bowland "Forest of Bowland"). The [Coniston Fells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coniston_Fells "Coniston Fells") are visible directly to the south. On the other side of South Top is a fine view of the [Scafells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scafells "Scafells"), [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Fells "Western Fells") and [North Western Fells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Western_Fells "North Western Fells"), with a portion of [Snowdonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowdonia "Snowdonia") visible between [Kirk Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Fell "Kirk Fell") and [Pillar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillar_/(Lake_District/) "Pillar (Lake District)"). The [Isle of Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Man "Isle of Man") is visible 60 miles (100 kilometres) away, as are the [Mourne Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourne_Mountains "Mourne Mountains") 120 miles (195 km) away (on exceptionally clear days). The final quarter is taken up by the coastal plain and the distant Solway Firth, backed by the hills of [Galloway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galloway "Galloway") such as [Merrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick,_Galloway "Merrick, Galloway") and [Criffel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criffel "Criffel"), and [Broad Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_Law "Broad Law") in the [Scottish Borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Borders "Scottish Borders"). [Goat Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goat_Fell "Goat Fell") on [Arran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Arran "Isle of Arran") can be seen at an angle of 313 degrees, 105 miles (170 km) away. The most distant view is of [Slieve Meelmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slieve_Meelmore "Slieve Meelmore") in the [Mountains of Mourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountains_of_Mourne "Mountains of Mourne") in [County Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Down "County Down"), Northern Ireland, 120 miles (195 km) distant. By moving to South Top a superb view of [Borrowdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borrowdale "Borrowdale") can be brought into sight.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-wainwright-1) [![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Summit_ridge_of_Skiddaw_%28geograph_2707510%29.jpg/250px-Summit_ridge_of_Skiddaw_%28geograph_2707510%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Summit_ridge_of_Skiddaw_/(geograph_2707510/).jpg) Summit ridge Many routes of ascent have been devised for Skiddaw; indeed, it is hard to devise a challenging approach in good conditions. The most popular tourist route starts from Keswick and first ascends behind Latrigg, before the climb continues over the slopes of Little Man to the summit. About 200 metres (660 ft) of ascent can be saved by driving to the top of Gale Road and beginning from the public car park just behind the summit of Latrigg. Another popular route (and the one recommended by Wainwright[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-wainwright-1)) is to follow Longside Edge, first ascending Ullock Pike, Longside and Carl Side before making the steep climb up from Carlside Col. Also from the north, a somewhat tougher alternative is to walk up Buzzard Knott between Southerndale and Barkbethdale: after crossing to the southern edge of the shoulder above Randel Crag ascend due east to the summit. Rather easier than either of these is the compass-walk due south from Cock Up (505 metres (1,657 ft)); reversing this route provides a safe descent, especially in bad weather. Scramblers may prefer simply to walk up Southerndale and climb Longside via a distinctive crevice seen easily from Skiddaw summit. From the south-west at Millbeck, Carlside Col can be reached directly. A start from nearby Applethwaite can also be used to provide a variation to the tourist route. From the north-west a tough but picturesque ascent can be made to the northern end of Longside Edge before following the ridge route to the summit. Finally, ascents from due east are possible for the walker who first makes for Skiddaw House, a good distance from either Keswick, [Threlkeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threlkeld "Threlkeld") or Peter House. Once Skiddaw House is reached a fairly direct line is possible, climbing over either Sale How or Hare Crag.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-wainwright-1) [![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Keswick_and_Skiddaw.jpg/250px-Keswick_and_Skiddaw.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Keswick_and_Skiddaw.jpg) Skiddaw with [Keswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keswick,_Cumbria "Keswick, Cumbria") at its foot From the north-east an unmarked but quite easy and fairly well-worn path starts at Whitewater Dash waterfall (on the [Cumbrian Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumbria_Way "Cumbria Way")) where the walker can follow the fence (along Birkett Edge just south of Dead Crags) past the Bakestall outcrop, and follow the fence until just before the unnamed top at 831 metres (2,726 ft). From the 831m top, a path leads directly to Skiddaw Man. Early forms of the name from the include _Skythou_ in c.1260 and _Skydehow_ in 1247.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-3) According to [Eilert Ekwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eilert_Ekwall "Eilert Ekwall"), Skiddaw's name is derived from the [Old Norse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Norse "Old Norse") elements _skyti_ or _skut_ + _haugr_ meaning either "archer's hill" or "jutting crag hill".[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-4) Diana Whaley likewise interprets it as "the mountain with the jutting crag", but also offers the alternative that the first element may be a personal name or Old Norse _skítr_ 'dung, filth, shit'.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-Whaley-5) [Richard Coates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Coates "Richard Coates") suggests that "it is possible that a [Cumbric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumbric "Cumbric") solution is to be sought."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-Whaley-5) [![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Skiddaw_House_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1519820.jpg/250px-Skiddaw_House_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1519820.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Skiddaw_House_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1519820.jpg) Skiddaw House Below Sale How, at an elevation of 470 metres (1,540 ft) is Skiddaw House, a stone building which has variously served as a shooting lodge, a shepherd's bothy and a [Youth Hostel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth_Hostels_Association_/(England_%26_Wales/) "Youth Hostels Association (England & Wales)"). Its windbreak comprises the only trees in Skiddaw Forest, and it is reached by a long access track up the [Dash Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dash_Valley "Dash Valley"). [![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/The_Kitchen_Range%2C_Skiddaw_House_%28geograph_4392542%29.jpg/250px-The_Kitchen_Range%2C_Skiddaw_House_%28geograph_4392542%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Kitchen_Range,_Skiddaw_House_/(geograph_4392542/).jpg) Kitchen range Built around 1829 by the [Earl of Egremont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Wyndham,_3rd_Earl_of_Egremont "George Wyndham, 3rd Earl of Egremont"), it was originally a keeper's lodge: a base for grouse shooting and for the gamekeepers who managed the extensive land owned by Egremont in Skiddaw Forest. Little is known of the house in the 19th century, but it was used by both gamekeepers and shepherds beyond 1860 and there were rooms for Egremont and the shooting parties.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-shf-6) [Canon Rawnsley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardwicke_Rawnsley "Hardwicke Rawnsley"), a founder of the [National Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Trust_for_Places_of_Historic_Interest_or_Natural_Beauty "National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty"), visited in about 1900 and mentions in one of his books the hospitality of the shepherd's family at that time.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-8) [Sir Hugh Walpole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Walpole "Hugh Walpole"), author of the Lake District novel _[Rogue Herries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogue_Herries "Rogue Herries")_, was a visitor in the 1920s and 30s and used the house as the scene, set in 1854, of the murder by Uhland.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-9) These arrangements for accommodation continued until the early 1950s. Several families brought up their children there until they were able to go to school, but the longest tenure was possibly that of Pearson Dalton, a shepherd and bachelor from the [Caldbeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caldbeck "Caldbeck") area, who came to stay for a month in 1952 and left in 1969 aged 75. He lived there alone for five days a week, only going home for long weekends with his sister in Caldbeck, then returning on the Monday to resume his duties. By that time farming practices had changed and the house was no longer needed; it declined, although there was intermittent use by various schools and outdoor groups.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-shf-6) In 1986 the house was leased by John Bothamley, who had created the [YHA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth_Hostels_Association_/(England_%26_Wales/) "Youth Hostels Association (England & Wales)") [Carrock Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrock_Fell "Carrock Fell") Hostel 13 kilometres (8 miles) away; and eventually the building was handed over to the YHA. It closed in 2002 following a disagreement over the lease. In 2007 it re-opened as an independent hostel run by the Skiddaw House Foundation, under the YHA's Enterprise franchising model.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-shf-6) In 2024, 1,200 hectares (3,000 acres) of Skiddaw Forest was purchased by the [Cumbria Wildlife Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumbria_Wildlife_Trust "Cumbria Wildlife Trust") for £6.25m, as part of a long-term rewilding project, which the trust says will see the re-introduction of hen harriers, black grouse, water voles, aspen and rare upland bumblebees. The plan includes planting 300,000 native trees over 250 hectares (620 acres) of the site (but specifically excluding the summit of Skiddaw). The peat bogs that cover one third of the site will be rewetted by blocking drains and holding back water so that the peat remains saturated. The purchase was partly funded by a £5m grant from [Aviva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviva "Aviva"), with a public appeal being launched to raise the balance.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-11) The forest forms part of the [Skiddaw Group SSSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group_SSSI "Skiddaw Group SSSI"), a [Site of Special Scientific Interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site_of_Special_Scientific_Interest "Site of Special Scientific Interest"). Skiddaw was a [civil parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_parish "Civil parish") until 1 April 1934, when it was merged with [Underskiddaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underskiddaw "Underskiddaw").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-12) In 1931 it had a population of 5.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-13) In "A Stranger Minstrel" (published 1800), [Samuel Taylor Coleridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Taylor_Coleridge "Samuel Taylor Coleridge") remarks on Skiddaw's characteristic "helm of cloud", and observes atmospheric effects and the play of sunlight across the landscape: "yon small flaky mists that love to creep / Along the edges of those spots of light, / Those sunny islands on thy smooth green heights."[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-14) Coleridge also mentioned Skiddaw in the valediction of his [mnemonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mnemonic "Mnemonic") poem "Metrical Feet," which he addressed to his son [Derwent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derwent_Coleridge "Derwent Coleridge"), who had been born nearby; he wrote, "Could you stand upon Skiddaw, you would not from its whole ridge / See a man who so loves you as your fond S.T. Coleridge."[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-15) Skiddaw is mentioned in the fourth book of [John Keats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Keats "John Keats")'s poem _[Endymion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endymion_/(poem/) "Endymion (poem)")_: "…with all the stress / Of vision search'd for him, as one would look \[…\] from old Skiddaw's top, when fog conceals / His rugged forehead in a mantle pale, / With an eye-guess towards some pleasant vale / Descry a favourite hamlet faint and far."[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-16) Skiddaw is also mentioned in the final lines of the poem _The Armada_ by [Thomas Babington Macaulay, Lord Macaulay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Babington_Macaulay,_1st_Baron_Macaulay "Thomas Babington Macaulay, 1st Baron Macaulay"): "Till Skiddaw saw the fire that burned on Gaunt's embattled pile, And the red glare on Skiddaw roused the burghers of Carlisle."[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw#cite_note-17) "Skiddaw" is also a former name for [Mount Wellington, Tasmania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Wellington,_Tasmania "Mount Wellington, Tasmania"), which also overlooks a River Derwent ([River Derwent, Tasmania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derwent_River,_Tasmania "Derwent River, Tasmania"), rather than [River Derwent, Report](https://worldexpeditions.com/regenerative-travel-projects/Restoring-Skiddaw-Forest-in-Cumbria#impact-report-anchor) ### Regenerative 2030 * Standing up for wildlife, restoring and connecting wild places * Creating and enhancing wildlife havens * Inspiring people about the natural world * Growing resources for action and advocacy * * * ### Addressing the UN Sustainable Development Goals ![Image 11](https://worldexpeditions.com/Icons/SDG/Small/sdg13ClimateAction.png)![Image 12](https://worldexpeditions.com/Icons/SDG/Small/sdg14LifeBelowWater.png)![Image 13](https://worldexpeditions.com/Icons/SDG/Small/sdg15LifeOnLand.png)![Image 14](https://worldexpeditions.com/Icons/SDG/Small/sdg03GoodHealthAndWellbeing.png)![Image 15](https://worldexpeditions.com/Icons/SDG/Small/sdg04QualityEducation.png) Climate Action:  Climate change is a global challenge that affects everyone, everywhere. Life Below Water:  Careful management of this essential global resource is a key feature of a sustainable future. Life On Land:  Sustainably manage forests, combat desertification, halt and reverse land degradation, halt biodiversity loss Good Health And Well-being:  Ensuring healthy lives and promoting the well-being for all at all ages is essential to sustainable development. Quality Education:  Obtaining a quality education is the foundation to improving people’s lives and sustainable development. * * * ### Impacts * To undertake baseline surveys with experts to create a detailed management plan * To improve heathlands by recreating high-altitude scrub and alpine-like grassland across 120 acres and return a habitat that is almost absent from the English uplands. * To create 620 acres of Atlantic rainforest and encourage natural regeneration which would significantly increase biodiversity. * * * ### Outcomes The overall vision is for Skiddaw Forest to be a true wilderness, where people can become lost in the natural world and immersed in a wealth of wildlife. Woolly cattle and natural processes shape the landscape and human intervention is minimal. Woodland, scattered trees and scrub cloak the fell sides, petering out to dwarf scrub and willows as altitude limits its growth. Deep peat locks away millions of tonnes of carbon carpeted by luxurious sphagnum mosses that soak up water. Mountain streams tumble down wooded cloughs into the natural river channels of the Caldew and Dash Beck. Both abound with migratory fish seeking out gravel beds in which to spawn. Birds abound. The mournful whistle of golden plover mixes with the bubbling cries of curlew, while hen harrier and merlin hunt low over the vegetation looking for small birds and voles. Amongst the scattered trees, black grouse gather to dance in the early morning trying to attract a mate, as red grouse fly purposefully above the deep heather shouting go-back, go-back when spooked. Pine martens hunt for food amongst the tangle of stunted oaks festooned with mosses, lichens and ferns. While eagles soar high in the sky watching for prey from afar. Skiddaw Forest forms a nucleus for montane restoration in all directions as the influence and breath-taking amount of wildlife is sought to be replicated by neighbouring landowners and farmers. This will positively impact people through improving their access to nature and offer an opportunity to encounter more diverse species. There is well established evidence to show that being close to nature benefits an individual’s well-being and therefore improves both their physical and mental health. Children will have the opportunity to experience more biodiversity, capturing their wonder of the natural world and creating a lifelong interest in nature. They will be able to learn about the animals, birds, insects and aquatic creatures that inhabit the land and water ways first hand, and not just from books. * * * ### Background The UK is one of the most nature depleted countries in the world with the loss of habitat and native species being consistently reported since 2003 through the State of Nature report, which is published every few years, a collaborative effort between over 60 organisations, including government agencies, academics, and wildlife conservation groups. To give some context more than half of the UK bee, butterfly and moth species have declined in the last 50 years. 93% of wild flower meadows have been lost since the 1950s. Native hedgehog numbers have plummeted by at least half in the UK and is now red listed. The Barn Owl has suffered a 75% drop in its population since the 1930s. Common frog, common toad and natterjack toad populations have been reported as being in decline since the 1970s. There are many more examples of the depletion of nature. Cumbria Wildlife Trust, with incredible support from generous benefactors, recently purchased Skiddaw Forest, an iconic location in the Lake District National Park, covering 3000 acres of wild landscape which contains England’s third highest mountain. Parts of this land have protection designations - Site of Special Scientific Interest and a Special Area of Conservation. The internationally known walk, the Cumbrian Way, passes through this newly acquired land. The restoration of the habitat at Skiddaw Forest is strategically important and nationally significant; it will contribute to the Cumbria Biodiversity Action Plan and the Cumbria Local Nature Recovery Strategy. Skiddaw Forest has been damaged by poor land management techniques. We have a unique opportunity to make changes for nature by bringing back a mosaic of habitats on a truly landscape scale. Despite its name, Skiddaw Forest has hardly any trees and one of our visons is to restore areas of Atlantic rainforest over 620 acres of the site. This is no quick fix and may take up to 100 years to fully achieve. Planting will be with sessile oak, birch, rowan, holly, alder, willow, and hazel in a manner that is sympathetic with the aesthetics of the landscape. This will allow a rich tapestry of life to grow on and around these trees and eventually ferns, mosses, liverworts, and lichens will seem to cover every surface, from the ground to boulders, crags, and even the trunks and branches themselves. This work will be registered with the Woodland Code for monitoring, with work and evaluation undertaken with a dedicated site officer. Skiddaw Forest supports a number of rare and unusual species, including a boreo-montane invertebrate community (of considerable ecological and biogeographical importance) and an important upland breeding bird community of high ecological value. It is a site of national interest and of importance for its geology as well as its ecology. It is of outstanding interest ecologically, being designated as both a Site of Special Scientific Interest and a Special Area of Conservation. Interest is focussed around a suite of upland habitats, with extensive upland heathland, upland blanket bog and montane grass heath being the most extensive. There are a number of rare plant species present, Cloudberry, Bog Rosemary and Dwarf Willow for example. A high-value upland breeding bird community is present, including curlew (a European red list species) golden plover, merlin and, in some years, the highly persecuted (and declining in number) hen harrier. The land is designated for its geological interest for a number of features, including periglacial features and as the type locality for the Skiddaw group of rocks. The area forms the headwaters of two designated river systems (The Caldew and Dash Beck). Restoration projects on this scale are very rare and allow us to follow the principles of the Lawton review - to take a whole landscape approach where wildlife habitats are bigger, better managed and more joined-up. Our successful restoration work at our nearby nature reserve at Eycott Hill Nature Reserve demonstrate that the Trust’s staff have the knowledge and experience to undertake a project of this scale. The overall work to restore Skiddaw Forest will take many years, indeed decades, to complete and will be achieved through a continuous flow of smaller, interrelated projects. * * * ![Image 16](https://worldexpeditions.com/portals/Blue%20Mountains%20Adventure%20Company/images/aboriginal-flag-350px.jpg) **As an Australian owned and operated organisation, we acknowledge the Traditional Owners of Country throughout Australia and recognise their continuing custodianship of the land, waters and culture for over 60,000 years. [![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/83/Blea_Tarn_Lingmoor_Fell.jpg/250px-Blea_Tarn_Lingmoor_Fell.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Blea_Tarn_Lingmoor_Fell.jpg)

Blea Tarn from [Lingmoor Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingmoor_Fell "Lingmoor Fell")

The following is a **list of [Sites of Special Scientific Interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site_of_Special_Scientific_Interest "Site of Special Scientific Interest") (SSSIs) in [Cumbria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumbria "Cumbria")**, [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"), [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"). In England the body responsible for designating SSSIs is [Natural England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_England "Natural England"), which chooses a site because of its [fauna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna "Fauna"), [flora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant "Plant"), [geological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology "Geology") or physiographical features.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Sites_of_Special_Scientific_Interest_in_Cumbria#cite_note-1)

As of July 2012 there were 278 SSSIs within Cumbria. Of these, 70 are listed purely for their geological interest and 170 for their biological interest. A further 38 have both geological and biological interest.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Sites_of_Special_Scientific_Interest_in_Cumbria#cite_note-2)

The county includes the whole of the [Lake District National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_District_National_Park "Lake District National Park"), as well as three [Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areas_of_Outstanding_Natural_Beauty "Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty"): the [Solway Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solway_Coast "Solway Coast"), part of [Arnside and Silverdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnside_and_Silverdale "Arnside and Silverdale"), and part of the [North Pennines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pennines "North Pennines").

For SSSIs in other counties, see [List of SSSIs by Area of Search](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_SSSIs_by_Area_of_Search "List of SSSIs by Area of Search").

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

_This article describes the [geology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology "Geology") of the [ceremonial county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceremonial_counties_of_England "Ceremonial counties of England") of [Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Durham "County Durham"). It includes the [boroughs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borough "Borough") of [Darlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darlington_/(borough/) "Darlington (borough)"), [Hartlepool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartlepool_/(borough/) "Hartlepool (borough)") and [Stockton-on-Tees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockton-on-Tees_/(borough/) "Stockton-on-Tees (borough)") but not those former northeastern parts of the county which are now in the county of [Tyne and Wear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_and_Wear "Tyne and Wear")._

The **geology of County Durham** in northeast [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") consists of a [basement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basement_/(geology/) "Basement (geology)") of Lower [Palaeozoic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palaeozoic "Palaeozoic") rocks overlain by a varying thickness of [Carboniferous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carboniferous "Carboniferous") and [Permo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permian "Permian")\-[Triassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triassic "Triassic") [sedimentary rocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedimentary_rock "Sedimentary rock") which dip generally eastwards towards the [North Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea "North Sea"). These have been intruded by a [pluton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluton "Pluton"), [sills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sill_/(geology/) "Sill (geology)") and [dykes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dyke_/(geology/) "Dyke (geology)") at various times from the [Devonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devonian "Devonian") Period to the [Palaeogene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palaeogene "Palaeogene"). The whole is overlain by a suite of unconsolidated deposits of [Quaternary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternary "Quaternary") age arising from [glaciation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaciation "Glaciation") and from other processes operating during the [post-glacial period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocene "Holocene") to the present.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-1) The geological interest of the west of the county was recognised by the designation in 2003 of the [North Pennines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pennines "North Pennines") [Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_of_Outstanding_Natural_Beauty "Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty") as a [European Geopark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Geopark "European Geopark").

The word 'geology' may be traced back to a coinage of [Richard de Bury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_de_Bury "Richard de Bury") who was a [Bishop of Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops_of_Durham "Bishops of Durham") in the 14th century. He introduced the term _geologia_ in his work _[The Philobiblon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Philobiblon "The Philobiblon")_ which he explained as 'the earthly science'.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-lawrence-2): 8

The oldest rocks at or near the surface within County Durham are [Ordovician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordovician "Ordovician") age (485 - 443 [Ma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megaannum "Megaannum")) [Skiddaw Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Group "Skiddaw Group") rocks found in a small [inlier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inliers_and_outliers_/(geology/) "Inliers and outliers (geology)") near [Cronkley Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cronkley_Fell&action=edit&redlink=1 "Cronkley Fell (page does not exist)") in upper [Teesdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teesdale "Teesdale"). They are recorded as the [Skiddaw Slates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiddaw_Slate "Skiddaw Slate"), better known from the [Lake District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_District "Lake District") 50 km to the west. A small quarry in these [phyllites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phyllite "Phyllite") was worked at one time to make slate pencils.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-3) Overlying these are [pyroclastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyroclastic_rock "Pyroclastic rock") rocks thought to belong to the [Borrowdale Volcanic Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borrowdale_Volcanic_Group "Borrowdale Volcanic Group").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-4)

No rocks from the succeeding [Silurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silurian "Silurian") Period (443 - 419 Ma) are seen at outcrop in the county.

No rocks of [Devonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devonian "Devonian") age (419 - 359 Ma) are seen at outcrop in the county though a [pluton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluton "Pluton"), the [Weardale Granite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weardale_Granite "Weardale Granite") forming the [North Pennine Batholith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pennine_Batholith "North Pennine Batholith") was intruded into Lower [Palaeozoic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palaeozoic "Palaeozoic") rocks around 410 million years ago during the Devonian Period.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-lawrence-2): 19  It forms a part of the larger 'North of England Plutonic Suite', whose members (which include the [granites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granite "Granite") at Shap and Skiddaw) were emplaced during the [Caledonian Orogeny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caledonian_Orogeny "Caledonian Orogeny").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-5) The buoyancy of this [batholith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batholith "Batholith") (it is less dense than the rock into which it was intruded) is considered to be responsible for the existence of the [Alston Block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alston_Block "Alston Block") which coincides with the [North Pennines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pennines "North Pennines") and which is essentially an eastward dipping [horst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horst_/(geology/) "Horst (geology)") bounded to the west (outside of County Durham) by the [Pennine Fault System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennine_Fault_System "Pennine Fault System"), to the north by the Stublick and Ninety Fathom faults (in Northumberland) and by the Butterknowle Fault and Stainmore Trough to the south.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-6)

There is a thick succession of rocks in County Durham which originated during the [Carboniferous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carboniferous "Carboniferous") Period (359 - 299 Ma). The detail of the rock succession varies from one part of the county to another and in no one location is the entire sequence detailed below in place. The sequence over the Alston Block is generally thinner than elsewhere.

The western half of the county forms a part of the [Pennine range of hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennines "Pennines") which are formed largely by the [sandstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone") and [limestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone "Limestone") of the [Great Scar Limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Scar_Limestone_Group "Great Scar Limestone Group") and overlying [Yoredale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoredale_Series "Yoredale Series") groups. Further east it is the younger Coal Measures rocks which are found at the surface. Further east again the Carboniferous succession is overlain by younger rocks but they are present at increasing depth to the North Sea coast and beyond.

Note that the subdivision of the British Carboniferous rock sequence has undergone considerable revision in recent years and many traditional [sequence names](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratigraphy "Stratigraphy") are now obsolete in formal use, though of course they remain widespread in the literature. What is now referred to as the Pennine Coal Measures Group would once have been referred to simply as the 'Productive Coal Measures' and the Yoredale Group was the 'Yoredale Series'. The 'Millstone Grit' of County Durham (minus the 'Great Limestone Member') has been renamed as the 'Stainmore Formation', having also been referred to somewhat confusingly as the Stainmore Group at one time.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-7)

A feature of much of the Carboniferous succession in northern England is its cyclicity which has involved regular changes between marine deposition and sedimentation from rivers. The phenomenon is manifest as [cyclothems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclothem "Cyclothem") and is especially prominent in the Yoredale Group sequence.

### Great Scar Limestone Group

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geology_of_County_Durham&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Great Scar Limestone Group")\]

A part of the [Carboniferous Limestone Supergroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carboniferous_Limestone "Carboniferous Limestone"), the [Great Scar Limestone Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Scar_Limestone_Group "Great Scar Limestone Group") consists of a number of different formations except over the Alston Block where a 107m thickness of largely [Asbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asbian "Asbian") age limestones and sandstones occurs and is known as the [Melmerby Scar Limestone Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Melmerby_Scar_Limestone_Formation&action=edit&redlink=1 "Melmerby Scar Limestone Formation (page does not exist)").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-8)

*   Great Scar Limestone Group
    *   Knipe Scar Limestone Formation
    *   Potts Beck Formation
    *   Ashfell Limestone Formation
    *   Ashfell Sandstone Formation
    *   Breakyneck Scar Limestone Formation
    *   Brownber Formation
    *   Scandal Beck Limestone Formation
    *   Coldbeck Limestone Formation

Limestone was widely quarried for the production of lime for agriculture and [lime mortar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lime_mortar "Lime mortar") for building. Industrial scale quarrying accompanied the growth of the iron and steel industries but has since declined. The [Frosterley Marble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frosterley_Marble "Frosterley Marble"), a [bituminous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitumen "Bitumen") [coraliferous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coral "Coral") limestone once worked at Harehope Quarry in Weardale is used as a decorative stone and can be found in many churches in the region. Concentrations of such corals as _[Dibunophyllum bipartitum](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dibunophyllum_bipartitum&action=edit&redlink=1 "Dibunophyllum bipartitum (page does not exist)")_ and of [brachiopod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brachiopod "Brachiopod") remains contribute to its attractiveness when sections are polished.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-9)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-lawrence-2): 40

Rocks assigned to the [Yoredale Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoredale_Series "Yoredale Series") overlie the Carboniferous Limestone succession. The Group is subdivided into a lower/older [Alston Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alston_Formation "Alston Formation") and a higher/younger [Stainmore Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stainmore_Formation&action=edit&redlink=1 "Stainmore Formation (page does not exist)"). The former is largely of [Brigantian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigantian "Brigantian") age whilst the latter is of [Asbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asbian "Asbian")/Brigantian to [Yeadonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yeadonian&action=edit&redlink=1 "Yeadonian (page does not exist)") age. The latter is broadly equivalent to the [Millstone Grit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millstone_Grit "Millstone Grit") of the central and southern Pennines. Note that in northeast England some hard rock units are traditionally described as 'sills', a local term for a hard band of rock of whatever origin. Nowadays geologists reserve the term for flat-lying igneous intrusions such as the Whin Sill which is described below.

*   Yoredale Group
    *   Stainmore Formation (formerly _Millstone Grit_)
        *   _various un-named sandstones and mudstones_
        *   Grindstone Sandstone (formerly _Grindstone Sill_)
        *   _various un-named sandstones and mudstones_
        *   Firestone Sandstone (formerly _Firestone Sill_)
        *   _various sandstones and mudstones_
    *   Alston Formation (formerly _Alston Group_)
        *   Great Limestone Member (formerly part of _Stainmore Group_ of _Millstone Grit_ - Pendleian)
        *   Four Fathom Limestone Member
        *   _various sandstones and limestones_
        *   Three Yard Limestone Member
        *   _various sandstones and limestones_
        *   Five Yard Limestone Member
        *   _various sandstones and limestones_
        *   Scar Limestone Member
        *   _various sandstones and limestones_
        *   Tynebottom Limestone Member
        *   _various sandstones and limestones_

Overlying the Yoredale Group rocks is a thick sequence of Coal Measures across which the [Durham Coalfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_Coalfield "Durham Coalfield") developed. The sequence in County Durham is divided into Lower, Middle and Upper formations. Each of the three are dominated by mudstones but contain abundant sandstones and [coal seams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_seam "Coal seam"). [Ironstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ironstone "Ironstone") bands occur in the lower part of the sequence. At least eleven [marine bands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_band_/(geology/) "Marine band (geology)") (shelly mudstones in general) occur within the Coal Measures. Of these, the 'Quarterburn' marine band defines the base of the Lower Coal Measures Formation, the 'Harvey' marine band defines its junction with the overlying Middle Coal Measures Formation and the 'Down Hill' marine band defines the latter's junction with the Upper Coal Measures Formation. The Quarterburn, Harvey and Down Hill marine bands correlate with the standard _Subcrenatum_, _Vanderbeckei_ and _Cambriense_ marine bands of elsewhere. The top of the entire Coal Measures sequence is an erosion surface.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-10)

*   [Pennine Coal Measures Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennine_Coal_Measures_Group "Pennine Coal Measures Group")
    *   [Pennine Upper Coal Measures Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pennine_Upper_Coal_Measures_Formation&action=edit&redlink=1 "Pennine Upper Coal Measures Formation (page does not exist)")
    *   [Pennine Middle Coal Measures Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pennine_Middle_Coal_Measures_Formation&action=edit&redlink=1 "Pennine Middle Coal Measures Formation (page does not exist)") (Duckmantian)
    *   [Pennine Lower Coal Measures Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pennine_Lower_Coal_Measures_Formation&action=edit&redlink=1 "Pennine Lower Coal Measures Formation (page does not exist)") (Langsettian)

Over the [Alston Block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alston_Block "Alston Block") the middle and upper Coal Measures are missing. Similarly in the [Stainmore Trough](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stainmore_Trough&action=edit&redlink=1 "Stainmore Trough (page does not exist)") on the [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire "Yorkshire") border, both the upper part of the Middle and the entire Upper Coal Measures are absent. The [rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilt%27s_Law "Hilt's Law") of coal increases in the west, a result of the heating of these strata by the Weardale Granite. Some such seams are semi-[anthracites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthracite "Anthracite"). Workings for coal date back centuries though the height of the industry was the nineteenth century. There are no deep pits remaining in the county though opencasting continues.

Various of the county's Coal Measures sandstones have been quarried for building stone, for example the Low Main Post sandstone in [Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham,_England "Durham, England") which was used in the construction of the [city's cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_Cathedral "Durham Cathedral").

### Late Carboniferous intrusive rocks

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geology_of_County_Durham&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Late Carboniferous intrusive rocks")\]

The 'Hett Subswarm' of [tholeiitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tholeiite "Tholeiite") quartz-dolerite dykes run WSW-ENE across country to the south of [Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham,_England "Durham, England"). The subswarm includes the [Hett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hett,_County_Durham "Hett, County Durham") Dyke and [Ludworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludworth,_County_Durham "Ludworth, County Durham") Dyke amongst others which cut Coal Measures rocks in a WSW-ENE alignment but do not pass into the overlying Permian succession.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-11)

Permian and Triassic
--------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geology_of_County_Durham&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Permian and Triassic")\]

As with the Carboniferous sequence, the subdivision of the British [Permian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permian "Permian") (299 - 252 Ma) and [Triassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triassic "Triassic") (252 - 201 Ma) has been considerably revised in recent years. Traditional sequence names have been replaced in formal use by new names, though the older names are frequently encountered in books and on maps. The full sequence of Permian and Triassic rocks forming the [New Red Sandstone Supergroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Red_Sandstone_Supergroup "New Red Sandstone Supergroup") locally is this (uppermost/youngest first):

*   [Mercia Mudstone Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercia_Mudstone_Group "Mercia Mudstone Group") (formerly _Keuper Marl_) (Triassic)
*   [Sherwood Sandstone Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherwood_Sandstone_Group "Sherwood Sandstone Group") (formerly _Bunter Sandstone_) (Triassic)
*   [Zechstein Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zechstein_Group "Zechstein Group") (Permian)
    *   Roxby Formation (calcareous mudstone, formerly _Upper Anyhdrite and Marl_)
    *   Sherburn Anhydrite Formation (in Stockton area only)
    *   Rotten Marl Formation (formerly _Rotten or Carnallitic Marl_)
    *   Boulby Halite Formation (formerly _Middle Halite_ in Durham area)
    *   Seaham Formation (formerly _Upper Magnesian Limestone_ - calcareous mudstone)
    *   Seaham Residue & Fordon Evaporite Formation (Edlington Formation in Stockton area (formerly _Permian Middle Marls_))
    *   Roker Formation (formerly _Hartlepool Anydrite & Roker Dolomite_)
    *   Ford Formation (formerly _Middle Magnesian Limestone_)
    *   Raisby Formation (formerly _Lower Magnesian Limestone_)
    *   Marl Slate Formation (formerly _Marl Slate_)
*   [Rotliegendes Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotliegend "Rotliegend") (Permian)
    *   Yellow Sands Formation (formerly _Basal Permian (Sands &) Breccia_)

The Yellow Sands Formation comprises [aeolian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeolian_processes "Aeolian processes") dune-bedded sandstones. The Yellow Sands Formation continues to be worked for building sand. These are overlain by the thin bituminous limestones of the 'Marl Slate' representing the start of a series of inundations of the area by rising sea levels. It contains abundant [fish remains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil_fish "Fossil fish").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-lawrence-2): 20

The sequence from the Marl Slate up to and including the Seaham Formation was formerly known as the [Magnesian Limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesian_Limestone "Magnesian Limestone"). The 'Zechstein Group' replaced the former Don, Aislaby, Teesside, Staintondale and Eskdale groups. Several of these units have proved economically valuable. [Anhydrite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anhydrite "Anhydrite") was sourced beneath [Hartlepool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartlepool "Hartlepool") and [gypsum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gypsum "Gypsum") near [Darlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darlington "Darlington"). The Magnesian Limestone forms a broken west-facing scarp running from the western edge of [Sunderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunderland,_Tyne_and_Wear "Sunderland, Tyne and Wear") southwards through [Houghton-le-Spring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houghton-le-Spring "Houghton-le-Spring") and [Hetton-le-Hole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hetton-le-Hole "Hetton-le-Hole") to [Coxhoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coxhoe "Coxhoe") where its outcrop is offset to the west by the Butterknowle Fault. [English Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Nature "English Nature") has defined this part of the county east of the scarp where the sequence is exposed at or near the surface, as the 'Durham Magnesian Limestone Plateau' in its assessment of '[character areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_character_area "National character area")'.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-12) The occurrence of gypsum and anhydrite reflects the extreme nature of the evaporation of the shallow [Zechstein Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zechstein_Sea "Zechstein Sea") on occasion though such [evaporites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evaporites "Evaporites") are economically valuable. They also present constraints on development as ongoing subterranean solution of these deposits causes occasional catastrophic ground collapse. Similar solution in Palaeogene times has created 'collapse breccias' of overlying strata.

[Dolomite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolomite_/(rock/) "Dolomite (rock)") from the Roker Formation has been quarried for building construction along the Durham coast. It has sometimes been referred to as 'Cannonball Rock' due to the appearance of calcitic concretions in certain beds. St Oswald's Church in Hartlepool is constructed from this stone.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-13)

### Permian intrusive rocks

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geology_of_County_Durham&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Permian intrusive rocks")\]

The Whin Sill and associated [igneous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igneous "Igneous") [dykes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dyke_/(geology/) "Dyke (geology)") were intruded into the existing sedimentary sequence during the [early Permian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cisuralian "Cisuralian") around 295 Ma.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-lawrence-2) The thickness of the [quartz-dolerite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartz-dolerite "Quartz-dolerite") sill averages about 30m. The sill underlies the larger part of the county at depth and appears to extend beneath the North Sea to the east. [Thermal metamorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metamorphism#Contact_.28thermal.29_metamorphism "Metamorphism") has altered the surrounding strata, the 'country rocks', to a distance of tens of metres or more. One such is the Sugar Limestone of upper Teesdale which weathers in characteristic fashion and hosts a rare assemblage of plants. Mudstones in contact with the sill have been altered into [hornfels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hornfels "Hornfels"), known locally as 'whetstone'.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-lawrence-2): 20  The presence of the Whin Sill gives rise to [High Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Force "High Force") where the [River Tees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tees "River Tees") drops in spectacular fashion over this erosion-resistant rock. The Little Whin Sill is a thinner, more geographically restricted intrusion of [dolerite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolerite "Dolerite") of similar age outcropping in upper [Weardale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weardale "Weardale"). A quarry near [High Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Force "High Force") in upper Teesdale works the dolerite (or 'whinstone') of the Whin Sill for roadstone, [aggregate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Construction_aggregate "Construction aggregate") and as larger blocks for coastal protection purposes.

### Northern Pennine Orefield

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geology_of_County_Durham&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Northern Pennine Orefield")\]

The Northern Pennine Orefield comprises an extended network of veins and 'flats' developed within the Carboniferous sedimentary sequence and is considered one of the finest examples of [Mississippi Valley type orefields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbonate_hosted_lead_zinc_ore_deposits "Carbonate hosted lead zinc ore deposits"). Epigenetic mineralisation (i.e. mineralisation at a shallow level) of veins and faults took place shortly after emplacement of the Whin Sill at the start of the Permian Period.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-lawrence-2): 20  Mining for [lead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead "Lead"), [copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper "Copper") and [zinc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc "Zinc") has taken place over several centuries across these uplands.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-14)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-15)

[Volcanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanism "Volcanism") centred on western [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") took place during the [Palaeogene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palaeogene "Palaeogene") Period and resulted in the intrusion of innumerable dykes, one of which is the [Cleveland Dyke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Dyke "Cleveland Dyke") which extends from [Galloway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galloway "Galloway") through County Durham to the [North York Moors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_York_Moors "North York Moors"). This intrusion of [basaltic andesite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basaltic_andesite "Basaltic andesite") which is up to 30m wide in places has been dated to 55.8+/- 0.9Ma[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-16)

The broad structure of the Alston Block has been described in the Devonian section above. The block is itself cut north to south a by a complex structure known as the 'Burtreeford Disturbance' which comprises both faults and folds.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-17) To the east of the block the cover of late Palaeozoic and early Mesozoic rocks dip into the [North Sea Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_the_North_Sea "Geology of the North Sea").

Much of the county is mantled with a layer of [glacial till](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Till "Till") though this is thinner on the higher ground in the west. There are also spreads of [glacially derived sand and gravel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaciofluvial_deposits "Glaciofluvial deposits"), especially across part of the lower ground in the east. [Alluvium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alluvium "Alluvium") deposited by rivers occupies the floors of valleys such as that of the [Wear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Wear "River Wear") whilst river terraces are frequent in the [Tees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tees "River Tees") valley. [Lacustrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake "Lake") [clays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clay "Clay") and [silts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silt "Silt") occur in parts of the east where for example, towards the end of the last ice age, Glacial Lake Wear and Glacial Lake Edderacres formed as drainage eastwards was blocked by an icesheet occupying the North Sea.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-18)

Peat has developed extensively across the higher ground of the North Pennines. A variety of coastal deposits are found around the Tees estuary and up the coast to [Hartlepool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartlepool "Hartlepool") and beyond. [\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-19)

Geoconservation and Geotourism
------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geology_of_County_Durham&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Geoconservation and Geotourism")\]

Some locations in County Durham are afforded statutory legal protection against adverse developments through being designated as one or more of the following:

### Local geological sites

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geology_of_County_Durham&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Local geological sites")\]

A [geodiversity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodiversity "Geodiversity") audit of County Durham produced many locations which are now afforded recognition as 'Local geological sites' (formerly referred to as '[Regionally Important Geodiversity Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regionally_Important_Geodiversity_Sites "Regionally Important Geodiversity Sites")' or simply 'RIGS'.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-20)

### Local nature reserves

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geology_of_County_Durham&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Local nature reserves")\]

LNRs may be designated for their biological or geological interest. In any case, more often than not, the biological interest is dependent upon the geological interest as at Wingate Quarry LNR north of [Trimdon Grange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimdon_Grange "Trimdon Grange") village where 'Magnesian Limestone grassland' may be found[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-21)

### Sites of Special Scientific Interest

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geology_of_County_Durham&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Sites of Special Scientific Interest")\]

Numerous SSSIs include citations referring to their geological interest. The extensive [Moorhouse and Cross Fell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorhouse_and_Cross_Fell "Moorhouse and Cross Fell") SSSI (shared with [Cumbria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumbria "Cumbria")) is one of the most important for a range of subjects. [Natural England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_England "Natural England") and other conservation bodies own and manage these locations. The [Durham Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_Coast "Durham Coast") is one such which is designated in part for its coastal [geomorphology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geomorphology "Geomorphology").

Bodies such as the North Pennines AONB Partnership and [Durham County Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_County_Council "Durham County Council") have published [local geodiversity action plans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGAP "LGAP") (or 'LGAPs') which summarise an area's geological interests and propose various measures to [conserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoconservation "Geoconservation") what is perceived to be valuable.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-22)

### North Pennines AONB and Geopark

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Geology_of_County_Durham&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: North Pennines AONB and Geopark")\]

The North Pennines AONB was designated as Britain's first [European Geopark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Geopark "European Geopark") in 2003 partly in acknowledgement of its geological and geomorphological interest. The AONB and Geopark extend beyond the boundaries of County Durham to include parts of [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland "Northumberland") and [Cumbria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumbria "Cumbria").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_County_Durham#cite_note-23)

Update: 7.10.24

The aim of the enclosures project is to enhance the recovery of upland heath plant communities by reducing grazing pressure; boosting biodiversity whilst supporting commoning**.**

The Lake District National Park Authority (LDNPA), the Caldbeck Commoners’ Association and Natural England are working together on this exciting project to fence off three upland areas of designated ‘Site of Special Scientific Interest’ on Caldbeck Common, totalling 36.2ha, for a period of five years. Fencing on common land typically requires Secretary of State, Section 38 approval however in this instance, as the area being fenced is less than 1% of registered common and for five years with the goal to improve the habitat, an exemption is made possible.

Caldbeck Common makes up part of the Skiddaw Group SSSI and Lake District High Fells Special Area of Conservation. It includes important habitats such as heather and moss moorland, blanket bog and juniper scrub. The area also supports large populations of upland breeding birds which are surveyed annually.

#### **How were the sites chosen?**

The areas for the enclosures have been carefully surveyed and selected for already having heathland plants present, such as heather and billberry, but with a low % ground cover. Because of this they are more likely to respond to a reduction of grazing pressure to make them denser, more robust and more species diverse. Heathland regenerated in this way is likely to become well-established and more able to withstand the reintroduction of the reasonably low level grazing once the fences are removed.

A further study was commissioned to  further assess and recommend the most appropriate areas to fence to ensure minimal negative impact on the graziers, landscape, cultural and historic, biodiversity and access. The sites are located on different fells with sufficient distance and changes in topography to prevent negative cumulative effects. These sites offer the best outcome for balancing objectives of livestock management, commoning, nature recovery and delivery of public goods, including cultural goods associated with landscape character and visitor access and experience.

#### **Protecting Open Access land**

To ensure continued open access (CROW Act, 2000), not only have the selected sites been carefully chosen to ensure minimal impact to visitors on the common but two pedestrian gates will be fitted at each site to allow visitors to pass through.

The results of this pilot will help to inform future management decisions on the common and repeated fencing of targeted areas could be a valuable tool, helping us work towards improving habitats across the common. This approach not only helps to boost biodiversity in targeted areas but also allows commoners to continue with culturally valuable practices with minimal impact.

#### **Chosen locations**

![Image 1: Caldbeck Common Enclosures](https://www.lakedistrict.gov.uk/__data/assets/image/0018/64017/CaldbeckCommon_enclosures_website-747.png)

###### Map: © Crown copyright and database right 2024 Ordnance Survey AC0000807483. You are not permitted to copy, sub-licence, distribute or sell any of this data to third parties in any form.

#### **Funding**

This project was funded by Farming in Protected Landscapes (FiPL) and LDNPA.

#### **Trialling reusable fencing**

The project has also provided an opportunity to demonstrate reusable metal fencing in one of the three locations in the hope that this more durable fencing can be used in future projects helping to reduce the LDNPA’s organisational carbon footprint. The fenced area on Birk Hill is considered the most suitable site to trial this innovative fencing due to its remoteness and lack of well used paths in the area. As a relatively new fencing system, LDNPA will evaluate the effectiveness of the reusable fencing and invite interested land managers and organisations to discuss the teams’ experiences. The metal post system is designed to be sustainable, long lasting and reusable. Its design enables it to be easily disassembled at the end of the five-year period and reused in future projects.

#### **Monitoring**

As part of this experimental project, LDNPA will be commissioning a baseline ecological condition assessment and repeated assessments throughout and at the end of the project, to monitor and evaluate changes in plant species and populations throughout the 5-year project and beyond.

Existing data and anecdotal evidence suggest deer populations are not currently an issue on Caldbeck Common especially in open fell with limited shelterbelts in the High Fells, where the fencing has been constructed. However, on recommendation, we will undertake a thermal drone survey to provide a base line for deer present across Caldbeck common and evidence of browsing within the fenced areas will be monitored and recorded.

#### **Sharing lessons learned**

The temporary exclusion of livestock on carefully chosen areas of upland heath is experimental in design and engaging with stakeholders and interested parties in process, lessons learned and providing training opportunities is a key element of the project. There will be an opportunity to be involved in knowledge-sharing events nearing the end of this project, where methods and outcomes will be discussed with commoners, local communities and nature conservation organisations. As the project progresses, there will be further information available on these events.
