### Landform, geology and soils ![Image 9: section contains a map](https://nationalcharacterareas.co.uk/wp-content/themes/nca_profiles/images/has-map.svg)

Note that numbers and figures in the body of the text are based on the 2014 profiles, unless otherwise stated. The maps contain live frequently updated datasets.

**Elevation**

Elevation ranges from just below sea level to a maximum of 978m at the summit of Scafell Pike, the highest peak in England. The average elevation is 308m above sea level (Natural England, 2011)

**Landform and process**

The complex geology of the Cumbria High Fells and the South Cumbria Low Fells consists of an eroded dome of ancient rocks. Ordovician marine sediments, lavas and volcanic deposits have been uplifted and metamorphosed by large granite intrusions. More recent glaciation has carved U-shaped valleys, now with rivers and ribbon lakes, radiating out from the central dome of fells. Glaciation features include cirques, ar̻tes, tarns and scree slopes, with roche moutonn̩es and moraine deposits in the valleys (Cumbria High Fells Countryside Character Area Description, Cumbria Fells & Dales Natural Area Profile).

**Bedrock geology**

The solid geology can be divided into the Skiddaw Group and Borrowdale Volcanic Group of the fells, with the low lying Eycott Volcanic Group and Carboniferous Limestone to the north and north-east.

The Skiddaw Group forms the smooth sided mountains of the north of the Lake District. These Ordovician age metamorphosed mudstones, siltstones and greywackes are of marine origin and the oldest rocks in the Lake District.

The rugged central fells area is comprised of a complex sequence of lavas and ash deposits of the Ordovician Borrowdale Volcanic Group. These are metamorphosed by a large granite intrusion that outcorps in Ennerdale, Eskdale, Shap and the Caldew Valley. The Eycott Volcanic Group, of a similar age, provides a narrow, less rugged and lower lying outcrop in the Caldbeck Fells, Eycott Hill and Binsey, to the north east of the Skiddaw Group rocks.

Rocks of the Skiddaw Group, Eycott Volcanic Group and Borrowdale Volcanic Group, host numerous mineral veins with ores of copper, lead, zinc and a variety of other metals, as well as the graphite deposit at Seathwaite in Borrowdale.

Carboniferous Limestone foothills, with karst features and limestone quarries, encircle the northern fells and extend into the adjacent Orton Fells NCA (Cumbria High Fells Countryside Character Area Description, Cumbria Fells & Dales Natural Area Profile).

**Superficial deposits**

Superficial deposits, which cover about 59 per cent of the NCA, are generally present in valleys and lower slopes. They include boulder clay (till), glacial moraines, and fluvioglacial sand and gravel. Fluvial alluvium is associated with active rivers. Significant areas of peat are present in the blanket bogs of the fells as well as the raised bogs to the south-east and east of the NCA (British Geological Survey, 2006).

**Soils and Agriculture Classification**

Typical brown podzol soils (intermediate between leached acid soils and more fertile brown earth soils) are widespread on lower slopes with extensive humic rankers (shallow peaty soils over non-calcareous bedrock) across higher slopes. Waterlogged raw oligo-fibrous peat soils (very acid soils where breakdown of organic material is limited) form blanket bog on some areas of high ground, particularly to the east of the area. Cambic stagnohumic gley soils (seasonally waterlogged soils with peaty topsoil lacking clay-enriched subsoil) are found locally in glacial valleys with narrow strips of typical alluvial gley soils (soils deposited by rivers with fluctuating water table) in some valleys (Natural England, 2012).

The major lakes, set in valleys radiating from the central dome of the High Fells, are the dominant features in the landscape. Numerous smaller tarns occupy glacially carved corries on the fells. This area has the highest rainfall in England. This, combined with steep gradients, impermeable geology and waterlogged upland soils, results in large amounts of run-off. The Cumbria High Fells NCA contains 5 river/lake Special Areas of Conservation (River Derwent and Bassenthwaite Lake, River Eden, River Kent, River Ehen and Nowt Water) as well as freshwater features within other SAC.

The Eden catchment includes the Ullswater Lake and Haweswater Reservoir. The upper catchment is dominated by the steep gradients of Skiddaw, Helvellyn and drains north to the Irish Sea via the Solway Estuary.

The River Derwent and its major tributaries rise in the high fells, draining into the Irish Sea at Workington: The Derwent Catchment includes Buttermere, Crummock Water, Loweswater, Derwent Water and Bassenthwaite Lake, as well as Thirlmere Reservoir. The South West Lakes catchment includes Ennerdale Water and Nowt Water. From Workington to Barrow-in-Furness this catchment contains a number of small, rural ‘flashy’ sub-catchments which drain in a south westerly direction to the Irish Sea.

Kent/Leven catchment includes Elterwater, Rydal Water and Grasmere.

The rivers Kent, Leven and Crake drain the southern fells of the Lake District, and drain south into Morecambe Bay via the Kent and Leven estuaries.

The River Lune drains only a small part of the south-east of the NCA area.

**Water quality**

Nitrate Vulnerable Zones (NVZs) are areas designated as being at risk from agricultural nitrate pollution. These can impact surface water (waterbodies and waterways located above ground) and groundwater (water bodies and waterways located below ground).

Waterbodies such as lakes can also be designated as “eutrophic waters” if the enrichment of the waterbody by nitrate pollution causes accelerated growth of algae, impacting the quality of the water and the balance of organisms within it.

**Distribution and size of woodland and trees in the landscape**

Woodland is found mainly on lower slopes and valley bottoms, with the higher fells relatively treeless. Remnant tree cover on the fells is found in a few isolated woodlands and gills, with scattered trees and juniper scrub replaced by dwarf willow at higher altitudes. Trees are found in discrete woodlands, plantations, groups and as scattered individuals, including pollards. Areas of wood pasture (grazed open woodland) include parkland, particularly around some of the lakes. Broadleaved woodlands are found particularly in Borrowdale, around Derwent Water, Ullswater and Haweswater and in the central Lake District around Ambleside and Grasmere and in the Duddon and Longsleddale valleys. Internationally important areas of juniper scrub are associated with the central Lake District, extending into the South Cumbria Low Fells NCA (Cumbria High Fells Countryside Character Area Description, Cumbria Fells & Dales Natural Area Profile, Natural England, 2012).

### Boundary features and patterns

Note that numbers and figures in the body of the text are based on the 2014 profiles, unless otherwise stated.

**Boundary features**

In the valleys, drystone walls enclosing the fields and the farmsteads, create a unifying element in the landscape and can often be seen as strongly marked patterns on valley sides. Hedges and individual trees, including pollards, are also part of the network of boundary features, and can provide connectivity between stands of woodland (Cumbria High Fells Countryside Character Area description; Countryside Quality Counts, 2003).

**Field patterns**

Patterns of rectilinear fields enclosed by dry stone walls. Small fields in the valley bottoms link through larger intakes and allotments to the open common land of the fells. Field patterns have developed and persisted since the early medieval period with a system of tenure of individually farmed in-bye fields in the valleys and extensive open common grazing on the fells. Above the fell wall the unenclosed rough grazing of the fells comprises the largest area of common land in England. The smaller inbye fields are predominantly agriculturally improved. The transition up the valley sides is marked by an increase in field size and decrease of agricultural improvement to the unimproved open fells (Cumbria High Fells Countryside Character Area description; Countryside Quality Counts, 2003).

**Habitat distribution/coverage**

**Fells**:  
Fells with extensive internationally important semi-natural habitats, with good potential for ecological connectivity. Fell habitat mosaic of mainly upland heath, blanket bog and acid grassland with valley and basin mires, flushes and springs interspersed with bracken beds, scattered trees and a few small isolated woodlands.

Habitat condition is slowly recovering, although the most sensitive (montane and blanket bog) habitats remain susceptible to grazing pressure. Extensive areas of blanket bog on the Skiddaw, Shap and Armboth fells. Particularly important for montane plant communities, restricted in England to here and the North Pennines. Montane heaths and grasslands are found on the Skiddaw, Helvellyn, Scafell and Grassmoor massifs. Cliffs and rock outcrops are a refuge from grazing for arctic-alpine plants, providing the only English locality for oblong woodsia, alpine catchfly, glaucous meadow grass and the endemic Borrowdale Hawkweed. Fells support important but declining breeding populations of curlew, ring ouzel and merlin. Raven and peregrines nest on the crags while ospreys are found on Bassenthwaite Lake.

**Woodlands**:  
An important NCA for native woodland, found mainly on lower valley sides and in sheltered gills, with valleys such as Borrowdale and Dunnerdale containing good woodland habitat networks. Historically the fells have lost most of their natural woodland cover with high level woodland restricted to small stands, such as Keskadale on the Buttermere Fells and Young Wood on the Skidddaw massif.

Juniper scrub can occur from the limit of tree growth down to the valley floor. Internationally important woodlands occur in the Borrowdale Valley and above Ullswater, while other large stands occur on the eastern shores of Haweswater and in the Duddon and lower Langdale Valleys. These support the best English examples of western oceanic bryophytes and old forest lichens.

The native woodland is important for western oakwood breeding birds, such as pied flycatcher, wood warbler, redstart and tree pipit. The rare netted carpet moth, which feeds on touch-me-not balsam, is found in some damper areas. Wet woodland occurs on some valley sides but is generally part of wetland systems around lakes. Wood pasture and parkland habitat is an important woodland element, with good examples near Rydal.

**Rivers and lakes**:  
The NCA contains the most extensive, diverse and biologically important range of water bodies in England. These form important ecological networks of connecting lakes and rivers. The lakes range from deep, large oligotrophic (nutrient-poor) lakes, such as Nowtwater to shallower, more mesotrophic lakes, such as Elterwater. Vendace and schelly are fish distinctive to the Cumbria High Fells, with Arctic charr also occurring in the South Cumbria Low Fells area. Small tarns are numerous and varied in altitude, depth, substrate and geology resulting in a wide variety of flora and fauna. The area includes key parts of the River Derwent (including Bassenthwaite Lake and Derwent Water), River Eden (including Ullswater) River Kent and River Ehen systems. These are of international importance for their biological features including salmon, otter, river, brook and sea lamprey, white clawed crayfish, floating water plantain and freshwater pearl mussel.

**Inbye grasslands**:  
Much of the grassland in the valleys and lowlands is agriculturally improved but small, fragmented areas of more species-rich grassland remain. This NCA has internationally important upland haymeadows, with important sites in Borrowdale and Bretherdale. Purple moor-grass and rush pasture is similarly scattered in small fields across several valleys and some examples support the rare marsh fritillary and small pearl bordered fritillary butterflies.

**Wetlands**:  
Wetland such as valley and basin mires, marsh and fen vegetation are important in the valley bottoms and lowlands. Extensive fen and swamp vegetation (as well as wet woodland) are found around many lakes and larger tarns, with good examples at the south end of Bassenthwaite Lake, Esthwaite Water and Elterwater. The area supports internationally important valley mire at Tarn Moss and nationally important lowland raised mire at Mungrisdale (Cumbria Fells & Dales Natural Area Profile).

### Settlement and development patterns ![Image 35: section contains a map](https://nationalcharacterareas.co.uk/wp-content/themes/nca_profiles/images/has-map.svg)

Note that numbers and figures in the body of the text are based on the 2014 profiles, unless otherwise stated. The maps contain live frequently updated datasets.

**Settlement patterns**

The pattern of settlement is largely restricted to the valleys and lowlands with isolated farms along the fell edge. Small villages, hamlets and farmsteads are scattered along access roads in the valleys, where the best farm land is found. The only towns are the small market towns of Keswick and Ambleside, whose populations are substantially increased by tourists at peak times (Cumbria High Fells Countryside Character Area description; Countryside Quality Counts, 2003).

**Main settlements**

The main settlements in the Cumbria High fells are: Keswick and Ambleside. The total estimated population for this NCA (derived from ONS 2001 census data) is: 27,881 (Cumbria High Fells Countryside Character Area description; Countryside Quality Counts, 2003, Natural England, 2012).

**Local vernacular and building materials**

Substantial farmsteads and older terraced cottages are typically constructed in stone with slated roofs. Local rocks, including different types of slate, have been used for farm buildings and walls, with sandstone, granite or limestone used for detail and finishes such as lime Nowh. Drystone walls and in places hedgerows form a visual and historic link between settlement and the countryside. Local building practices are seen in chimneys, windows and walling, as well as in hogg houses, peat houses, packhorse bridges and bank barns. Other than stone-built churches and chapels, few buildings from before the 17th century remain. The main town of Keswick has medieval origins but consists mainly of Victorian two and three storey slate buildings, built in response to the sudden influx of tourists at that time. The Lake District also contains some fine examples of villa architecture as well as wood or stone boathouses around some lakes (Cumbria High Fells Countryside Character Area description; Countryside Quality Counts, 2003).

### Key historic sites and features ![Image 37: section contains a map](https://nationalcharacterareas.co.uk/wp-content/themes/nca_profiles/images/has-map.svg)

Note that numbers and figures in the body of the text are based on the 2014 profiles, unless otherwise stated. The maps contain live frequently updated datasets.

**Origin of historic features**

Neolithic stone circles such as Castlerigg and Swinside are the earliest built monuments in the area. Neolithic stone axe production, from volcanic tuff in the central Lake District, produced highly polished stone axes widely traded to southern England, Scotland and Ireland.

Bronze Age clearance cairns and settlement remains, are evidence of the more extensive establishment of farming on the lower slopes. Bronze Age stone circles include those at Burnmoor in Eskdale.

Romano-British period sites include major forts at Troutbeck, Ambleside, Hardknott and Ravenglass, civilian settlements at Ambleside and Ravenglass, major roads, such as High Street, plus enclosures and field systems in the lower fells and valleys.

Medieval and later field boundaries are based on a persisting farming system of in-bye grazing in the valleys and extensive open common grazing on the fells. Fellside “intakes” date from the 16th to 18th century.

Widespread Norse place names such as “Thwaite” (clearing) as well as hog back tombstones and crosses (for example, at Gosforth) date from the late 10th Century onwards.

Industrial remains dating from the medieval period onwards include mines, quarries, spoil tips, for example, Coniston Copper Mines valley, smelting sites (bloomeries), charcoal pits and water-powered forges and mills. Iron manufacture Now supported by charcoal production from coppiced woodlands, with a post medieval increase in woodland cover for this industry and fuel. In comparison with other NCAs in the north-west there is an unusually small amount of industrial landscape. 18th-century Picturesque movement features include villas, ornamental plantings and designed landscapes and views.

Features associated with the influential Romantic Movement poets include houses, for example, the Wordworth’s Dove cottage, burial places and landscapes, which inspired ideas and poetry.

National Trust properties are a specific legacy of the birth of the conservation and environmental movement in the Lake District, in response to the construction of Thirlmere Reservoir in the mid 1870s.

The relatively large number of Scheduled Monuments, particularly on the unenclosed land, is due to the lack of intensive land use in these areas over time (Draft Historic Profile, Countryside Quality Counts, Countryside Character Area description).

[Field Collecting](https://www.mindat.org/msgboard-5.html)SSSIs and collecting
==============================================================================

![Image 13](https://www.mindat.org/images/anonymous.png)

20th Nov 2007 23:06 UTC[Colin Robinson](https://www.mindat.org/user-4265.html) OP
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------

As a collector and dealer of minerals on ebay (and elsewhere) I recently received a communication from a 'Heritage" organization requesting that I stop listing specimens from a particular north of England location as the site is a SSSI (Site of Special Scientific Interest) and pointing out that to remove or sell such material since designation as a SSSI was in fact a criminal offence.  
  
  
My problem (apart from the obvious one of despising bureaucratic interference in all its forms) is that unless I collect a piece myself, how do I know when it was collected? Also, and perhaps more importantly, how do I know a site is a SSSI? This last year I have visited 4 sites which, it turns out, are SSSIs and there is no indication of any kind as to that status. They say ignorance of the law is no excuse but it's an odd law that says you can't do certain things but we're not going to tell you what they are.

![Image 14](https://www.mindat.org/images/anonymous.png)

20th Nov 2007 23:21 UTC[Alfredo Petrov](https://www.mindat.org/user-275.html) [🌟](https://www.mindat.org/user-275.html#7) Manager
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I don't know the relevant British law but in the USA, I think, it would still be legal to sell such things if they had been collected before the area became protected. A few laws are applied retroactively, but most are not. Is this not the case in Britain?  
  
  
Difficult, if you have to prove when something was collected. Another reason to save old labels, I suppose; and old field trip photos.  
  
  
There is a lot of information about Britain's SSSIs on Wikipedia - They are listed there. According to this source, about 7% of the national territory is already covered by either biological or geological SSSIs! Also, your own private property could get included too! Theoretically, you could buy the land an old mine sits on, with the intention of carrying out future specimen mining, and then find out it's going to be a SSSI and you can't do any development without consulting the heritage protection folk. Sounds rather draconian. (Where were these people when all the hedges were torn out? I was sorry to see those go.)  
  
  
Cheers,  
  
Alfredo

![Image 15](https://www.mindat.org/avatarcache/1207.jpg?1586270970)

20th Nov 2007 23:42 UTC[David Von Bargen Manager](https://www.mindat.org/user-1207.html)
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Well, there are only 4113 sites in the UK.  
  
  
[http://www.english-nature.org.uk/special/sssi/searchresults.cfm?sssi\_name=&frmcounty=](http://www.english-nature.org.uk/special/sssi/searchresults.cfm?sssi_name=&frmcounty=)

![Image 16](https://www.mindat.org/images/anonymous.png)

21st Nov 2007 00:24 UTC[Chester S. Lemanski, Jr.](https://www.mindat.org/user-461.html)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

One world order and control - beware!!!!!!

![Image 17](https://www.mindat.org/images/anonymous.png)

21st Nov 2007 00:40 UTC[Alfredo Petrov](https://www.mindat.org/user-275.html) [🌟](https://www.mindat.org/user-275.html#7) Manager
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

English Nature does make a case for the benefits of collecting ("responsibly") in certain areas. Presumably this does not include dealers hauling off lorry loads of material. Actually seems somewhat reasonable to me, although it remains to be seen how many "in situ veins and mine dumps" are included in their SSSIs. Their recognition that actively eroding areas can actually benefit from collecting is a lot more intelligent than the attitude of some bureaucrats in the USA, who will punish any collecting at all in protected areas. In my experience, sites get closed because of the activities of a few greedy, hyperactive and destructive collectors taking far more material than they can use, often dumping the excess at some other locality, and leaving rubbish behind.  
  
  
From their website:  
  
  
  
  
Irresponsible specimen collecting  
  
Irresponsible collecting of fossils or minerals is a serious problem on certain sites. In extreme cases, irresponsible collecting can result in partial or complete destruction of a geological interest feature.  
  
  
Responsible specimen collecting, is not considered to be a damaging activity on the majority of geological SSSIs, which are classified as exposure sites. Indeed, on actively eroding coasts, where important material would be lost to the sea if not collected, responsible specimen collecting is an essential part of geological conservation. For example, the Dorset Jurassic Coast Project has developed a code of conduct for fossil collecting and a database on which to register finds.  
  
  
  
  
Similarly, in working quarries, important geological material can be lost if it is not collected. There are several sites, for example Grinshill Quarries SSSI, Shropshire, where the owners provide access to material. In addition, there a number of disused quarries where the owners still provide material for study and collection. An example is Cross Hands Quarry SSSI, Warwickshire. In all cases, permission from the owners must be sought in advance before visiting the site.  
  
  
  
It is generally only on certain finite sites, where the resource is limited and practically irreplaceable, that irresponsible specimen collecting can cause serious damage to or even total destruction of the resource. Many sites of mineralogical importance, both in situ vein material and mine dumps, and certain fossil sites fall into this category. Such sites can be easily damaged and there are sites where the resource has been almost completely removed by collectors. Examples of finite sites where unconsented collecting activities have had serious impacts on the mineralogical interests include Hope's Nose SSSI, Torquay, Devon, Clevedon Shore SSSI, Somerset and parts of the Skiddaw Group SSSI, Cumbria.  
  
  
  
It is frequently impossible for site owners to prevent determined collectors from removing material without consent. Since January 2001, the new Countryside and Rights of Way Act gives much greater powers to take legal action against individuals who cause damage to SSSIs. While the threat of large fines may act as a deterrent, it is preferable that all collectors develop an ethical and sustainable approach to collecting. The irresponsible activities of a few people can destroy the resource for all others to study and enjoy, now and in the future.  
  
  
  
Although the resource on many finite sites is strictly limited, Natural England recognises the need to continue to use such sites for scientific gain and will generally give consent to collect, providing that there is an authentic reason to do so. There are several sites where Natural England has been involved in promoting organised responsible collecting. For example, organised collecting at Writhlington SSSI, Somerset, has resulted in numerous important fossil finds.  
  
  
  
Ultimately, it is the responsiblity of collectors to act in a responsible manner, adhering to the Best Practice Guidance for Fossil and Mineral Collecting.

![Image 18](https://www.mindat.org/images/anonymous.png)

21st Nov 2007 15:01 UTC[Bruce Grant](https://www.mindat.org/user-3574.html)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

For information on SSSI's in the UK go to the following link. Be warned however, that in checking the tick box at the bottom to access the citation data, you are acknowledging all of the constraints which are listed there !!!  
  
  
[http://www.english-nature.org.uk/text\_version/special/sssi/sssi6.asp](http://www.english-nature.org.uk/text_version/special/sssi/sssi6.asp)

![Image 19](https://www.mindat.org/avatarcache/864.jpg?1434755554)

21st Nov 2007 15:39 UTC[Lloyd Llewellyn Expert](https://www.mindat.org/user-864.html)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Any 'dates of collection' which were posted along with specimen (whoever might have collected them) pictures of mine on Mindat have recently been removed because of a similar enquiry. Similarly, any site pictures involving any activity which could be construed as dodgy, even down to those where the dog is obviously not on a public right of way.  
  
  
Although I've been 'guilty' of buying specimens from you, Colin (and jolly pleased I've been with most of them, too), I should point out that there is a distinction between collection for one's own use and collection for trade & profit. The latter is more likely, I think, to raise the ire of the conservationists, even though you might be making available material to the general public which might otherwise be lost (forever).  
  
  
I'm afraid that displaying sensitive information on a forum as public as eBay is asking for trouble in these days of the Nanny State and litigious landowners.  
  
  
(Looking forward to the day when having a mineral collection is about as socially acceptable as owning a collection of birds' eggs)

![Image 20](https://www.mindat.org/images/anonymous.png)

21st Nov 2007 16:24 UTCMRH
--------------------------

Yes, Lloyed, and perhaps someday trainspotting will be deemed far too "disruptive" as well (all far too absurd)!  
  
  
While I fully agree there ought to be preservation of SITES, to retroactively make owning materials from these sites "taboo" is going too far. We're not talking "Ivory" here, nor the level of exploitation that may trip species close to regional extinction (bird egg collecting). Surely a "different" model is required here.  
  
  
I've long considered the members here at mindat to largely consist of those who "do their part" to educate and preserve our mineralogical heritage, those who may be MOST likely, among the general population, to hold concern for preservation of sites which may be under threat, but hardly the problem! The Idea that photo's were actually removed from this site for concern of this legislation is damning evidence to it's "ill fit" to the subject at hand.  
  
  
As the question was posed in our discussions of institutional collections of late, preservation yes, but for who's benefit, if it is to be this restrictive?  
  
  
MRH

![Image 21](https://www.mindat.org/avatarcache/1.jpg?1751654012)

21st Nov 2007 16:44 UTC[Jolyon Ralph Founder](https://www.mindat.org/user-1.html)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I don't think anyone has suggested (or could legally enforce) retroactive legislation regarding specimens collected before specimen collection was prohibited within an area - the emails being sent around presumably are just warnings to remind people that current collecting is not allowed. You shouldn't have any fear about owning or selling specimens that were collected before the rules changed.  
  
  
Jolyon

![Image 22](https://www.mindat.org/avatarcache/864.jpg?1434755554)

21st Nov 2007 17:36 UTC[Lloyd Llewellyn Expert](https://www.mindat.org/user-864.html)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Although it's a different issue from SSSI's, there are certain well-known localities where, to the best of my knowledge, collecting has NEVER been allowed (by the owners, not conservationists). There are several pages of mineral photos from just one of these on Mindat.

![Image 23](https://www.mindat.org/images/anonymous.png)

21st Nov 2007 17:37 UTC[Stephen Moreton Expert](https://www.mindat.org/user-1526.html)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

When SSSIs were under the control of the DETR (now DEFRA) they told me in writing that SSSI designation does not automatically preclude collecting. When a site is designated "SSSI" a list of "Operations Liable to Damage" is gone through and boxes ticked. Each one has a number, and covers things like forestry, landfill, argiculture etc. No. 25 is specimen collecting.  
  
Unless no. 25 is ticked, then specimen collecting is not banned. Apparently only about 3 % of geological SSSIs have this designation. English Nature should be able to advise. Of course, if it turns out that your site does have this designation then I am sure that whatever specimens you have from there were collected long ago, before it became a SSSI.

![Image 24](https://www.mindat.org/images/anonymous.png)

21st Nov 2007 20:26 UTCMRH
--------------------------

Thanks Jolyon and Stephen, for clearing up the issue. Seems SSSI is similar to the protection/conditions of National Park and Historic Site designations here in the U.S., (although some folks here have also misunderstood ownership of previously collected materials along the same line as this).  
  
  
There are collection items in other disciplines where retroactive policies over legal ownership have been put in place, so I can understand the confusion. There are also some arenas, like religious and cultural "relics", where retroactive ownership policies are still not strict enough (outside institutional collections that is), nor restrictions pursued with sufficient vigor. It's an ongoing process worthy of discussion.  
  
  
Along Lloyd's line, philosophically speaking at least, here is where "I" think we bump heads between legal rights and overall justice. Imagine if a policy of "no specimen recovery" had been instituted at Tsumeb, for whatever daft reason. Perhaps they would be perfectly within their "legal" rights to do so, but what a great injustice would have been served as well. While I might tend to perceive ownership rights as a bit too restrictive/exclusive in some instances like this, unfortunately I'm likely in the minority. Most American at least, despite their democratic underpinnings, are devoutly Autocratic when it comes to land ownership, and don't give a "fig" about the commonwealth in this arena.  
  
  
I'm very happy that some measure of protection has been instituted at many sites, but surely it is upon our own shoulders to both support them, and to see that they are not too zealous, or have too many unintended negative consequences (a discussion worth having).  
  
  
  
MRH

![Image 25](https://www.mindat.org/avatarcache/864.jpg?1434755554)

22nd Nov 2007 09:17 UTC[Lloyd Llewellyn Expert](https://www.mindat.org/user-864.html)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Good to hear from you, Stephen. Hope you're back on the road to a full recovery.  
  
  
Come the Spring, we shall have to meet-up and have a day or two out-and-about together (non-'No-Collecting' SSSI's, of course!) :)  
  
  
Maybe we could set the agenda for the Old Farts for 2008?

![Image 26](https://www.mindat.org/images/anonymous.png)

22nd Nov 2007 09:56 UTC[Stephen Moreton Expert](https://www.mindat.org/user-1526.html)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hi Lloyd, the rate my bones are healing at (not at all) and the set-backs I have had (infection then a DVT) make me doubt a return to collecting anytime before next summer. I only just got out of my 3rd spell in hospital on Tuesday. I should know in January if my most recent op (bone graft) has worked or not.  
  
  
I have no qualms about collecting at SSSIs where the OLD25 designation has not been ticked. English Nature should be able to inform about the status of English SSSIs, Scottish Natural Heritage about Scottish ones (I think you'll find that the Loch Roag sapphire local is forbidden), and whatever the Welsh equivalent is can advise about Welsh locations (Tremadoc is certainly one where OLD25 applies - better to leave the minerals to the frost and rain it seems).  
  
  
Northern Ireland has ASSIs - Areas of Special Scientific Interest. As far as I am aware similar rules apply. The Dept of the Environment is in charge there. The Scawt Hill (scawtite etc) site is protected. The Mournes are also under a blanket ASSI, but collecting there is not forbidden. When I wrote to the Dept of the Environment they were refreshingly pragmatic about the Mournes - it's a huge area, the amount of vuggy granite at Diamond Rocks is enormous etc. They just prefer one to stick to boulders if possible and generally obey the country code.  
  
  
The Irish Republic has recently acquired NHAs - Natural Heritage Areas, with draconian penalities for those disturbing them. What constitutes "disturbance" is unclear. Most such locations so far are wildlife or botanical. A few fossil ones are in the pipeline. Mineral ones may follow, but as many of the traditional sites have long go been obliterated by farmers anyway, any such "protection" will be a case of closing the stable door after the horse has bolted. The famous Sheshodonnel East mine (that glorious yellow and green smithsonite on purple fluorite) became history in 2005 when the farmer bulldozed the tiny tip down the shaft and levelled the site. It is thanks to mineral collectors that many pieces were saved before that happened. Had the site been "protected" collecting would have been banned and the farmer (who detests officialdom) would have still flattened the site regardless.  
  
  
As you can tell, I tend to take a cynical attitude to "protecting" sites by banning collecting, when the real dangers come from agriculture, forestry, land reclamation etc, or simply the ravages of time. The best way to preserve minerals is to collect them while you can.

![Image 27](https://www.mindat.org/images/anonymous.png)

23rd Nov 2007 21:34 UTC[Colin Robinson](https://www.mindat.org/user-4265.html) OP
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Many thanks for all your input. Having been a collector for over 40 years I'm aware of all the potential problems we face and also most aspects of the legislation regarding SSSIs. Stephen's points are very valid. Much of the legislation is open to interpretation and as long as one is not bringing in heavy equipment or blasting outcrops I can't see much of a problem. I think the originator of the warnings about selling was merely sabre-rattling and possibly even doing it off his own back with no official sanction. The problem with bureaucrats of any kind is that they soon seem to develop an over-inflated sense of their own importance!

![Image 28](https://www.mindat.org/images/anonymous.png)

24th Nov 2007 11:58 UTC[Stephen Moreton Expert](https://www.mindat.org/user-1526.html)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

It would not surprise me if the jobsworth who rattled his sabres at Colin was indeed just acting on his own, petty volition. My inclination would be to completely ignore him. Unless caught red-handed at a "protected" site ripping it up (which, of course, we would never do), the chances of prosecution are remote. There was a case recently when a fossil collector got convicted for selling fossils from a site in Wales, but in his case he had put them on e-bay in his name and they could be matched with fresh saw marks at the site. Otherwise, how are the officials to know the specimens were not got years ago before the site got "protected"? The burden of proof is theirs', not the collector's. I vaguely remember also a fuss in Scotland when some prig from Scottish Natural Heritage accused a jeweller of illegally collecting a sapphire from the Loch Roag site. Turned out the stone had been found just outside the SSSI boundary and the jeweller threatened to sue SNH which then had to hastly retract and apologise. All very satisfying. There has also been much hullaballoo about the LDNPA's ban on collecting in the Caldbecks, but anyone who knows the area will know just how unenforceable it is. I have also been assured by collectors selling material from there that their specimens are all "old-time", "Elizabethen you know" (yes, Elizabeth II), collected "long ago" (long ago last summer perhaps?), "turn of the century" (which one?) ... When friends got a threatening letter from the LDNPA after having a photo of a very fine pyromorphite published in a well-known journal they were thrilled, and considered framing it. Needless to say the LDNPA were impotent and nothing more happened. Remember, they have to prove you guilty, you do not have to prove anything to them. There are moves now by the N. Pennines Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty Trust to curb collecting in the N. Pennines, but they have no legislative powers and so their whining can be ignored. The best way to deal with such killjoys is probably to ignore them, and if you happen to have something from a "protected" site then obviously it was collected before the site acquired its "protected" status.

# **A Bibliography of Cumbrian Coleoptera**

## **No. 8 Issue 1 August 2022**

![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/16996705327760585583/16996705327760585583.pdf-0-0.png)

#### Cumbria Biodiversity Data Centre Occasional Publication



![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/16996705327760585583/16996705327760585583.pdf-0-1.png)
_**Cumbria Biodiversity Data Centre Occasional Publication No.8 (2022**_ **)** _**1**_

### **A Bibliography of Cumbrian Coleoptera**

##### **R.W.J. Read** 43 Holly Terrace, Hensingham, Whitehaven, Cumbria, CA28 8RF. Email - jread@uwclub.net Compiled October 2020. Abstract: This document is a compilation of the relevant literature published on Cumbrian coleoptera in the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries. Keywords : bibliography, coleoptera, Cumbria, including Cumberland and Westmorland. Recommended citation : Read, R.W.J. (2022) A bibliography of Cumbrian Coleoptera. Cumbria Biodiversity Data Centre. Occasional Publications No.8 Issue 1.

### Contents


Contents 1


Introduction 2


Chronological list of publications on coleoptera in Cumbria published in the 19th, 20th

and 21st centuries. 3


Acknowledgement 73


Index of Authors 73


_**A Bibliography of Cumbrian Coleoptera                                                         2**_

### Introduction


Apart from the bibliography on the naturalist and natural history of Cumbria by Alan Armsby,
(Armsby 2015) and which contains a great many references to Cumbrian coleoptera, to date there
appears to be no published comprehensive bibliography dealing with the coleoptera of the county. A
short series of annual bibliographies compiled on a county by county basis on the coleopterous
literature of the northern counties, which included the old counties of Cumberland and
Westmorland, were published in _The Naturalist_ journal, Anon. (1888) which covered the years 1884
– 1887, and Roebuck (1892) listed the relevant publications for 1888 – 1891. The only published
bibliography dealing with the Coleoptera of a British county that this author is aware of is by Chris
Reid (Reid 1983) who compiled a list of the literature dealing with the beetles of Buckinghamshire.


This bibliography is a compilation of the relevant literature published in the 19th, 20th and 21st
centuries on those species of coleoptera known to occur in Cumbria, which mainly includes, the old
Watsonian vice counties of Cumberland 70 and Westmorland 69. It has been compiled from a large
number of journals (both national and regional), survey reports (published and unpublished), printed
books and on - line computerised documents: approximately 1,400 references are listed in the
present document. The principal national entomological journals which have been consulted are –
_The Entomologist’s Monthly_ _Magazine, The Entomologist, The Entomologist’s Record and Journal of_
_Variation_, _Entomologist’s Gazette, The Entomologist’s Annual, British journal of Entomology and_
_Natural History Society,_ and _The Coleopterist._ The main regional journals which have been checked
are _The Carlisle Naturalist, Lakeland Naturalist, Transactions of the Carlisle Natural History Society,_
_The Field Naturalist, The Naturalist (Yorkshire Naturalist Union), Birds and Wildlife in Cumbria_
_(Cumbria Naturalists Union), Transactions of the Manchester Entomological Society, Transactions of_
_the Natural History Society of Northumberland, Durham and Newcastle upon Tyne, Transactions of_
_the Tyne side Naturalist’s Field Club and Lancashire and Cheshire Fauna committee (Annual Report_
_and Reports of the Recorders)._ Several important and classic works dealing with the coleopterous
fauna of the British Isles have also been consulted: the mains ones being by Curtis (1823 – 1840),
(Fowler (1887, 1888, 1889, 1890 & 1891), Fowler & Donisthorpe (1913), and Stephens (1827 – 1835)
and (1839). These tomes contain many records of beetles that were known to occur in the county at
that time. In particular the work by John Curtis (loc cit) gives the locality details of a number of
beetles that were collected in the old county of Cumberland by the well known and eminent Carlisle
naturalist / entomologist Thomas Coulthard Heysham (1791 – 1857), and whose life and work have
been documented in detail by Hodgson (2021) and Murray (1909). The work by Stephens (1827 1835 loc cit) on British Coleoptera which was published in five volumes also contains a large number
of records of beetles from the county. In his Manual of British Coleoptera Stephens (1839 loc cit)
gives records of many beetles from Cumbria, and although he omitted the names of collectors, he
did include the old Heysham localities such as Baron Wood, Cardew Mires, Dalston Hall Woods and
Cummersdale, and he also gives 109 references to Carlisle. A great many periodicals and various
books dealing with coleoptera have been accessed via the excellent on - line digital Biodiversity
Heritage Library. This has been an extremely useful resource for tracking down the more older and
out of print literature. Also, the extensive work by Bousquet (2016) dealing with the literature on
Coleoptera published between 1875 and 1900 has also been very useful in obtaining accurate
information regarding early publications. In this bibliography no attempt has been made to
distinguish with regards the quality of the publications cited and both direct and incidental
references have been included. Also, no attempt has been made to correct any misspellings or
change any – outdated scientific names, and all references are fully cited as would be required in a
peer reviewed journal. The majority of the references listed in this bibliography relate to the recent
beetle fauna, but it also contains several references to the literature published on sub – fossil
coleoptera from the county. These references relate to beetles found in post glacial deposits from
sites, mainly around the St. Bees area of West Cumbria. A few references have also been included
that deal with the remains of beetles and other insects that were found during the extensive


_**Cumbria Biodiversity Data Centre Occasional Publication No.8 (2022**_ **)** _**3**_


archaeological excavations carried out by the York Archaeology unit at Annetwell Street and other
sites in the city of Carlisle, and at the Roman fort of Papcastle near Cockermouth.

The purchase of Skiddaw Forest is now complete
==============================================

Wednesday 18 December 2024

  

We now officially own the 3,000 acre site in the northern Lake District

          ![Image 7: Image of Skiddaw with purple heather in the foreground](https://www.cumbriawildlifetrust.org.uk/sites/default/files/styles/scaled_default/public/2024-12/Skiddaw-by-Harry-Shepherd-%288%29.jpg?itok=zrLHXQv9)

The purchase of Skiddaw Forest is now complete © Harry Shepherd

> We’ve reached another important landmark in the story of Skiddaw Forest: our purchase has formally completed. This is wonderful news, as we begin the important work of restoring this iconic site in the northern Lake District Fells
> 
> Stephen Trotter
> 
> CEO, Cumbria Wildlife Trust

We're pleased to announce that our purchase of Skiddaw Forest is now complete. This landmark is a huge win for nature and wildlife, making Skiddaw the highest nature reserve in England.

In a six-week fundraising campaign, an [incredible £1.25m was raised](https://www.cumbriawildlifetrust.org.uk/news/summit-success-we-reached-our-ps125m-goal) by the public, in support of our 100-year vision for the site. To mark the completion of the purchase, we've launched a [virtual tour of Skiddaw](https://app.lapentor.com/sphere/skiddaw-forest?scene=671014e6156e052413042e1d), now live on our website. In this video, you can find out about our plans to create a haven for wildlife over the next 100 years, from the comfort of your own home.

Prior to the fundraising campaign, we'd already secured £5 million, thanks to a long-term partnership between The Wildlife Trusts and Aviva, and additional support from charitable funders.

We can now start planning and carrying out the restoration of the site. This will include bringing back 620 acres of lost Atlantic Rainforest to the lower slopes of Skiddaw Forest. In addition, over 2,200 acres of other habitat will be restored including montane scrub, wildflower grassland, heather moorland and 992 acres of peatbogs.

**Stephen Trotter, CEO of Cumbria Wildlife Trust,** says:

_“We’ve reached another important landmark in the story of Skiddaw Forest: our purchase has formally completed. This is wonderful news, as we begin the important work of restoring this iconic site in the northern Lake District Fells._

_“We’re starting by carrying out in-depth, baseline surveys across the site, from small mammals such as otters, weasels and stoats, to the so-called ‘lower plants’ such as bryophytes, lichens and liverworts, which play a vital role in the ecosystem. In addition, we’ll survey water quality and flow rates and check the depth and erosion of the peatland. So the exciting work is already getting underway, in this long-term project which will come to maturity in the coming decades and well into the next century._

_“We’re extremely grateful to Aviva and our other funders, and to the over 7,000 members of the public who donated to the purchase of Skiddaw Forest, enabling us to take this once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to restore nature on a truly landscape scale. Thank you so much to all of you and we look forward to working with our many local partners, farmers, volunteers and others to make this vision a reality that everyone will enjoy for generations to come.”_

Fundraising continues for the restoration work on the site. Our vision is to create a mosaic of healthy, resilient and revitalised mountain habitats. The 620 acres of temperate rainforest will be created with native trees that are adapted to live in an upland landscape. Due to the altitude of planting, the trees will be low-growing and fit sympathetically with the aesthetics of the landscape.

Training of seed-collecting volunteers started in the autumn (see pictures below) and will continue next year. The native seeds will be taken to new tree-growing hubs in Plumgarths near Kendal, Cold Springs Community Nature Reserve in Penrith, and a site near Keswick where the saplings will be grown on, before eventually forming part of the new temperate rainforest at Skiddaw.

Our baseline surveys have also begun: we've been working with scientists from Cambridge University who have sampled cores of peat at Skiddaw, which they'll analyse to find out what plants and trees were growing there many years ago - see pictures below.

We'll be carrying out more baseline surveys next year and there'll also be more opportunities for community and volunteer involvement with our restoration work. Training will be provided and all facilities are designed to be accessible to all. Please keep an eye on our website.

## 54 55 57 58 66 73 78 80 83 98 99 54 Antenna 2021: 45 (2) 

Hello and welcome to Antenna 45 (2). As I’m typing this editorial over the Bank Holiday weekend, a palpable feeling of change is in the air. Insects are on the wing, my daffodils and tulips are in bloom, and our garden has just seen an extremely rare visitor – my Mother-in-Law dropping off the kids’ Easter Eggs. As we begin to ease out of lockdown, I’m even hopeful that I might still get students out to the university farms before the term is over! Other recent changes of note are that we have introduced ‘Opinion Pieces’ to Antenna (with initial offerings from Hugh Loxdale and Simon Leather), and that the George family have sampled their first ‘Cricket Cookies’ from Bug Farm Foods. If you have an opinion piece on an entomological topic that you’d like to share, we can recommend submission to ‘antenna@royensoc.co.uk’, and if you fancy treating your taste buds to something scrumptious, but with a bit more entomological content than a McVities, then my wife, my 8 and 11 year olds and I can all highly recommend https://www.bugfarmfoods.com/shop/cricket-cookies-mocha-chilli-crunch/. We’re bulging with entomological content here too. We get this issue underway, as always, with Correspondence, with Rowan Edwards’ Letter in Issue 44 (2) continuing to inspire you to write in. In her President’s Letter, Helen Roy takes the opportunity to invite applications from potential future Trustees, writing on behalf of the RES Council. As someone who’s kept Acromyrmex in the past, Stuart Reynolds’ latest Spotlight is a joy to read, looking this time at ‘Multilateral symbiosis and coevolutionary chemical warfare in fungus-farming ants’. We follow this with articles from Vazrick Nazari and Ian Hodkinson on insects in palaeolithic art and Thomas Coulthard Heysham, a Cumbrian naturalist and insect collector. Our new ‘Opinion Pieces’ comes next, covering conservatism in entomology and the combined conditions of ‘Entomyopia and Entoalexia’. This issue’s Society News continues to demonstrate how well RES meetings and events organisers have responded to lockdown restrictions and adapted to remote gatherings, with Charlie Woodrow, Max Tercel and Manuela Carnaghi clearly turning challenge into opportunity to host a very successful, and international, ‘EntoCareers’. Erica McAlister’s remote Verrall Lecture was also a global hit, attracting 230 attendees from sixteen different countries (with a review of Erica’s recently-published ‘ The Inside Out of Flies ’ provided towards the end of this issue). For his latest Honorary Fellow Interview with Jane Memmott, Peter Smithers opted for an ‘al fresco’ Zoom alternative, swapping the computer screen for a park bench in Bristol. Society News also features an interesting overview of the RES Insect Identification Service, exploring whether Covid-19 has had an impact on use of this service. Sadly, we also report the passing of a number of eminent entomologists, with obituaries included for Alan Clements, Charles Baker, Steve Wratten and RES Vice-Patron, Lord Selborne. Past RES President Walter (Wally) Blaney also passed away towards the end of 2020, with an obituary expected for 45 (3). Finally, we’d like to express huge thanks again to all of our authors and contributors for their ongoing efforts to keep the copy coming despite Covid. Please do keep on sending us those submissions – be they Letters, Articles, Reports or (from now on) Opinion Pieces. Dave George

# Correspondence 

# Linnaean taxonomic system 

Dear Editor, In his letter about “errors in the Linnaean taxonomic system” affecting nomenclatural database architecture ( Antenna 44 (4): 151-152), Rowan Edwards said, “Until the Linnaean System is placed into 3NF, attempts to create solutions which rely on a 3NF system will continue to fail.” The “Linnaean System” (as codified for insects in the ICZN, International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (iczn.org)) is a frequent ‘whipping boy’ for people with complaints about taxonomic stability and desires for metaphysical certainty, but such complaints are often misplaced, as is the case here. Edwards’ letter describes revised circumscriptions of taxa due to new taxonomic research (in his example, the splitting of 

Nomada facilis from Nomada integra in 2017). No nomenclatural system can foresee the future and guarantee the stability of names against the progress of scientific discovery. For this reason, the ICZN wisely does not stipulate any rules regarding the circumscription of specific, generic, or family-level taxa. The names Nomada integra and Nomada facilis refer to individual specimens, which are, in fact, unique identifiers for those names in zoological nomenclature. How taxonomists, conservation biologists, software engineers, etc., choose to apply those names to additional specimens is not a nomenclatural problem. It is certainly a nuisance, from the perspective of a database manager or curator, to have to make changes in your data or collection labels when taxonomy advances. But just as a cartographer cannot stop changes of place names or movement of borders, and therefore needs to revise maps from time to time, so the system of nomenclature we use for a taxon is (one hopes) up-to-date and correct at the time that taxon’s name is published. After that, all bets are off. And, just as what was Poland in 1930 is not the same as what is Poland today, so an insect identified in 1930 might not be considered to belong to the same species in 2021. Such changes are not “errors”, just concepts that have evolved over time. Also worth observing is that the potential for nomenclatural change is a good reason to collect and preserve voucher specimens. If all that is available as a ‘record’ is a sighting or field ID, then that data point becomes marooned in the taxonomic context of the time the observation was made. For example, if Nomada facilis is indeed a distinct species from Nomada integra ,then any unvouchered record of ‘ Nomada integra ’ prior to 2017 will be eternally ambiguous. By contrast, specimens in a museum collection can be examined and reclassified, as needed. Andrew Brower, Ph.D., F.R.E.S. Assistant Director, National Identification Services (NIS) USDA APHIS PPQ Plant Health Programs 

# Ovipositors of sawflies 

Dear Editors, I am an engineer working for my PhD at Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh. I am studying the ovipositors of sawflies in order to learn new principles for the design of cutting tools. One of my supervisors is Prof. Julian Vincent, a Fellow of the R.E.S., who suggested I should write to Antenna .One approach is to study the movements of the insect while it saws into the plant. If anyone has film of a member of the Symphyta ovipositing, and will share it, I would be very grateful if they please contact me at mv2003@hw.ac.uk. Yours sincerely, Martí Verdaguer Mallorquí 

# Whitefly wanted 

Dear Editors, I am Mia Graham, a 1st year PhD student at the University of Stirling. My research is exploring the likelihood that greenhouse whitefly, Trialeurodes vaporariorum , will evolve resistance to commercial biological control agents (fungal biopesticides and parasitoid wasps) and what the evolutionary basis for any resistance might be. To carry out my research I require whitefly samples from across the UK. If you could help and provide whitefly, please contact me at mg72@stir.ac.uk and follow me on twitter @entomia. Yours sincerely, Mia Graham 56 Antenna 2021: 45 (2) 

# Insect Pests in Historic Houses and Museums 

Dear Editor, Readers of Antenna may be interested to know that a new poster “Insect Pests in Historic Houses and Museums” has recently been published by English Heritage. The poster is the third in the series which started in 1998 with “Insect Pests found in Historic Houses and Museums” with support from the Museums and Galleries Commission and Central Science Laboratory (CSL). It was well received by museums and the heritage world who could use it as simple guide to identify the pests they found in their collections and buildings. The poster was used widely in the UK and other countries and by 2008, over 5,000 copies had been distributed. It was then decided that the poster needed a major revision to include more recently established pests such as the Guernsey carpet beetle Anthrenus sarnicus and the Brown carpet beetle or ‘Vodka beetle’ Attagenus smirnovi. The colour and layout of the poster, re-titled “A Helpful Guide to Insect Pests Found in Historic Houses and Museums”, was changed and new images of the pests were used, supplied by Fera/Collections Trust. This poster proved very popular, and over the next 10 years, 25,000 printed copies were distributed to 15 countries; it was also available to download from the English Heritage website. In 2019, the poster once again required a revision to include more new pests, such as the grey silverfish Ctenolepisma longicaudatum . English Heritage had already commissioned a series of exceptional insect images from the Oxford University Museum of Natural Heritage (OUMNH) for their book “Pests in Houses Great and Small”, published in 2018, and these were used in the new poster edition. The opportunity was taken to completely change the layout of the poster to focus on the image of a cutaway infested house which had also been commissioned for the book. The insects could then be linked to their favoured environments and food, making the poster more intuitive and useful to the non-specialist. The new poster is proving to be very useful in generating interest in insects, what they eat and where they live. It has also helped to highlight the differences between pests, invasive species and beneficial ones. David Pinniger, Cookham, Berks 

The poster is now available online at https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/siteassets/home/learn/conservation/collections-advice— guidance/eh-pest-poster-fin_web_lr.pdf Printed copies are available from English Heritage Customer Services quoting the Product number 506506. 0370 3331181 · customers@english-heritage.org.uk Antenna 2021: 45 (2) 57 

# Letter from the President – Become a Trustee – 

Helen Roy (on behalf of Council) 

My first year as President of the Royal Entomological Society is almost over. I have worked with the most incredible team of Trustees and staff and mostly managed to navigate the bye-laws (although admittedly often with lots of assistance)! It has been a very busy year for Council and the wider Society. There have been lots of changes (including to the bye-laws!) and so many highlights. From celebrations through the virtual National Insect Week and sharing stories in entomology (see Antenna 45 (1)) to the many wonderful Special Interest Group Meetings and inspiring Student and Early Career Entomologist Event and all the many and varied Society publications, including our fantastic Society magazine. Trustees, committee members, special interest group convenors, regional secretaries, editors, reviewers, judging panels for RES awards – so many people, including all of you as members, give time as volunteers to ensure that the Royal Entomological Society is a thriving community. It is a privilege to be part of the Trustee team overseeing the work of our Society through the Council. There are currently eleven Trustees. Their dedication to the Society is incredible. Their commitment to entomology and the membership is simply exceptional. I have benefitted enormously from their kindness and friendship. There has been lots to do but much laughter and joy along the way. Perhaps you might like to have more involvement with the Society? We are pleased to announce some exciting opportunities, the first of which will be a more modern and inclusive way of recruiting new Trustees from the membership, starting soon. There will be several opportunities, including President-Elect, Treasurer, Meetings, Publications, and a brand new position of Early Career Trustee. I warmly encourage all of you to consider applying for these places on our Council. You have to belong to the Society but you don't have to be a Fellow, or a Professor, or be a regular contributor to our journals. The Society needs Trustees who: • care deeply about our Society, and will champion it • will support other Trustees and staff, and challenge them constructively too • want to be part of developing and implementing a strategy for the next five years • can analyse information and consider recommendations, and make the best decisions for our Society • are willing to engage with essential but non-entomological topics such as finance, sustainability, looking after our staff, and looking after The Mansion House • are willing to give up time, and take on responsibility. Council is a place where Members and Fellows work together to make our Society successful and nurturing. All the Trustees enjoy their role, and find it fulfilling and rewarding. Any of us would be delighted to chat with potential candidates about the commitment required, and about any aspect of being a Trustee. There is a section on the website (www.royensoc.co.uk/ becomeatrustee) dedicated to recruiting new Trustees. This gives details of the positions where Council (and RES Committees) needs new people, and how to apply. Please take a look at this site now, and revisit it regularly as further opportunities will arise. We will also provide regular updates through our newsletters. The roles will start in August 2021, at the AGM. I would like to take this opportunity to thank all the current Trustees for their incredible dedication and commitment to the Society – it is such a privilege to work with them all. The Society is committed to equality, diversity and inclusion and here three women from the wider group of amazing trustees share insights and encourage you to consider stepping forward. Gia Aradottir (National Institute of Agricultural Botany): 

For me it is a great privilege to be a Trustee of the Society. I have been a Member since I was a student, hugely enjoy being involved with a friendly community of other entomologists, and feel I have benefitted from the experience of others in the Society who have been incredibly generous with knowledge and advice. This is why I wanted to become more involved with the Society and became a Trustee. It has been very rewarding to work with a great team of Trustees, staff and committee members on all aspects of the promotion and development of entomological science. There are so many different areas to get involved with, so if anyone is interested in joining a committee or Council as a Trustee, I would highly recommend putting your name forward. 

Rebecca Farley-Brown (Field Studies Council): I’ve enjoyed my spells as a Trustee, it is so interesting to see the breadth and diversity of work across the Society and I particularly enjoy looking at ways we can promote insects to everybody. All the Trustees bring a variety of experiences to the role. We learn so much from one another and it is such a privilege to work together putting the membership first in all our decision-making. 

Julie North (Entomologist, Consultant Ecotoxicologist and Artist): Being a Trustee of this prestigious Society, is for me an honour and a privilege. I feel extremely fortunate that in these times of challenge and change, I’ve been able to work alongside such a dedicated group of people to make a meaningful and lasting difference to the Society, both in terms of its governance and its ongoing development to become a progressive, dynamic and inclusive organisation of which we can all be proud. For anyone who has a love of insects, works in the field of entomology and/or would really like to make a commitment to serving the Society, my advice would be to come forward and have your voice heard – a very warm welcome awaits! 58 Antenna 2021: 45 (2) 

# Consider her ways! Multilateral symbiosis and coevolutionary chemical warfare in fungus-farming ants 

# RESEARCH SPOTLIGHT 

The entomological origin of agriculture? 

It’s a familiar trope that insects invented farming long before humans existed. By ‘farming’ I mean the deliberate cultivation of other organisms for food; several major insect groups are said to be farmers because they cultivate crops of fungi. Mueller et al. (2005) and Biedermann & Vega (2020) attempt to define insect farming very carefully in terms of exactly what ‘cultivate’ means, but to me this word sufficiently conveys the essence of this purposive activity. As we will see later, I myself think it’s useful to consider agriculture as a kind of niche construction (Rowly-Conwy & Layton, 2011) in which the farmer either consciously or unconsciously engineers the farm ecosystem so that it becomes a receptive niche for a “farmed” crop. My own interest in this topic arose from thinking about the apparent unsustainability of our present intensive human agriculture (Pretty, 2008). Since insects have been farming for at least tens of millions of years, their version of farming is obviously sustainable; it seems to me that there is much to learn from insect farmers. Fungus-cultivation has arisen on at least nine separate occasions during insect evolution (Mueller et al., 2005). Ambrosia beetles (perhaps 3,000 species of bark beetles within the families Curculionidae and Scolytidae) account for seven of these, while termites (330 species in 11 genera of Macrotermitinae) appear to have made the transition to farming only once. But the rosette for agricultural success among insects inevitably goes to the Attini, a tribe of myrmicine ants restricted to the Americas that includes 19 extant genera and more than 240 species, all of which cultivate and depend on what appears to be a monoculture of a single fungal species (but see below for more about monocultures). All the Attini are symbiotically associated with parasol mushrooms (basidiomycete fungi from the genus Leucocoprinus ), from which the colony derives almost all their nutrition. 

Leaf-cutting ants and their fungi 

The fungus-farming way of life, which appears to have arisen in the Attini on a single occasion around 55-65 MY ago (Mueller et al., 2018), represents an evolutionary innovation that allowed entry to a previously unoccupied fungus-farming niche. Among the attines, there is a deep phylogenetic divide between the lower and higher attines. The more numerous species of the lower Attini produce smaller individual ants, have smaller colonies and are associated with more diverse fungi with functionally diploid cells and typical mycelial structure; most are capable of living alone outside of the ant symbiosis. The higher Attini, by contrast, are physically larger insects living in larger colonies; importantly, their nest fungi are derived from just two clades, are highly polyploid and asexual, and their hyphae have modified tips (“gongylidia”) that supply the ants with highly nutritious food. It has been natural to suppose that this deep systematic divide reflects the consequence of association with more cooperative, more “cultivable” fungi. 

Stuart Reynolds 

Department of Biology and Biochemistry, University of Bath Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways and be wise. 

The Bible (King James version), Proverbs 6:6. Antenna 2021: 45 (2) 59 

Not quite congruent with this systematic division into lower and higher attines is another evolutionary transition; in all lower Attini, but also in the less highly derived higher attine genus Trachmyrmex , the ants supply their associated fungus with only dead or decayed plant materials. But the true leaf-cutting ants, a group of ~50 species from only two highly derived genera, Atta (Fig. 1A) and Acromyrmex, feed their own cultivated fungus exclusively on fresh, often green plant material, gathered specifically for this purpose using modified jaws that resemble a gardener’s pruning shears (Fig. 1B). Their societies are based on more numerous physical castes (Fig. 1C), reflecting the diverse requirement of cutting and transporting leaves, cultivating the fungus garden, and defending the nest. The leafcutters appear to have split from the rest of the tribe ~14-24 MY ago. Today, leafcutters are said to be responsible for about 25% of all herbivory in Neotropical forest ecosystems (Swanson et al., 2019). Their subterranean nests (Fig.1E) are huge, occupying areas up to 600 m 2, and are excavated down to depths of up to 15 m; each nest may contain millions of workers stripping the leaves from vegetation for up to 250 m all around to feed hundreds of separate fungus garden chambers within the nest. There, the ants engage in fungus-cultivation (Fig. 1F), cleaning and macerating the cut leaves, depositing enzyme-rich rectal fluid to initiate digestion, tending and weeding fungal mycelium, removing gongylidia to feed themselves and their larvae, and finally removing spent leaf material and depositing it in refuse dumps. The ability to utilise freshly cut plant materials as fungus-food may have been driven by a new association of the ants with a more derived fungus that could make use of this material. The variety of lifestyles of the attine-associated fungi certainly follows a trend in which increasingly derived species have committed themselves ever more completely to fungus farming, leading to the huge ecological success of the leaf-cutting ants. The evolution of these fungi is complicated; fungi that are clearly members of the species L. gongylophorus 

can be assigned to different strains, or cultivars, which can be clearly differentiated using DNA techniques. These cultivars were formerly thought to be strongly associated with particular attine species. Now, however, it appears that there is appreciable systematic crossover. There are five principal clades of L. gongylophorus cultivars (Mueller et al ., 2018) .

Clade A is mostly found in the nests of the true leafcutters, 

Atta and Acromyrmex spp., but is also associated with some nests from the more advanced, but non-leaf-cutting ant 

Trachymyrmex. Clade B was formerly thought to be associated only with Trachymyrmex , but has now been found to be present in some true leafcutter nests. “Clade 1cultivars”, “Yeast cultivars” and “Clade 2 cultivars”, collectively described as “lower attine cultivars”, previously thought to be associated only with basal attine genera, are now realised also to occur in more derived Trachymyrmex 

species. Moreover, a number of probably separate 

Leucocoprinus species occur exclusively in the nests of these basal attine species. I have described this fluid systematic situation in some detail because, as has been pointed out by Mueller et al.
