Some entomological history 

That leaf-cutting ants have a special relationship with fungi has been known for almost 150 years. The British mining engineer Thomas Belt (1873) was first to propose, in his splendid book The Naturalist in Nicaragua, the idea that leafcutters do not eat the plant materials they carry back to their nest, but instead derive their nutrition from fungi that grow upon the cut leaves. In describing this he specifically drew attention to the idea that the ants are practising a form of agriculture: “…they are in reality mushroom growers and eaters ”. Interestingly, there’s a connection here with Charles Darwin. Belt was a good naturalist and, although not a member of Darwin’s inner circle, corresponded with him regularly (you can read their letters in the wonderful Darwin Correspondence Project, https://www.darwinproject.ac.uk/). Belt’s book was published on 18 th December 1873, and over Christmas at his family home in Down, Kent, Darwin devoured the book in just a few days. Predictably, the great man was much interested in Belt’s theory of fungus-farming by insects and was probably the first to grasp its evolutionary significance. Hence, on 1 st 

January 1874, Darwin wrote in a letter to his long-standing supporter and frequent correspondent, Fritz Müller (then resident at Blumenau, Santa Caterina, Brazil): “I have directed to be sent to you Belt’s Nicaragua , which seems to me the best Nat. Hist. book of travels ever published. Pray look to what he says about the leaf-carrying ants storing the leaves up in a minced state to generate mycelium, on which he supposes that the larvæ feed. Now could you open the stomachs of these ants & examine the contents so as to prove or disprove this remarkable hypothesis? ”Müller did as was requested, replying on 20 th April 1874 (remember the time that the post would have taken): “ As to leaf-cutting ants, I have always held the same view which is proposed by Mr. Belt, viz. that they feed upon the fungus growing on the leaves they carry into their nests, though I had not yet examined their stomachs. Now I find that the contents of the stomach are colourless, showing under the microscope some minute globules, probably the spores of the fungus. I could find no trace of vegetable tissue which might have been derived from the leaves they gather; and this, I think, confirms Mr. Belt’s hypothesis. ”Darwin sent on Müller’s letter (which was mostly about other matters) to the editor of Nature , where it was duly published (Müller, 1874). One wonders whether Darwin thought that this was a good way of provoking interest in the ant–fungus symbiosis, without specifically drawing attention to his own thoughts on the matter. Darwin had for some time been concerned about his inability to see how altruism could evolve under natural selection. In The Origin of Species he had apprehensively commented: “ Natural selection cannot possibly produce any modification in any one species exclusively for the good of another species... If it could be proved that any part of the structure of any one species had been formed for the exclusive good of another species, it would annihilate my theory...” (Darwin, 1859, pp: 200-201). In early 1874 he was in the process of preparing the second edition of his book 

The Descent of Man (Darwin, 1874) and was much concerned about this problem. In the case of leafcutters, he may well not have recognised that the transfer of nourishment from the fungus to the ants is in fact an example of mutualism rather than fungal altruism. As far as I know, Darwin never wrote about leafcutters in his own work. Interestingly, Alfred Russel Wallace, that other notable nineteenth century alumnus of a South American field trip, also read Belt’s book immediately on publication, and contributed a long book review (it ran to almost 3,000 words) to Nature , which by mentioning Belt’s idea about leafcutters became the first published mention of insect fungus farming (Wallace, 1874 – it is dated 22 January). Unlike Darwin, he was grudging in his appreciation of Belt’s book, commenting that “ we sincerely trust that the author may soon find himself in a position to work more systematically at some of those branches of science which he has here touched upon ”. In three pages, Wallace devotes only a few words to Belt’s fungus-farming hypothesis. He briefly says of the discovery: “…he arrives at the conclusion that the ants do not feed on the leaves which they gather in such enormous quantities, but that they use them to form beds for the growth of a minute fungus on which they and their young live” ; one senses that he was probably sceptical of Belt’s conclusion. The nineteenth century’s other great evolutionist evidently did not see fungus-farming as a problem for the theory of evolution. 

A fungus monoculture? 

Belt, dying at only 45 years of age in 1878, did not survive to investigate leafcutter biology any further. 18 years elapsed before the topic was taken up again, but it then matured rapidly. In 1892 two amateur naturalists resident in Trinidad, J.E. Tanner and J.H. Hart (a second-hand account of their work is given in Anon, 1893) separately reported that they had been able to watch “parasol ants” ( Atta cephalotes ) in the act of eating the fungus (notice that neither Belt nor Müller had claimed to have seen this). In the same year, Müller's nephew, the mycologist Alfred Möller (1893), also reported the same thing and went on to describe the fungus in considerable detail. So far no-one had mentioned the idea of a nutritional symbiosis between ant and fungus. Thus, it was important that Möller particularly noted that the tips of fungal hyphae in leafcutter nests were modified into structures apparently specially formed for the ants to eat. Another crucial element in the story was to discover how the leafcutter nest first acquires its fungus; von Ihering (1898) was the first to report that virgin queens leaving the nest for their mating flight carry a small piece of mycelium in their infrabuccal pocket, so that the fungus is deliberately vertically transmitted to the new nest. The whole “fungus farming” story was synthesised by William Morton Wheeler (1907; 1910) who evidently considered that leafcutters and their associated garden fungus had by now been proven to be “true symbionts”. It is evident that Wheeler considered that term to be synonymous with mutualism, and by this he meant that shared materials produced shared rewards. 

Mutualism: exchanged gifts and shared rewards 

The essence of Wheeler’s “true symbiosis” between leaf-cutting ants and the garden fungus is that the fungus allows the ants to consume some of its own biomass in return for provision by the ants of plant leaves for its own nutrition. For such a mutualism to persist, the cost of cooperating must be less than the gain for each participant. The trick, like a clever birthday present, is to supply something that is inexpensive to the donor but of great value to the recipient. In this case, the ants continuously supply the fungus with freshly collected leaves and other plant material. Since the ants can’t digest fresh plant materials on their own (no ants are autonomously herbivorous), providing bits of plant is a gift that costs nothing except the energy expended on going out and getting them, and possibly incurring additional risks of predation and parasitism (leafcutters are specifically parasitised by phorid flies – Bragança et al., 2016). In return the fungus gives itself. It produces special hyphae, rich in carbohydrates, lipids, amino acids and other soluble nutrients, which can be used by the ants either to fuel their own activity or feed to their offspring. It’s true that this is potentially expensive, but the supply of leaves is under the control of the ants, which unlike the fungus are mobile so they can easily supply asuperabundance of food for the fungus. That both partners make a good profit is shown by the fact that both ants and fungus rapidly increase in biomass once a nest has been established. In the longer term, nests proliferate and higher attines eventually dominate neotropical food chains. This is evolutionary success writ large. But a dependent mutualism also involves sacrificing ecological potential. In this case, the ants give up flexibility of diet, becoming almost completely dependent on the fungus for their food. They also rely on the fungus to detoxify the secondary defensive chemicals that are so commonly produced by plants; the ants appear to have reduced their complement of detoxification genes (Nygaard et al., 2011), while the fungus has expanded its own detox set (De Fine Licht et al ., 2013). An obvious sacrifice made by L. gongylophorus is that of genetic diversity. The fungal cultivars associated with higher Attini have multiple haploid nuclei per cell (i.e. they are functionally variably polyploid) and as a result they cannot reproduce sexually, effectively preventing genetic interchange between clonal lineages of the fungus. Differing clonal strains of fungus, in some cases even from the same ant species, achieve self-recognition through the use of different molecular markers on their surface, repelling strains from different colonies. Because leafcutters live at high density, it is always possible for ants to encounter cultivars of garden fungus from different colonies, but should these strains be accidentally introduced to the nest they are rejected, because the ants maintain their own fungus strain’s ability to distinguish self and non-self by inoculating the fungus garden with rectal fluid containing the resident fungus’s own self-recognition markers, thereby suppressing invaders before they can grow (Poulsen & Boomsma, 2005). Multi-clone fungus gardens have never been observed; such an outcome is predicted by evolutionary theory (Leigh, 2010) as a means of restraining the potential for cheating (i.e. taking more than their fair share of the mutualism’s proceeds). Associated with polyploidy is the inability of the fungus to reproduce sexually; this also restrains genetic diversity. The fact that the fungi are polyploid and asexual regardless of the symbiont ant species tells us that the mutualism between L. gongylophorus and the Attini probably arose only once. But the ploidy of the fungus increases with progressive domestication, and the fungus strains associated with higher attines are markedly more polyploid than are those of the lower Attini (Kooij et al., 2015). Why is this? One possibility is that having multiple copies of the genome increases the potential for using alternative alleles of adaptive genes to allow the exploitation of a wider range of resources (Albertin & Marullo, 2012). The parallel between the polyploidy of the leafcutter fungus and that of the crop plants of human agriculture is striking (Renny-Byfield & Rendel, 2014). 

A new paradigm 

So far, I have retold Wheeler’s classic story, in which Atta and 

Acromyrmex ants preside as “farmers” over a symbiotic fungal “monoculture”. This idea was introduced by Möller (1893), and the “m” term was still in use when Hölldobler and Wilson (1990) described, in their magisterial survey The Ants, how the ants engage in various mechanical and chemical “weeding” activities to remove invading microorganisms, in essentially the same way as they groom each other when practising “social immunity” to potential pathogens (Cremer 

et al., 2007). Emphasis was laid on the secretion by the metapleural glands of the worker ants of chemicals such as phenylacetic acid (antibacterial), and 3-hydroxydecanoic acid (antifungal), often described as being used by the ants as a kind of disinfectant to control unwanted microbes. The implication is one of top-down agriculture, much like that practised by humans, in which farmers attempt to eliminate weeds, and crop pests and diseases through their own efforts. Being ants, of course, leafcutter farmers are always described as being busy, taking “meticulous care” of their crops. Fernández-Marin et al. (2009) indeed noted that when non-mutualist fungi are present, the ants can spend almost all of their time grooming. But even as Hölldobler and Wilson (1990) were writing, the monoculture story was about to come unravelled; over the last 30 years, as knowledge of ant fungus farming has deepened, what had previously looked like a straightforward bilateral mutualism no longer appears so simple. In the 1990s it was realised that that the world of the leafcutter is not after all a bilateral symbiosis between ant and fungus as Wheeler had described and research into this interesting question quickly intensified. There are many more recent accounts, among them two books solely about leafcutters by Wirth et al. (2003) and Hölldobler and Wilson (2010). The literature on leaf-cutting ants now runs easily to thousands of papers. Among these, reviews by Currie et al. 

(2003), Mueller et al. (2005) and Heine et al. (2018) stand out, but there are far too many others for me to list them all here. Reflecting this, studies on the domestic economy of leaf-cutting ants have emphasised three important ways in which we now know that fungus farming by ants differs from human agriculture. First, the agricultural ecosystem of the ants is more complex than the typical human farmer’s field; leafcutters do not aim for a monoculture at all. Second, rather than being a top-down system regulated by the farmer, the ant-farmed fungus garden appears to be a bottom-up collaboration in which the key players are mutualistic microbial symbionts. Most recently, the long-term resilience of this multilateral mutualism to invasion by parasites derives (perhaps surprisingly) from its ability to recruit new beneficial partners from outside, and from the ability of the members of its microbiome to share traits through horizontal gene transfer. Key findings that led to this scientific revolution were described in two papers from Cameron Currie, then at the University of Toronto, Canada. In the first of these (Currie et 

Antenna 2021: 45 (2) 61 al., 1999a), it was revealed that an ascomcycete fungus of the genus Escovopsis is a specialist necrotrophic parasite of L. gongylophorus , being found in a significant proportion of nests of all leaf-cutting ants. Several species of Escovopsis have now been distinguished, as well as one in a new genus 

Escovopsioides , all ant-associated (Augustin et al., 2013). When attending ants are absent from colonies with Escovopsis the garden fungus is overgrown by the parasite in only 1 or 2 days. When experimentally introduced to nests, the parasite causes serious damage, and is in some cases lethal to the colony. It has subsequently been shown that Escovopsis not only directly consumes L. gongylophorus , but additionally secretes multiple diverse antibiotics that are toxic not only to the garden fungus, but also to beneficial bacteria in the leafcutter microbiome (see below), and in one case to the insects themselves (Heine 

et al ., 2018). Unlike the garden fungus, which is vertically transmitted, however, Escovopsis is not detectable in newly founded nests; although there is extensive genetic variation between isolates of Escovopsis , this does not correlate either with ant species or L. gongylophorus isolate, showing that transmission of the parasite between nests is horizontal, probably being acquired from the external refuse heaps of their own and other nests (Augustin et al., 2013). 

Escovopsis thus appears to be a chronic problem for leafcutters. It has all the characteristics of an originally obscure agricultural pest that has greatly prospered from the increase in frequency of its host due to the spread of farming. What defences does the leafcutter fungus-farming system use to control it? In the other landmark leafcutter paper of that year, Currie et al. (1999b) showed that all attines are associated with an additional symbiotic partner, a novel actinobacterium soon dubbed Pseudonocardia, which secretes multiple antibiotics specifically preventing growth of Escovopsis (reviewed by Batey, 2020). Like the pest fungus itself, it appears that this biological pest control agent was adopted into the leafcutter mutualism soon after the outset of attine agriculture. This innovation amounts to the installation of aprophylactic public-health protection system. Like human public health systems, however, it has a cost. The additional symbiont consumes resources that would otherwise have been available to the original bilateral pair of mutualists, while there are also trade-off costs connected with modifying ant development and behaviour in order to cultivate the more complex mutualistic community. One such cost is the modification of the ant’s body as a 

Pseudonocardia carrier, as is seen in Acromyrmex (but not 

Atta ) workers. Thread-like chains of the bacteria’s cells are carried by the ants in specially adapted cuticular crypts from which they grow out all over the body surface (Fig. 1D) (Currie et al., 2006). It is possible that this is a co-evolved adaptation that acts principally to allow the vertical transmission of a single strain, encouraging mutualistic co-evolution. But the crypts are not just bacterial receptacles; exocrine glands situated directly under the crypts supply the symbiont with nutritional resources. It is possible that this secretory adaptation (which itself is costly) not merely provides resources to encourage the symbiont, but actually allows the ant to regulate the actinobacterium’s growth through control of its nutrition, thereby reserving the use of its antibiotics to times when they are most needed. This would minimise selection pressure on the pest, reducing the likelihood of resistance. The ant might monitor the need to supply materials to the actinobacterium simply by detecting reduced nutrient flow to itself from the fungus garden, or perhaps as part of a physiological stress response. It is interesting that the larger, even more highly derived Atta 

leafcutters do not possess these crypts, and it has been shown that members of this genus instead engage more heavily in grooming and metapleural gland secretions when challenged with Escovopsis and other fungi (Fernandez-Marin et al., 2009). Interestingly, in Atta , there is some evidence that Pseudonocardia may live deep within the body, perhaps in deep cuticular pockets (Marsh et al., 

2013). In such an environment, antibiotic secretion by the 

Pseudonocardia symbiont might be controlled even more effectively than in the surface crypts of Acromyrmex .

Sole reliance on a single Pseudonocardia -derived antibiotic as a defensive agent against Escovopsis would not be a good strategy; it is likely to be defeated in the end, either because a locally tolerated strain of the parasite would eventually evolve resistance to the antibiotic, or because a new strain of the parasite that is already resistant would be encountered. Since leafcutter nests are long-lived (ten years or more), a more flexible defence plan is needed. The most obvious way forward would be for the defensive symbiont to secrete several different antibiotics. Ideally, all of these antibiotics would be used simultaneously, or at least in varying succession. Resistance would be much less likely to evolve under such a regime. Pseudonocardia does indeed secrete more than one antibiotic. Fascinatingly, a genetic mechanism that can apparently produce a large range of antibiotics has now been discovered in both Pseudonocardia 

and Streptomyces bacteria associated with Acromyrmex octospinosus (Seipke et al. , 2011; Pathak et al., 2019). In each species, the genes required to make multiple structural variants of a single antibiotic are present in multiple gene clusters. Each cluster has a set of “core” genes responsible for the antibiotic molecule’s common structural core, but also incorporates other variable genes that are responsible for directing the synthesis of different antibiotic analogues. Each gene cluster thus appears to specify a different antibiotic. In addition to the polyene fungicide Nystatin P, Pseudonocardia 

also secretes multiple, structurally similar depsipeptide antimicrobials such as dentigerumycin, gerumycin A, gerumycin B, and gerumycin C. The sequence similarity of the encoding gene clusters suggests they may all have originated from a single ancestral cluster. Remarkably, the leafcutter’s facultative beneficial symbiont Streptomyces has no fewer than 14 very similar, but non-identical, versions of a gene cluster (each containing 15-17 genes) encoding structural variants of the very toxic antifungal Antimycin A. It’s not yet clear whether a single Pseudonocardia or 

Streptomyces strain can manufacture all of the possible antibiotics at the same time, or whether there is some kind of mutually inhibitory switching system. The importance of these gene clusters in the defence of the mutualism is clearly shown by a population genomic study by Caldera et al. (2019) on Pseudonocardia from the Central American lower attine species, Apterostigma dentigerum . This study revealed evidence of local geographic mosaic adaption to co-evolved Escovopsis populations, and also that, despite limited genetic variation in the actinobacterium’s core genome, the sequences of the antibiotic synthesising gene clusters are highly variable, having evidently undergone selective sweeps, presumably due to antagonistic coevolution with Escovopsis .Another possibility would be for the mutualist leafcutter system to recruit additional strains of beneficial microbes into its microbiome should the opportunity arise. One can easily imagine that Pseudonocardia strain-swapping might be advantageous in the event of an Escovopsis outbreak, for example. According to Poulsen et al. (2005), however, different strains of Pseudonocardia cannot coexist within a single colony of higher attine ants, implying the existence of competition between actinobacterial strains. Sure enough, 

Pseudonocardia strains are found to secrete antibiotics that inhibit the growth of other conspecific strains. Such an outcome is predicted by orthodox evolutionary theory of mutualism, in which it is against the interests of a symbiont to share its mutualist niche with others (Leigh, 2010). Exactly as predicted, tolerance between Pseudonocardia 

strains is better if the two are closely related. Invasion of an existing healthy symbiosis by a new strain of antibiotic-producing actinobacterium is therefore unlikely. It is possible, however, that if the resident Pseudonocardia species has already been depleted by antibacterial agents secreted by a particular strain of Escovopsis , then the mutualist cooperative might be able to adopt a different and better-defended environmental Pseudonocardia strain, to replace it. Alternatively, completely different antibiotic-secreting bacteria might take the place of the original strain of 

Pseudonocardia , should this be necessary. The microbiome of the ants’ farming mutualism sometimes also contains other bacterial and fungal species that are not always present, even in a single ant species in a particular location. Antibiotic-secreting actinobacteria of other genera such as 

Streptomyces are known to occur in leafcutter fungus gardens. Since these non-core organisms may help to defend the mutualistic farming system against invasion by 

Escovopsis , it would be advantageous if there existed some system that enabled them to be recruited when needed. Other even less closely related beneficial bacterial and fungal species have also been documented in leafcutter nests. In one example, a member of the Gram-positive bacterial 

Burkholderia cepacia complex, a group of soil organisms that frequently produce antibiotics, was found to be present in >50% of Brazilian Atta sexdens colonies. This organism secretes an unknown antifungal agent that inhibits growth of Escovopsis and several other fungi, but which does not adversely affect L. gongylphorus (Santos et al., 2004). Such additional facultative symbionts cannot be obligatorily required to defend the garden fungus against pest attack, because they are not always present, but they may possibly contribute to prophylactic defence against Escovopsis and other ‘weedy’ microfungi. Mattoso et al. (2013) have pointed out that additional non-core microbiome members of this type may contribute fitness to the ant partners quite separately from the agricultural mutualism by protecting the insects against disease-causing organisms such as entomopathogenic fungi. This incidentally suggests one possible evolutionary route to mutualism that does not depend on immediate adoption of an agricultural lifestyle. Since Currie’s ground-breaking papers of 1999, much has been learned. For example, we now know the chemical identities of many (but certainly not all) of the numerous antibiotics concerned. There is a good account of the relevant antibiotic chemistry in Batey (2020). 

Assembly of the beneficial microbiome: the screening model 

The recognition that mature ant–fungus mutualist systems contain multiple additional strains of microbes that are essential to protect the system from parasitic invasion focuses attention on how the founding queen, with her plug of matrilineal garden-fungus, initially inoculates the microbiome of her own newly-formed fungus garden with the necessary, additional “right” microbes. We would like to know not only how these organisms are encouraged, but also how the “wrong” microbes are excluded. 

Antenna 2021: 45 (2) 63 Goes et al. (2020) have suggested that unsuitable microbial species might be recognised through recognition of volatile organic chemical (VOC) signals emitted by unwanted microbes, or possibly semiochemicals (“alarm pheromones”) from the garden fungus itself, and that the significance of novel VOC signals might be the subject of associative learning. Although not impossible, this seems to me to be unlikely, as such a system would require sophisticated recognition systems that would inevitably provoke the evolution of evasive strategies by would-be parasites. Moreover, it would be difficult for a system of this type to cope with the arrival of either potentially beneficial new members that hadn’t been encountered before, or new parasites and pests. It seems more probable to me that the mutualistic community is engineered through some self-assembly mechanism that promotes the unassisted build-up of a beneficial microbiome, and then allows its membership to evolve according to circumstances. This would be, in other words, the construction of a suitably resilient agricultural niche. Such a system might be based on recognition of the consequences of altered microbiome membership. An obvious candidate for this would be to look for altered nutrient flow within the fungus-garden; something that the ants must be able to monitor anyway as a part of their fungus-cultivation duties in the garden. A drop in the availability of nutrients would be a sure indicator that something was wrong, and this would be a signal to remove the offending parts of the garden. Detection of a greater than usual requirement to remove old garden materials would be a good time to recruit new antibiotic-secreting microbiome members, perhaps by sampling soil. Any such mechanism must be sufficiently simple and robust to persist for millions of years while the outside environment (including parasites and pathogens) undergoes continuous evolutionary change. With this in mind, it is interesting that theory-led modelling approaches (e.g. Archetti et al., 2011a; 2011b) have shown how any biological host can manage the composition of its associated microbiome by engineering a niche that favours antibiotic-secreting organisms. In this “screening” model of beneficial microbiome assembly (the theory is borrowed from economics), the host simultaneously offers a reward for participating in the associated microbiome, while also imposing a cost on participation. Interference competition then occurs between inhabitants of the microbiome, and under the right conditions, “right” microbes will outcompete “wrong” ones. This is a bit like establishing a social club that has a membership fee; joining the club has a payoff, and this is greater if the membership is exclusive, but in order to join you have to be able to afford membership in the first place. The higher is the potential payoff, the higher is the membership fee. The probable reward in the leafcutter case is the generous availability of nutrients for microbial growth. The membership fee is likely to be antibiotic secretion plus the cost of resisting or tolerating the toxic effects of existing antibiotics. This approach has been applied to the case of higher attines (specifically Acromyrmex ) by Scheuring & Yu (2012), who show that in the presence of supplied nutritional resources, an initial 2-species combination of a beneficial symbiont and a parasite is bistable, tending either to complete domination or complete loss of one or other of the two species. Screening leads to a strong founder effect and provided the inoculum of the beneficial microbe is sufficiently large, this alone is sufficient to afford protection from the parasite. The screening fee is imposed by establishing vertically transmitted antibiotic secreting 

Pseudonocardia as one of the three founding members of the club. Successful establishment of the maternally-derived strain of actinobacteria assures the elimination of a previously encountered strain of Escovopsis . This is evidently what normally happens in nature; newly founded Acromyrmex 

nests remain closed for an initial period, and during this time any vertically transmitted Escovopsis is eliminated, and the parasite is not found in newly opened nests. However, it remains possible that those nests that inherited an insufficient inoculum of Pseudonocardia do not survive to be sampled. Once the colony has acquired a population of worker ants that forages outside for leaves, a wider range of resistance than was provided by the vertically transmitted actinobacteria is highly desirable, in case new strains of 

Escovopsis are encountered. Additional antibiotic secreting members can now be recruited to the microbiome from the environment through screening. An important point not discussed by Scheuring & Yu (2012) is that when an additional member joins the microbiome club, there is always a risk that this will result in the elimination of an existing member that is unable to defend itself against the new antibiotic secreted by the old bacteria. One obvious way to minimise this risk would be to ensure that the genes encoding both antibiotic production and also the corresponding resistance factors, are generously shared among microbiome members (but not pathogens and parasites). Fascinatingly, it has been found that the gene clusters encoding the variable antimicrobial agents secreted by core and facultative members of the leafcutter microbiome are in some cases encoded on transposable elements (TEs), enabling their movement between genomes (Pathak et al ., 2019; Goldstein & Klassen, 2020). In Streptomyces , the gene clusters responsible for synthesising the multiple variable antibiotics discussed above, are flanked by DNA sequences such as transposases, integrases, and endonucleases, which suggests that they can be horizontally transferred within and between genomes. Such mobility would contribute to the longevity of these genetic elements in wild populations of bacteria in the soil, increasing the size of the genetic pool of antibiotic synthesis and resistance elements, and thus providing an insurance policy against their loss. Since mobilization of TEs occurs more readily under stressful conditions such as attack by Escovopsis , it is possible that the widespread distribution of pest-control genes that defend the leafcutter mutualism against attack by this specialist parasite acts as a further insurance policy against pest-control failure. I think it’s fairly obvious from the above account that there are lessons to be learned from leaf-cutting ants for the management of antibiotic and pesticide resistance in human agricultural and medical situations. In short, public health and productive agriculture are best assured by encouraging the genetic diversity of naturally beneficial organisms, thus constructing niches that are naturally resistant to pests and diseases.

Antenna 2021: 45 (2) 65 Lepidoptera in Upper Palaeolithic Art 

Vazrick Nazari 

P.O. Box 45063, Ottawa, Ontario K2M 2Y1 Canada email: nvazrick@yahoo.com 

Introduction 

Palaeolithic art is arguably the oldest artistic tradition in the world with roots in the African Middle-Palaeolithic (Wildgen 2004; Morriss-Kay 2010). Earlier forms of incipient art, such as simple symmetrical tools (i.e. hand-axes, spear-points etc.) or basic geometric patterns carved on animal bones from the late Middle Palaeolithic (after 100,000 BP) are also prevalent in African sites such as Blombos and Diepkloof (e.g., Henshilwood & d’Errico 2005; Texier et al. 2013). By the Upper Palaeolithic, the artform expands not only geographically (e.g. to Sulawesi, Australia and Europe), but also in subject matter. The apparent contrast between the simple Middle Palaeolithic artifacts and the artistic explosion of the Upper Palaeolithic in the form of realistic figurines and colourful and elaborate cave paintings, such as those in 

Altamira and Lascaux caves, prompted anthropologist Jared Diamond to term this temporal boundary “ The Great Leap Forward ” (Cela-Conde & Ayala 2007), although this was later contested (Bar-Yosef 2002; McBrearty & Brooks 2000). The underlying cognitive change responsible for the flourishing of art, and possibly also language and music at the same time, in early Homo sapiens is still debated. A succession of cultures in the Upper Palaeolithic are recognized, mainly based on their stone tools (Fig.1). The earliest, the Aurignacian in Europe, lasted roughly from 45,000–28,000 BP (Wood 2011). The hunter-gatherer Aurignacian culture also included artists who created the magnificent decorations at Chauvet cave in the Ardèche Valley of France, one of the earliest known painted caves in Europe. Several Aurignacian sites with parietal art have been identified in France, Spain, Italy, and Eastern Europe (Fig. 2). Subsequent Gravettian (30,000–22,000 BP), Solutrean (22,000–17,000 BP) and Magdalenian (17,000–12,000 BP) tool cultures followed the artistic traditions of Chauvet 

painters. Before the discovery of Chauvet in 1994, Lascaux 

(18,000 BP) was thought for a long time as the high point of artistic expression in the Palaeolithic. Chauvet also upset the notion that representational effectiveness in art gradually improved over time from the early Palaeolithic to the end of last Ice Age (Lewin & Foley 2004; von Petzinger & Nowell 2014). For an art that lasted more than 20,000 years and over vast distances, it would be naive to expect a solid unity or a linear progression: no precise correlations exist between a culture’s technology and its art, and the age and style of Palaeolithic art do not always coincide (Valladas et al. 1992). Nevertheless, many characteristics are common through all Palaeolithic cultures that produced cave art. Artists mostly represented animals and abstract geometric designs. Humans were seldom depicted and when they were, they appeared deliberately sketchy or caricatural, possibly because they did not play the same role as the animals in the myths and religious practices of the time (Bahn & Vertut 1997). Among the available animals around them, Palaeolithic people often chose to represent the large herbivores that they hunted, including horses, bison, mammoths, aurochs, ibex and all varieties of deer. A survey of 72 caves in France and neighbouring countries of over 2,000 animal images (Leroi-Gourhan 1982) has revealed that horses (610) outnumbered the rest, with bison (510) and mammoths (205) in second and third place. Megaloceros , rhinos and snakes were less common, and carnivores (lions, wolves, hyenas, bears and foxes) were rare. Fish accounted for only eight, and birds for six (two in Lascaux , four in Trois Frères ). Chauvet , which was discovered subsequently, contained more game animals, but also several carnivores, rhinos, and even an owl (Clottes 2010). Portable art, including ivory figurines or etched bone fragments discovered in many Aurignacian sites across Europe, also depicted these animals in a variety of ways (Guthrie 2005). Beside these easily identifiable animals, numerous abstract signs exist on Palaeolithic cave walls that have been a challenge to decipher. At first sight, these simple geometric symbols (e.g. circles, dots, spirals, zigzags, triangles, cross-hatches etc.) do not seem to convey any immediate meaning. Several attempts have been made to organize and classify these symbols into discrete categories to help infer their 

66 Antenna 2021: 45 (2) meaning (e.g. Leroi-Gourhan 1958; Guthrie 2005; Roussot 2013), yet even the most comprehensive of such classification systems fail to accommodate some rogue outliers (von Petzinger 2010). Speculation on what these symbols may represent include toxic mushrooms, hallucinogenic plants, or magic drums (Vieira 1996). Insects are said to be missing altogether in Palaeolithic art (Clottes 1999; but see Marshack 1991; Bahn & Vertut 1997), despite several unambiguous recorded cases: A Troglophilus 

grasshopper on the bison bones from Trois Frères (Bégouön & Bégouön 1928; Kühn 1954; Schimitschek 1977), spider and flies in Barranco de la Gasulla , Castellon province, eastern Spain (Schimitschek 1968), honey bees in various scenes of honey-collecting from the late Palaeolithic – early Neolithic sites of Cueva de la Araña and Barranco del Fondo 

in Spain (Schimitschek 1977; Dams 1983; Crane 1983, 1999), and Magdalenian pendants in the shape of beetles, buprestids and ladybirds from Germany ( Engen in Baden Hegau) and France ( Grotte du Trilobite , Arcy-sur-Cure and 

Laugerie-Basse ) (Schimitschek 1977; Cambefort 1994). Some of the cruciform signs from Lascaux can be assigned to horseflies, dragonflies and other insects (Leroi-Gourhan 1980; Montserrat 2011) (Fig 3a-e). The oldest unambiguous depiction of a lepidopteran in rock art is Neolithic (~7,000 BP) (Schimitschek 1978) (Fig 3f). The conspicuous absence of Lepidoptera in Palaeolithic

Among the many categories of geometric symbols in Palaeolithic caves, some of the “aviforms” (motifs resembling birds) and “tectiforms” (motifs made up of straight lines, such as rectangular shapes) seem to resemble schematic insects with two or four wings, similar to moths in resting position. Züchner (2000) assigned several of these signs to “butterfly-or-bird-type” symbols. Based on their method of production, these may be classified as paintings, engravings, bas-relief, or portable pieces. 

Paintings are images created by applying a variety of coloured organic materials and mineral pigments (e.g. ochre, charcoal, manganese, etc.) to rock surfaces. Aviform paintings resembling butterflies occur in Chauvet (32–31,000 BP) , La 

Antenna 2021: 45 (2) 69 Pasiega (17,000 BP) and Le Portel (11,600 BP). Two such signs in Chauvet , modern day France (Fig. 4a, b), have been suggested to represent birds in flight (Gély & Azéma 2005; Clottes 2010; von Petzinger & Nowell 2014). However, the vastly different style used in drawing of an owl in the same cave (Wheye & Kennedy 2008) does not support this notion. Züchner (2000) also placed in this category two red aviform signs from La Pasiega in northern Spain (Fig. 4c). A spade-shaped sign from 

Le Portel in Spain (Fig. 4d) (Bahn & Vertut 1988), which strongly resembles a Sphingid moth at rest (Fig. 5a) also falls within this category. Clottes et al. (1990) speculated that these signs may be the realistic predecessors to the varied family of the so-called “ signes en accolade ” (bracket signs), a.k.a. “ Le Placard type” after Le Placard cave in France; Guthrie (2005), however, dismissed these as stylized female anatomy. 

Engravings are images carved by scratching the rock surface with sharp tools, or by tracing with fingers in soft clay. Tectiform engravings from Trois Frères in France (20,000 BP) (Fig. 6a) drawn around the head of a lion (Bégouön & Breuil 1958; Leroi-Gourhan 1968; Monserrat 2011) have been interpreted as Sphingid moths, specifically the eyed hawk moth Smerinthus ocellatus (Howse 2010). However, closer examination of the published images of these signs (Bégouön et al. 2014) failed to confirm some of the detail highlighted by Howse, e.g. the hind wing ‘eyespot’ seems to be only a chip in the rock surface. These signs have also been dismissed as representations of female genitalia (Guthrie 2005). A different style of engraving includes scratch-mark tectiforms comprised of multiple parallel lines, a design common in four neighboring caves in modern day France, namely Font-de-Gaume (~17,000 BP), Rouffignac (13,000 BP) , Combarelles 

(13–11,000 BP) and Bernifal (15–10,000 BP) (Barrière 1983; Roussot 2013) (Fig. 6b–d). These geometric signs normally include a straight central axis, at least one pair (and sometimes up to three pairs) of sloping anterior arms at about a 45-degree angle, and usually a straight line at the base. The base is sometimes connected to the arms forming a pentagon, and sometimes lines connect from the middle of the arms to the base of the axis, reminiscent of lepidopteran hind wings. Traces of what may be antennae or legs are often present. Capdeville (1986) classified these signs into three categories: arrow shaped (ramified), triangular, and pentagonal. The pentagonal signs may also have caudal semi-circles. The most common interpretations for these signs include dwellings (hence the term ‘tectiform’, “roof-shaped”) (Capitan & Breuil 1902), proprietary signs (Capitan et al. 1903), tents (Mortillet 1903), evil-spirit traps (Obermaier 1918), magic (Zervos 1959), hunting traps (Bégouön 1923; Vinaccia 1926; Kühn 1929; Lindner 1941), symbols of femininity and masculinity (Leroi-Gourhan 1958), and stylized female genitalia (Guthrie 2005). However, their distinct style, relative (smaller) sizes compared to other illustrated animals, and their placement – e.g. on mammoths in Bernifal and on bison in Font-de-Gaume (Fig. 7) – suggest that this class of geometric signs may represent insects, possibly flies, dragonflies, or moths. Some of the tectiform signs following this general pattern in Font-de-Gaume and 

Bernifal are made up of tightly-packed series of painted dots rather than scratched lines (Fig. 6c) (Roussot 2013). One such sign in Bernifal (Fig. 6d), with annulated arms and base, closely resembles a mating pair of Amata moths; others bear some resemblance to plume moths at rest (Fig. 5b–d). 

Bas relief are images sculpted out of the rock surface. Two reniform (kidney-shaped) bas-relief sculptures located side by side on the wall in the main chamber of the Roc de Vézac cave in France (21–20,000 BP) represent a unique production style and are reminiscent of butterflies (von Petzinger & Nowell 2014). The difference in production technique of these signs may at first glance obscure their similarity, but when their physical form is compared with the “butterflies” from Chauvet ,they seem to have many traits in common: both are made up of adjoining circular/oval shapes with a rounded triangular bulge that extends downwards from the main part of the figure. A closer examination of these signs reveals that they are enclosed in a horizontal cartouche, with a third unfinished “butterfly” on the right side whose outline is barely visible (Fig. 8). 

Portable pieces with insect imagery are very rare. Beside the grasshopper on a bone fragment found in Trois-Frère (Fig. 3a), there are very few other records of insects in Palaeolithic portable art, including possible insect larvae (reindeer botfly?) carved on bone fragments found in several German and French caves (Guthrie 2005). The only recorded Palaeolithic portable art associated with Lepidoptera are Upper Solutrean (~18,000 BP) pendants made out of animal bone fragments from Altamira , that are presumed to represent butterfly chrysalids (Lasheras & González 2005; Monserrat 2011), although in my opinion they do not much resemble butterfly pupae at all. Discussion 

The beauty and expressiveness of Palaeolithic paintings in 

Chauvet and Lascaux speak directly to contemporary observers, yet despite the empathy they may evoke, their meanings and the intent of their makers is simply unknown. Some animals are depicted much more frequently than others, and some are very rare or missing altogether. Animals are often painted or engraved without any understandable reference to one another. The art does not give an accurate account of the world around the artists: The sun, stars, and moon are never shown, nor the ground line. Other than a few tentative identifications, there are very few confirmed examples of mountains, huts, rivers, recognizable representations of tools, weapons, or personal adornment (Clottes 1999; García-Diez & Vaquero 2015). Instead, the cave walls contain a myriad of abstract signs and symbols whose interpretations are controversial. Butterflies are symbolic creatures in many cultures, standing in some contexts for beauty and metamorphosis and in others for the transitory nature of happiness. Butterfly metamorphosis has captured the human imagination since the beginning of recorded history, and representations of butterflies and moths in early art date as far back as the Neolithic age. Insects, including lepidopterans, would have been also plentiful during the Pleistocene. Colourful butterflies would have fluttered outside the caves, and moths would have been abundant – some likely even lived with these early humans, infesting their clothing or dried food supplies. It is possible that Palaeolithic man did try to depict them as part of the animal world; however, the execution of the concept was perhaps so rudimentary that today we are unable to associate the resulting symbols with insects. Several categories of geometric signs do remind of insects, including those classified under tectiform, aviform or reniform (von Petzinger 2009). The definitive identity and meaning of these signs, however, remains obscure. The tectiform signs on mammoths and bison in French caves provide a clue to their identity. Flies and mosquitoes are the universally acknowledged symbols of nuisance. Flies were revered in ancient Egypt for their tenacity (Kritsky & Cherry 2000) and were a symbol of death in European medieval marginalia (Yanoviak 2013). The Palaeolithic people would have seen mosquitoes around their living spaces and flies on rotting carcasses of the animals they hunted. Perhaps the signs on mammoths and bison are meant to represent flies on dead beasts. The reniform symbols in Roc de Vezac may be interpreted as two butterflies in the midst of a mating dance. The tectiform sign in Bernifal may depict a mating pair of Amata 

moths. These moths and butterflies are still present in Dordogne today. The Palaeolithic people would have observed these critters individually and in copula . These early humans, with the same cognitive capacity as us, would have known what the mating pair were doing. For them, this simple act would have represented fertility, generation of new life, and the magic of procreation. Scenes of copulation, whether of animals or humans, abound in Palaeolithic art (Guthrie 2005). Maybe they chose the iconic posture of a pair of mating moths as the symbol of their clan. Speculations aside, the question remains: if these signs were really meant to represent lepidopterans, why did the Palaeolithic artists choose to depict them in an abstract and ambiguous way, while the paintings of the large mammals are executed in such exquisite realistic detail? And if they are not insects, what are they? Whatever their meaning and intention, we can now only wonder.

72 Antenna 2021: 45 (2) Thomas Coulthard Heysham of Carlisle (1791-1857): a Cumbrian naturalist and insect collector 

Ian Hodkinson 

i.d.hodkinson@ljmu.ac.uk 

At the end of the 18th century little was known about the insect fauna of Cumbria. 1 Thomas Heysham’s father John produced the first list of the ‘Animals of Cumberland’ in 1794 but insects were barely mentioned. The Kendal journeyman cobbler and natural history collector John Fitz-Roberts, nearly a hundred years previously, had been solicited by James Petiver to provide Cumbrian insects for inclusion in his Musei Petiveriana (1695-1703) but this had produced little by way of results. Similarly, the Kendal-born botanist William Hudson, author of the highly regarded Flora Anglica (1762), toyed briefly with the idea of publishing a companion work covering the insects and sent around a hundred specimens, representing several Orders, to Linnaeus. These specimens are now in the Linnean Society collection but no coherent account of these insects was produced at that time. Fast forward to 1901 when the Victoria History of Cumberland 

included an extensive list of the insect species of the county compiled by Frank Henry Day, one of our Society’s past Fellows. 2 Thomas Coulthard Heysham’s name dominates the primary records and it is clear that it was he who established the foundations of early entomology in Cumbria. Thomas was a man of independent means, inheriting both his father’s curiosity in natural history and the financial means to pursue his interests largely uninterrupted. He was a gifted natural historian who studied and collected birds, fish, seaweeds, mosses and molluscs as well as insects. He also brought the occasional rare or unusual plant to the attention of botanists, and specimens of welsh poppy (pl. 743) and of a whorled caraway, Carum verticillatum (pl. 680), collected from Kingmoor, Carlisle, were used by John Curtis to adorn the insect plates of his British Entomology . Entomology and ornithology, however, were Thomas’s main passions and they served a complementary purpose: birds collected for taxidermy provided specimens of several unusual species of lice (Phthiraptera) that were passed on to Henry Denny and included in his monograph of the British species (see later). Thomas clearly had an excellent eye for the unusual. Frank Day, who was to become Honorary Curator of Carlisle Museum and a recognised authority on the Cumbrian insect fauna, wrote in an appreciation of Heysham’s life that ‘There is no doubt that he was a painstaking and reliable collector of insects. He possessed a good library and his identification of his captures were invariably correct … at that time when entomology was in its infancy, exact and trustworthy records were difficult to obtain’. 3 He adds that ‘It is noteworthy that his records are mostly of uncommon species, the more generally distributed ones being seldom mentioned’. This preoccupation with rarer species has led some to question the occasional Heysham identification, particularly where north Cumbria localities appeared as distant outliers in an insect’s distribution pattern. Day, after many years working on the Cumbrian fauna conceded, however, that ‘as the years went on, and my acquaintance with Cumberland insects extended, and one after another of Heysham’s finds rewarded my search, the extreme reliability of his records became apparent and although one or two species remain that have not been since found in the county, these may be accounted for by the changed condition of the localities’. He cites the water beetles that have disappeared from Cardew Mire, which is now a flooded aggregates quarry! A good example of a Heysham species that was long-doubted but which has subsequently been accepted as British is the rare water skater 

Limnoporus (then Hydrometra ) r ufoscutellarius (Latr.). 4 His British record for the striking ichneumonid wasp 

Pseudogonalos hahnii (Spin.) (then Trigonalys anglicana ) was similarly questioned, but vindicated many years later. 5

Antenna 2021: 45 (2) 73 Thomas Heysham’s insect collecting localities (Fig. 1) were highly concentrated around Carlisle and he does not appear to have ventured far outside his home county. He was a strong walker and most of his sites he visited on foot. His strength and endurance are illustrated by his long walks along the River Caldew from Carlisle to one of his favourite haunts, the summit of Skiddaw – a distance of about 70 km round trip. This mountain in the Lake District had been visited earlier by John Curtis in the company of his wealthy patron James Charles Dale, where they had recorded the carabid beetle Leistus montanus Steph. Thomas was determined to discover it for himself, necessitating several repeat visits before he finally succeeded. 6

North Cumbria, nevertheless, provided a wide diversity of habitats in which to collect insects. Heysham’s frequently-visited localities included the marshes along the Solway Firth, such as Burgh and Rockcliffe marshes, and the mosslands and mires adjacent to this coast, such as Drumburgh Moss (now a National Nature Reserve), Orton Moss (now an SSSI) and Rockcliffe Mire. A much favoured site for aquatic beetles and bugs was Cardew Mire, near Thursby. Woodland sites adjacent to the River Eden, including Baron and Coombs Woods, proved particularly productive, as did the demesne of Rose Castle, south of Dalston, the then country home of the Bishop of Carlisle. The main Cumberland rivers, the Eden, Caldew, Petteril, Irthing and Esk, radiating from Carlisle, provided the corridors that allowed Thomas access to the surrounding countryside. Many of his scarcer species were collected along the river banks and from localities easily accessed from the rivers. Thomas was, by all accounts, a retiring person who remained a bachelor. He nevertheless developed avoluminous list of correspondents and contacts with whom he exchanged notes and specimens. A large collection of this correspondence still survives. 7 He was by nature an observer and collector rather than a writer of scientific papers; the task of writing he largely left to others. His printed work is sparse, with just the occasional records of unusual insects, such as a series of notes in Entomological Magazine . These included the abundance of small mountain ringlet butterfly Hipparchia cassiope (now Erebia epiphron (Knoch)) near Sprinkling and Sty Head Tarns in the English Lake District, captures of bedstraw hawkmoth Deilephila (now Hyles ) gallii (Rott.) near Cumwhinton, Cumbria, the provenance of a pair of scarce swallowtail butterflies Papilio (now Iphiclides ) podalirius (L.) reputedly taken in Britain, and the presence of a rare sawfly 

Cimbex femoratus (L.) near Carlisle. 8 His most noted publication was on a bird species, the dotterel, an uncommon bird of the higher mountains of the Lake District. 9 The importance of his entomological work, however, is best judged from the writings of those to whom Thomas sent a great many rare and little-known species. Prominent among these were three of his friends who were the main instigators involved in re-establishing the Royal Entomological Society of London as presently constituted, namely James Francis Stephens, John Curtis and William Yarrell. They were each involved in the inaugural meeting held by a small group of interested entomologists on 3 May 1833 at the British Museum. Despite his entomological involvement, Yarrell was primarily interested in birds and fish, towards which Heysham made substantial contributions of Cumbrian records and observations in Yarrell’s History of British Birds 

and his British Fishes .10 John Curtis and James Stephens, by contrast, were already making highly significant contributions to British entomology through their exquisitely illustrated multi-volume publications entitled British Entomology (1824-1839) and Illustrations of British Entomology (1828-1846), respectively. It was to this pair that Heysham sent many of his notable insect specimens, which subsequently featured widely in their volumes. Curtis’s British Entomology was originally issued between 1824 and 1839 as 192 monthly parts comprising 770 full-page plates. Later editions were compiled into, usually, eight bound volumes and often contain a mixture of original and revised plates. 11 Here I have found it easiest to refer to the plate number for individual species, which are consistent throughout, and have relied on Watson and Dallwitz’s list of updated Curtis insect names. 12 Curtis included Heysham’s locality data for twenty-seven uncommon species, including additions to the British fauna, and used his specimens to illustrate new and particularly interesting species. One of these, the snipefly Rhagio heyshami sp.n. (pl. 705), collected at Carlisle, is now synonymised with Rhagio notatus (Meig.) (Fig. 2d). The same locality figures in the common name of another beetle, the staphylinid Bryaxis (now Trichonyx ) sulcicollis 

(Reich.) (pl. 315), the Carlisle Pselaphus (Fig 2c). Perhaps, the most celebrated species was the rare marbled wormwood moth Heliothis (now Protoschinia ) scutosa (Denis & Schiff.) (pl. 595), first collected from the banks of the River Caldew near Dalston, Cumberland (Fig. 2b). A Heysham specimen, sometimes doubted on the basis of its locality, but later verified, twice passed through auction many years later, each time for a considerable sum. 13 Other notable Heysham specimens illustrated were the carabid beetle, Notiophilus rufipes sp.n. (pl. 254) from ‘the neighbourhood of Carlisle’(Fig. 2e), the staphylinid beetle Lesteva leachii sp.n. (now Deleaster dichrous (Grav.) (pl. 303) from the banks of the River Eden (Fig. 2a), the stratiomyiid fly, Sargus reaumuri (now S. bipunctatus (Meig.)) (pl. 305) taken at Rockcliffe Moss, adjacent to the Solway (Fig. 2g), and the dragonfly Libellula 

(now Leucorrhinia ) rubicunda (L.)) from an undisclosed locality almost certainly near Carlisle (Fig. 2f). This latter

74 Antenna 2021: 45 (2) species, commonly known as the northern white-faced darter, is a species of great current conservation interest that has recently been reintroduced into Drumburgh Moss, one of Heysham’s favoured north Cumbrian collecting sites, and Foulshaw Moss in south Cumbria. Occasional Heysham specimen illustrations, including ‘ Lesteva leachii ’ and ‘ Heliothis ’

scutosa , were reused by Curtis to illustrate his two later books on the Genera of British Coleoptera and Lepidoptera .14 

The publication of Stephens’s Systematic Catalogue of British Insects in 1829, to which Thomas was a listed subscriber, contained a few ‘Heysham’ records and provided a spur for Thomas to send more material for inclusion in the 

Illustrations .15 Stephens’ magnum opus , published in 11 volumes between 1828 and 1846 included records of 412 species collected by Heysham, almost exclusively in north Cumbria. 16 Many were again uncommon or notable species, primarily among the Coleoptera and Lepidoptera. When Stephens published his Manual of British Coleoptera in 1839, he omitted the names of his collectors, but all the old Heysham localities were there, such as Baron Wood, Cardew Mire, Dalston Hall Woods and Cummersdale, as well as 109 references to Carlisle. 17 

It is interesting, however, that Thomas reserved many of his most interesting specimens for other specialists. Henry Denny received eighteen species of Phthiraptera collected from birds that Heysham had procured, particularly gulls, auks, ducks, divers and waders. Heysham specimens used by Denny to illustrate his monograph on the British species included Nirmus (now Carduiceps ) cingulatus (Denny) from black-tailed godwit (Fig. 2j), Nirmus (now Brueelia )

cyclothorax (Burm.) from brambling (Fig. 2i) and Docophoris merguli Denny (now Austromenopon nigropleurum Denny) from a little auk shot in Cumbria (Fig. 2h). 18 The most unusual capture, however, was of Docophorus (now 

Upupicola ) upupae Schr. on Eurasian hoopoe, a rare vagrant in Cumbria. Similarly, James Duncan was a recipient of several species of less common stratiomyiid fly from wetland localities around Carlisle, especially Cardew Mire. 19 Thomas sent weevils to John Walton, who included several unique specimens in his series of papers on the British fauna. Notable species, mostly collected from near Carlisle, included Trachodes hispidus L., Dorytomus tremulae Payk., 

Magdalis carbonaria L. and the then rare and attractive 

Rhynchites (now Involvulus ) cupreus (L.), taken from mountain ash and sent alive to Walton in a pill box. 20 Pride of place, however, goes to the Red Data Book species Procas granulicollis Walt. ‘found amongst moss and decayed vegetable matter’. 21 

Lepidoptera were another of Thomas’s specialisms, where again his observations were never mundane. He commonly found the Duke of Burgundy butterfly Neomoebius (now 

Hamearis ) lucina (L.) along the banks of the River Eden and he discovered the wood white butterfly Leucophasia (now 

Leptidea ) sinapis (L.) near Carlisle. 22 In both cases these represented the northernmost British records at that time, observations that were repeated many times in the Lepidoptera literature. He made the earliest records of the scarce migratory butterflies Camberwell beauty Vanessa 

(now Nymphalis ) antiopa (L.) and clouded yellow Colias croceus (Geoff.) in Cumbria. 23 His records of the red underwing moth ( Catocala nupta (L.)) at Davidson’s Bank near Carlisle, alongside that of the yellow-tail moth ( Euproctis similis (Füss.)) stood as the sole Cumberland records for many years. 24 Sometimes Thomas’s records contained snippets of additional information, such as in his description of the small mountain ringlet butterflies at Sty Head and Sprinkling Tarns, its Lake District stronghold. He noted the abundance of this extremely local mountain-dwelling butterfly and commented that while the females appeared worn the males were in more pristine condition. 25 

Thomas Heysham was one of the first to use ‘sugaring’ of tree trunks to attract and collect moths. 26 It had been known for a few years that moths were attracted to sugary and fermenting materials, but it was a letter from Henry Doubleday to Thomas that formally described and established the technique. Writing on 11th August 1841, Doubleday stated that ‘by taking some sugar and water and brushing it on the trunks of trees, or sprinkling it on the bushes, you attract an immense number of moths, and about an hour after sunset they remain quite quiet, and with a light you may select what you want’. 27 No doubt Heysham employed the technique to obtain some of his unusual captures. While Heysham sent specimens to many colleagues he also received material from others. A curious letter from Henry Doubleday describes him sending Thomas part of a series of scarce copper butterflies Lycaena virgaureae L. that he purchased, believing them to have been taken in the fens around Ely. The provenance of these specimens is unknown and L. virgaureae remains a highly dubious historical British species. 28 Another letter, dated 1833, thanks William Orton Aiken of Huntingdonshire for sending ‘remarkably fine and exceedingly well set’ specimens. He noted, however, that the abdomens of elephant hawk moths Deilephila elpenor (L.) had detached and damaged other specimens, for which he blamed the inevitable vicissitudes of coach transport. 29 He often employed others to trap insects for him, particularly moths. One especially interesting associate was James Cooper, a handloom weaver living at Little Orton, west of Carlisle. He collected moths on the local common and regularly sent them on to Heysham. Cooper later studied taxidermy and was appointed the curator of Warrington Museum. 30

Antenna 2021: 45 (2) 75 Heysham records of Hymenoptera are frequently mentioned in later publications and a few examples illustrate the breadth of the novel material he collected. Uncommon aculeates taken around Carlisle include the broken-belted bumblebee, Bombus soroeensis Fab., the short-haired bumblebee, Bombus subterraneus L. (then B. collinus ), the solitary Andrena denticulata (Kirby) and the cuckoo wasp 

Chrysis (now Chrysura ) austriaca (Fab.) 31 The latter species is now excluded from the British list and may represent a misidentification of the scarce Chrysura radians (Harris). 32 

Sawflies include Cimbex femoratus , the strikingly coloured 

Tenthredo maculata Geoff. and the alder wood wasp, 

Xiphydria camelus L. Ichneumon species were especially prominent with the subfamilies Pimplinae, Tryphoninae, Ophioninae and Ichneumoninae all represented. 34 

Towards the end of his life Thomas Coulthard Heysham became increasingly reclusive. He died quietly on 6 April 1857 at his home at 45 Fisher Street Carlisle and his death was reported to the entomological world with brief notices in the Entomologist’s Weekly Intelligencer, The Gentleman’s Magazine, The Illustrated London News and more locally in the Liverpool Mercury, Westmorland Gazette and Carlisle Journal , in which an unfortunate error was corrected two weeks later, originally stating that he suffered from repeated fits of delusion (corrected to seclusion). 35 More complete appreciations of Heysham’s life include a short memoir by James Murray entitled A Bygone Cumberland Naturalist , and an extended piece in the Carlisle Journal .36 

Following his death, his extensive library and natural history collections were sold by auction at J.C. Stephen’s saleroom on King Street, Covent Garden, London. The sales were widely advertised in the local and London press and attracted much interest. 37 The library sale was held on 12 July 1858, with The Entomological Society a major bidder. Sheffield Neave, in his history of our Society, noted that this was ‘perhaps the first large purchase of books’ for the library and that ‘£46 7s was expended’. 38 There is no definitive list of volumes purchased, but included was a ‘magnificent copy’ of Jacob Hübner’s Sammlung Europäischer Schmetterlinge , a large multi-part colour plate book of European butterflies and moths. Heysham’s copy of Curtis’s British Entomology 

was also purchased for £13 and bears his characteristic bookplate (Fig. 3). 39 The British Insect sale on 23 November 1859 followed previous successful auctions of Heysham’s birds and their eggs, fish and shells earlier that year. 40 The collection, housed in four large mahogany cabinets, contained ‘all the Orders including many great rarities’. 41 Among lots sold was the ‘celebrated specimen’ of ‘ Heliothis ’ scutosa taken by Heysham at Carlisle, which fetched 28s. It is uncertain who purchased it but a specimen found its way into the collection of John Bradshaw Hodgkinson of Preston, an auctioneer’s porter and one of our past Society’s Fellows, and was auctioned for 55s in 1897 following his death. 42 The British Museum was a major purchaser of Heysham specimens, with the accessions (1859-42) mentioning 325 Ichneumonidae, 225 Coleoptera and 185 other Hymenoptera. 43 An attached note states that ‘This collection of Ichneumonidae contained many species of great rarity including four of Trigonales Anglicannus (sic) [now 

Pseudogonalos hahnii (Spin.)] & five of a species of 

Mesostenus new to Britain’. It seems that some rare material went to other bidders, who then presented specimens to the British Museum. Two former Society Fellows, Robert Bakewell and Edward Coldwell Rye, offered respectively a series of eight specimens of the short-haired bumblebee, 

Bombus collinus (now B. subterraneus L.) and a specimen of the longhorn beetle, Clytus (now Plagionotus ) detritus (L.). B. subterraneus , a denizen of species-rich grassland, which was declared extinct in Britain in 2000, has since been successfully reintroduced into areas of Dungeness and Romney Marsh in Kent and East Sussex. Thomas shares a granite memorial with his father in Richardson St. Cemetery, Carlisle. The substantial four-sided block, around 2m high, with a shallow pyramidal apex, bears his inscription on the southern face, together with the accolade ‘EMINENT NATURALIST’. 44 Despite his interests, Thomas never became a Fellow of the Entomological or Linnean Societies, although he subscribed enthusiastically to most books on entomology and to the publications of the Ray Society. One is left with the impression of a quiet, introverted man, obsessed by his studies in natural history who, despite on occasion serving as Mayor and Alderman of Carlisle, shunned the spotlight, preferring his own company and avoiding frequent travel outside his native area. His original contribution to early entomology in the north of England was, nevertheless, substantial.
