# PIECES 

# Hanging on to your crocodile and hippo gods †; conservatism in science, including entomology 

# OPINION 

† The title of this article refers to the Court of the Pharaoh Akhenaten (reigned c. 1351– c. 1334 BC), husband of Queen Nefertiti and father of Tutankhamun, who encountered considerable opposition from the priesthood (who worshipped all kinds of animal deities, e.g. Sobek and Taweret), when he promoted the concept of monotheism in the form of the sun god Aten ( cf . en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akhenaten). As such, Akhenaten is considered by some to be a kind of proto-ecologist, in that he realised that life on Earth (or most of it anyway, and possibly all of it) ultimately derives from the sun. 

Nowadays, the majority of informed six to seven-year-olds have probably heard of the word ‘mutation’ and doubtless many of them know what this means, certainly in relation to the Covid-19 virus and the horrid global pandemic that it has caused. Yet, because of the current widespread usage and discussion of the word, more especially in relation to the evolution of new, potentially more transmissible or pathogenic strains of the virus, it got me thinking again about mutation in my own taxa of special interest, the aphids (Hemiptera: Aphididae). But, and amazingly in this light, twenty years ago when I and colleagues, especially Gagan (Gugs) Lushai, tried to publish our papers on this topic, we were met with a wall of opposition. One of our papers was submitted – and rejected – seven times from mainstream journals, including Nature .Only when we organised an international meeting on 

intra clonal genetic variation, jointly funded by the RES and Linnean Society, whereupon our two main papers finally appeared in print, did the vehement opposition mysteriously ebb away! (Loxdale, 2003a & b; Lushai et al. , 2003). Hitherto, the broad consensus was that so-called clones, including aphid clones, were ‘genetically identical’, as unlikely as this scenario would appear. Some people were seemingly strongly opposed to any views to the contrary. Perhaps this had something to do with the then recent media hype about Dolly the Sheep (Kolata, 1997) and that there were too many vested interests riding on this sensational achievement to brook any views, or even empirical evidence, that this may not actually be so in eukaryotes (e.g. Major, 2002). A few years earlier, when trying to publish my and colleagues’ findings on long vs. short distance migration in aphids, studied using molecular genetic markers (allozymes and later microsatellites), we also met quite a lot of opposition from referees, including one who stated “ Clearly the authors have taken leave of their senses !” And this despite the fact that we had clear empirical evidence to show that different aphid species displayed different population genetic patterns depending on their different flight urges and abilities. This was something that had anyway already been demonstrated empirically by Roy (L.R.) Taylor (1924-2007) and co-workers in the 1960s-80s following comparative species analysis of Rothamsted Insect Survey (RIS) 12.2m high suction-trap data (reviewed in L.R. Taylor, 1986; cf. also R.A.J. Taylor, 2007) and measurements of aphid flight behaviour, as well as endurance and response to visual stimuli from wind tunnel experiments on various species of flying aphids by Jim Hardie and co-workers at Silwood Park (Hardie, 1993). No one would surely argue today against the fact that different bird species have different migratory urges and abilities. But the then consensus amongst many aphidologists, certainly prior to the widespread and comparative use of molecular genetic markers, was that aphids tended to travel long geographical distances, borne on the wind above their low flight speed in still air (Loxdale et al., 1993), a view enhanced early on in the 20 th century by observation by ecologists such as Charles Elton FRS (1900-1991) of winged aphids on ice floes in Spitzbergen (Elton, 1925). True, some species do migrate long distances, but not all, as now shown empirically with molecular markers. Rather, other species seem to undergo short- to medium-range dispersal (reviewed in Loxdale et al ., 1993, 2017; Loxdale & Lushai, 2007). My most recent battle with the scientific cognoscenti is over the terms generalism and specialism ( cf. Loxdale et al ., 2019 and references therein). In this paper, last of a trilogy on the topic, I and co-authors argue that generalism in 

78 Antenna 2021: 45 (2) reference to aphids and their hymenopterous wasp parasitoids is a misnomer. At the most fundamental level, this is because as soon as a population of a living organism occupies a distinct and unique ecological niche, be that as a full species or lower level of evolutionary divergence, i.e. subspecies, semi species, race, etc.….then that is the specialism, regardless of diet breadth. If the organism is an animal, it may be mono - oligo - or polyphagous , and in the last instance, even omnivorous, but it is never generalist....in our view. But people seem very reluctant to change their stance on this one, possibly because of the yin & yang, good & bad, right & wrong, black & white phenomenon: if there is ‘specialism’, then there surely has to be the opposite condition, i.e. ‘generalism’. But as my wife Nicola argues, if generalism existed, evolution would effectively stop, since it is the process of specialism that governs evolutionary adaptations and population divergence, by whatever means (allopatric, sympatric, parapatric). David Attenborough in his many TV series never uses the ambiguous term ‘generalism’ – not that I have ever heard him use anyway – but often states that such and such a species is a specialist, sometimes highly so. Hence, there are clearly degrees of specialism in nature, ultimately leading to incredible ‘fine-grained’ ecological specialisations, sometimes involving intimate co-evolutionary relationships (Thompson, 1994). It is well described in the broader literature how individuals or groups of people, including the military, were incredulous or downright negative about the importance of technical or scientific advances such as – for example – the screw propeller for ships, submarines, powered flight, antiseptics and antiseptic surgery, and in fact the germ theory itself ( cf. Germ theory denialism, Wikipedia) and very recently, the unjustified reluctance of certain European governments and institutions not to utilise the perfectly viable AstraZeneca Covid-19 vaccine in favour of other ones (www.nytimes.com/2021/02/25/world/europe/germany-coronavirus-vaccines astrazeneca.html). In his thoughts about organic evolution, Charles Robert Darwin (1809-1882) ‘ believed that entomologists were opposed to his views’ …but later he realised …. ’that his perception was based, in part, on three reviews, including one that he erroneously attributed to an entomological critic, and that not all entomologists were opposed to his ideas.’ (Kritsky, 2008). Indeed, he wrote to fellow evolutionist Ernst Haeckel (1834-1919) in Jena, Germany in May 1867 stating that ‘ The belief in the descent theory is slowly spreading in England, even amongst those who can give no reason for their belief. No body of men were at first so much opposed to my views as the members of the London Entomolog. Soc; but now I am assured that with the exception of 2 or 3 old men all the members concur with me to a certain extent. ’ (www.darwinproject.ac.uk/letter/DCP-LETT-5544. xml; see also Kritsky, 2008) In more recent times, the Visiting Group at Rothamsted (a four-yearly visiting group of eminent scientists whose job was/is to comment on the quality and relevance of the research being done in the various departments) apparently recommended that the work on synthetic pyrethroids headed by Michael Elliott CBE, FRS (1924-2007) of the Insecticides & Fungicides Department be terminated. Only the continuing support of the then head of that department, Dr Charles Potter (1907-1989), who disregarded their advice, enabled a range of very important and valuable chemicals to be synthesised, leading to huge worldwide sales and successful control of many global insect pests (Pickett, 2016). But having said that, as is the way of the world, winning discoveries and ideas will not always be backed and others that appear potentially viable and are backed, spiritually and financially, eventually prove untenable or indeed even untrue (e.g. so-called ‘cold fusion’; cf. Wikipedia entry). Another celebrated case of not seeing the scientific potential and importance of a scientific discovery, here, like evolution, one of universal relevance (and which I was privileged enough to hear first-hand from the scientist involved himself when I was a young man studying for my DPhil degree in Oxford in the late 1970s), concerns a lecture given by the late, great Sir Hans Adolf Krebs (1900-81) about the publication of his work on the citric acid cycle in 1937...or ‘Krebs cycle’, as it is often known ( cf . Wikipedia entry; cf. also Kornberg & Williamson, 1984). Towards the end of his lecture, given with gusto in his distinct German accent in the lecture theatre of the Biochemistry Department, he told the well-attended audience how, on originally sending the manuscript of his famous paper to 

Nature ....it was duly rejected! (Borrell, 2010). Later in 1953, he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology & Medicine “ for his discovery of the citric acid cycle ” shared jointly with Fritz Albert Lipmann (1899-1986) for the latter’s work for his “discovery of co-enzyme A and its importance for intermediary metabolism .” With a glint in his eye, he concluded by saying that he had both the original rejection letter from Nature and the certificate for his Nobel Prize framed and on opposite sides of the writing desk in his office. Doubtless there are many other examples in science in general, including entomology, of such lack of foresight and imagination, or decided opposition to the furtherment of hypothetical ideas and proof of concepts using empirical data. I would be very interested to receive any further examples from Members and Fellows of the RES of such cases.... in effect, revealing that we scientists are not necessarily as broadminded, nor free of prejudice and bigotry, or even religious constraints, as other members of Society at large are, much as we would like to believe otherwise. We are, as a group, not infallible, and that perhaps also, what we initially fail to perceive as a good idea or important discovery is unintentional rather than intentional in terms of our individual or even collective lack of support. Lastly, science is often a ‘belief-led’ practice, being set against the backdrop of the social norms and politics of the age in which it is done, whereby only the doggedness and persistence of the individual scientist concerned eventually triumphs in getting their ideas accepted, or these ideas are eventually accepted posthumously, perhaps long after the scientist in question has ‘shuffled off this mortal coil’ ‡. It was Max Planck (1858-1947), the great late 19 th -early 20 th C. theoretical physicist, who said, somewhat cynically perhaps: “ A new scientific truth does not triumph by convincing its opponents and making them see the light, but rather because its opponents eventually die, and a new generation grows up that is familiar with it .” (Planck, 1968).

# PIECES 

# Entomyopia and Entoalexia – two potentially life-threatening conditions 

# OPINION 

This article was stimulated by two recent events. First, a conversation I had at a pre-lockdown curry evening organised by the amateur band that my wife plays in. My neighbour was a well-educated modern languages teacher in her early forties. We discussed our various jobs and she evinced surprise that anyone would want to work with insects and, even when I explained the myriad benefits of understanding insect biology and ecology to her in terms of food security, vector control, detritivores, integrated pest management, pollination etc., she was still unconcerned about the lack of training provision for entomology and the dwindling number of young entomologists in the population. I also highlighted the growing disconnect between people and nature. Her response was that it was just the way it was and that people had other interests now! I was, despite the fact that I have bemoaned the lack of funding for invertebrate research and training for some time now (e.g. Leather 2009ab, 2013, 2014), totally amazed and down-hearted. The 

80 Antenna 2021: 45 (2) second event was when one of my entomological colleagues reported to me how shocked he had been, when describing the recent opening of our new entomology building at Harper Adams University to his next-door neighbour, a retired engineer, that the neighbour expressed great surprise that anyone would want such a facility and why anyone would want to spend that amount of money to enable entomological research. I have written before about my worries concerning the decline of interest in natural history and entomology (Leather & Quicke, 2009, 2010) and entomologists have with increasing urgency been warning about the startling declines in insect abundance for almost twenty years (e.g. Thomas et al., 2004; Thomas, 2005). More recently, the warnings about insect decline have highlighted the global ecological Armageddon that is likely to follow if the reported declines in insect abundance are allowed to continue unchecked (e.g., Cardoso & Leather, 2019; Cardoso 

et al ., 2020; Didham et al ., 2020; Wagner, 2020). Despite a great deal of media attention, there have been very few signs of concrete action. Consequently, I feel that it is now well past time to do something urgently about this lack of understanding among the public, the educational establishment, funding councils and the government. We are, as entomologists, all too aware of entomophobia, the irrational fear of insects; in fact some Orders have their own specific titles, e.g. lepidopterophobia, the fear of moths and butterflies. I personally came across this condition when I was giving a talk to a local garden club. I always make a point of wearing an insect-themed shirt on these occasions, usually one covered in illustrations of brightly coloured butterflies. It turned out that one of my audience suffered from such extreme lepidopterophobia that she had to face the back of the room throughout my talk. A less extreme form of entomophobia, which is often fuelled by irresponsible media stories, headlining with fear-inducing names such as “murder hornets”, is the common attitude that the only good insect is a squashed one. Not only is institutional invertebratism (Leather, 2009, 2013) still alive and well but we now have two potentially life-threatening conditions that desperately need curing. 

Entomyopia 

noun 

entomological short-sightedness • a condition in which insects are viewed either as pollinators or as nuisances • a lack of foresight or discernment as to the importance of entomology : a narrow view of entomology 

Entoalexia 

noun 

entomological blindness • a condition in which a person or organisation is totally oblivious to the importance of entomology and insects 

Symptoms 

The closing of entomology departments and research groups A reduction in the numbers of entomologists employed by universities and research institutions An ageing population of practicing entomologists A lack of understanding by the public about why the study of entomology is important to their well-being A lack of teaching of invertebrate biology at secondary schools and at undergraduate level A lack of government funding A tendency for members of the public to scream and/or flinch when insects enter their personal space A tendency for members of the public to kill insects when found in their personal space A failure by the majority of the population to appreciate the beauty and wonder of insects Investing hundreds of millions into medical research to keep people alive for longer (a very good thing) without thinking about how the extra mouths are going to be fed without similar levels of investment in crop protection research (a very bad thing) Funding in conservation and whole organism biology and ecology heavily biased towards “large charismatic mega-fauna” Schoolchildren able to name the ten most endangered mammal species in the world but unable to recognize and name the ten most common insect species in their own country 

Treatment 

A concerted effort by all entomologists to explain to the general public, the educational establishment, funding bodies, the media and government why we need urgently more entomologists and why the study of entomology is crucially important to our well-being. I would go further than that and suggest that we need to redouble our outreach activities and actively lobby those who hold the purse strings and those that represent us in government. Yes, national entomological societies such as the Royal Entomological Society in the UK are doing much more to promote entomology than they used to but much more remains to be done. The Amateur Entomologist’s Society has also been active in this area for more than eighty years. My message to all entomologists is act now before it is too late. Entomyopia is apparently not a new disease. While researching this paper, I came across this gem from 1882. “No science is so generally slighted, ignored, and misunderstood as is Entomology. Hysterical humanitarians, novelists, poets, political agitators, classical students, speak in terms of contempt or horror of the ‘fly-hunters’” (Anon, 1882). As an aside, I would be remiss if I did not point out that mycology, plant pathology and plant nematology are also extremely vulnerable and just as important to our well-being as entomology. 

Prognosis 

At the current level of investment into treatment and cures, very gloomy. On the plus side, NERC has just awarded a £2.3 million grant to study the causes of insect decline (UKRI, 2021), but this is only a drop in the ocean compared with the funding and resources that are needed (Montgomery et al ., 2020). Ironically, the coronavirus pandemic and subsequent lockdowns has, at least in the short-term, made more people aware of the importance of the natural world.

After a period of volunteering with Operation Wallacea (www.opwall.com) in Indonesia, working on coral reef ecology, he joined the Field Studies Council (FSC) on a temporary contract as a Tutor, then a Senior Tutor, at Nettlecombe Court in the Exmoor National Park, becoming Assistant Head there in 2006. (Natural History Museum) 3rd March 2021 Report by Richard Harrington 

The pandemic inevitably stymied the Entomological Club’s Verrall Supper, the very essence of which is convivial in-person interaction, but it couldn’t see off our Society’s companion Verrall Lecture. Quite the reverse. With around 230 people from 16 countries glued to their computers, it was possibly a record attendance. The lecture is usually held at the Natural History Museum, London, so it was appropriate that the speaker was one of its own, Erica McAlister, Senior Curator of Diptera and Siphonaptera. Her specialism was also appropriate, as George Verrall (1848 – 1911) was, of course, an eminent dipterist, and a founder of the Entomological Club in 1887. He described over 550 species of fly and catalogued the UK Diptera, listing 2,991 species in 1888. There are now reckoned to be 7,216. Erica’s talk was a whirlwind tour of the extraordinary diversity and morphology of flies, starting at the head end and working back to the anus which, in the case of many larvae, looks rather like a face and can be used to distinguish species. The weird and wonderful structures and adaptations which she described included the enormous eyes of the Big-headed flies (Pipunculidae); the vestigial mouthparts of the Botflies; the lengthy mouthparts of the South African Nemestrinidae, which are the longest in relation to body length of any insect and used to pollinate flowers with long corollas; the venom of Robber flies (Asilidae); the long legs of the Dolichopodidae, some of which show a fantastic tangle of ribbons, protrusions and hairs, the functions of which are not known; the hairy legs of the Dagger flies (Empididae); 

# Meetings

84 Antenna 2021: 45 (2) the wingless Bee louse ( Braula coeca ) and, arriving now in the nether regions, the fat bottoms of the Soldier flies (Stratiomyidae); the huge ovipositor of the fruit fly 

Anastrepha curvicauda (Tephritidae) and the corkscrew aedeagus of some Blow flies (Phoridae) such as Megaselia . To see the whole range, get Erica’s books. Such morphologies, whilst fascinating and fun, have a purpose and teach us a great deal about the ecology and evolution of this hugely successful and vitally important insect order. Concentrating on the absurd may not do justice to more “normal-looking” flies (if there are such things), but is a great way of encouraging newcomers of all ages, and established entomologists, to take a closer look. Insects don’t have to have bright and beautiful wings to draw people into their world and do what needs to be done in relation to conservation and control. Unsurprisingly, many questions were posed. Erica’s favourite flies are the Robber flies (for their sheer power and aggressiveness) and the Botflies (for their cuteness). She doesn’t have a least-favourite. She recommends the Hoverflies (Syrphidae) or the Soldier flies for budding young naturalists, as there is plenty of identification help available as well as active recording schemes. Erica is convinced that flies can play a larger role in human diets, and there are already factories all over the world devoted to this. Many other subjects were covered, but the final question was revealing. Does Erica have an ambition to play host to a Bot fly? “Oh gosh yes – it’s every dipterist’s dream.” I suggest that the parents of budding young naturalists are kept in the dark on that one. The Verrall lecturer is the annual recipient of the President’s medal and, in a lovely final touch to the meeting, the medal miraculously passed from the hands of the President into those of the speaker, via the ether. The Verrall lecturer also gets a complimentary ticket to the Verrall Supper, in this case deferred until next year. I wonder when Black soldier flies will be on the menu? As a postscript, this Verrall Lecture was not only the first ever to be given entirely online, but also the first to be followed up with a “Young Verrall Lecture”. Co-hosted by the Amateur Entomologists’ Society, of which Erica is the current President, over 100 joined the Saturday afternoon fun. It was basically a repeat of the main event but with slightly more references to bottoms and poo. Even some of the questions were the same. The future of entomology looks bright! # Online 17 th – 18 th March 2021 

Report by Charlie Woodrow, Max Tercel and Manuela Carnaghi 

On the 17 th and 18 th of March 2021, early-career and student entomologists from around the world attended a new virtual event titled ‘EntoCareers’; a forum of speakers, activities, and networking for the next generation of entomologists. Held via Zoom, this conference aimed to present different routes into an entomological career, introduce the RES to a new global audience, and discuss the barriers that many underrepresented groups face to enter the field. It was also an opportunity for students to meet each other, discuss their research, and take part in group activities. We were overwhelmed to see 325 people sign up for the event, with over 100 going on to attend all of the first day of talks, and more than 30 staying for the activities and quiz. The event started with an insight into ‘Innovation and Industry in Entomology’. This session, introduced by RES PG rep Charlie Woodrow and chaired by Dr Gia Aradottir, brought speakers from Syngenta, Spotta, Oxitec, and The Bugfarm to discuss the industry routes for entomology graduates. This session was followed by an activity and competition in which attendees were put into virtual breakout rooms in groups, and given the task of creating an insect-inspired piece of technology. Attendees were encouraged to share their creations with us via email and social media. We received four very creative entries for the competition, which was subsequently judged by the post-graduate representatives. The winning design was the ‘Multi Arthropod Silk Spray’ (or MASS), an anti-microbial silk-inspired bandage that can be applied directly onto wounds! Following the innovation and industry talks, attendees were given the chance to ask questions to some past presidents of the RES during the ‘Presidents of Entomology’ session. This discussion, chaired by RES PG rep Manuela Carnaghi, was a brilliant insight into the history of entomology, providing advice for students, and hopes for the future. The panel featured five past presidents of the Society, as well as current president, Professor Helen Roy.

# Jane Memmott 

## by Peter Smithers 

A life outstanding in the field 

It was late September when I set up this interview with Jane. Zoom had worked well with the previous two interviews, but it’s just not the same as talking face to face. So, as both Jane and I are based in Bristol, we decided that it would be safe to meet outside to conduct the interview. A date was set, and on a bright and surprisingly warm autumn afternoon I found myself walking on to Brandon Hill (the city centre nature reserve and park) to meet Jane in the shadow of the local landmark, Cabot Tower. We quickly located a park bench in a sunny location and settled ourselves at either end to discuss Jane’s life in entomology. 

Early life and children 

“Before school, my family spent a long summer holiday in the Burren in County Clare in Ireland. We camped in a farmer’s field and spent the entire summer outdoors. I remember chasing Burnet moths, digging holes and looking at fish in the lakes. They were just wonderful days. At primary school we had a nature table, and I was always a good provider of things for it. There was a hedge that ran along the back of the playground and I remember finding a woolly caterpillar on it, which I collected and kept in a jar. I was then amazed when it pupated, and the most gorgeous moth emerged. It could have been parasitised, but I was lucky, and the moth made it to adulthood. At that age, a gorgeous moth is what you need. I was five years old when I found that first caterpillar and I am still collecting them today – and amazingly it’s part of my job to do so. Most children at primary school are interested in mini beasts but then they tend to outgrow that interest, they leave it behind or maybe it just becomes a bit nerdy, but I never lost it. In fact, I wonder if there is a gene for it as my brothers are not at all interested but my nephew is really fascinated. Is it nature or nurture? Something seems to happen when you are young which switches it on, and once it’s got you, you are never bored. There is always something to grab your interest. If I find myself stuck in a traffic jam, I often look out the window and identify the plants in the roadside verge. Last year I was running between meetings on campus when I spotted a yellow flower I had not seen before. I stopped, picked one of the flowers and went on to my meeting. It turned out to be yellow figwort which is a Mediterranean plant that has never been recorded from the Bristol area before. That was such a buzz; it was just lovely. When my children were at nursery, they reared a hawk moth from a caterpillar, so we took the moth home to release in the garden. It swooped majestically across the lawn, but mid swoop a robin shot out of hiding and plucked it from the air, then swept back into the bushes. The kids were horrified, but it was an early introduction to food webs. At my previous house I ran a moth trap over the summer, and at that time the Avon Wildlife Trust ran an outreach team that went into schools in deprived areas in Bristol. I would empty the moth trap and place a selection of moths in a cool box, which the team would collect and take into the schools. I tested the approach first with my own children at their school. If you take a box of chilled moths into a school and 

88 Antenna 2021: 45 (2) take the lid off, it’s like Pandora’s box. A cooled moth sitting on a child’s hand will rapidly warm up and take flight. The children were amazed and delighted as the moths launched themselves across the school playground.” 

University 

“Durham was my first choice, but I did not get in, so I applied to Leeds and gained a place. I wanted to ensure I was a reasonable distance from home, but by coincidence my dad had been a student there reading engineering and now one of my daughters is there too. I really enjoyed my time there. I read zoology, as ecology had not yet appeared as a separate subject. I really enjoyed the zoology course, but I had to do a range of other subjects which included biochemistry and microbiology which I did not bond with. In fact, I initially failed my first-year biochemistry exam, but I was not alone as twelve of the eighteen zoology students failed this exam, and to this day I still harbour a deep loathing of the Krebs Cycle. The first year practicals were amazing. We were given lots of material collected from the marine field station at Robin Hood’s Bay. So, we saw sea mice, lugworms, and other marine life that I had never encountered before, and we also learnt about the life cycles of anemones and other inverts with pelagic larvae, which was just brilliant. I enjoyed all the invertebrate sessions, anything with lots of legs was great. I also liked the sessions on birds and mammals, but it was the invertebrates that did it for me. My final year project was on an invertebrate. I looked at communication in Madagascan hissing cockroaches, examining the neurophysiology of their hiss.” 

A very good year 

“By my third year I just could not face doing finals and applying for a PhD at the same time, as I had reached overload by then. So, after graduation I took a year out and went travelling to Morocco, Peru and Costa Rica. The trip to Morocco was just a group of family and friends who decided to drive a Land Rover to a remote small village in the Atlas Mountains. We were just travelling, it was time out to unwind, a chance to see other cultures and new habitats. We visited ancient cedar forests and saw Barbary apes which were all new to me. It was also amazing encountering Bedouin and seeing how they lived in those very austere environments. Back in the summer of my first year at University, I had an internship at the Natural History Museum working on psyllids (Homoptera) from New Zealand. I had spent my time there mounting these small insects on slides, ready for identification. So, as I had that connection with the Museum, I wrote to them on my return from Morocco asking if they had any jobs, and to my delight I was offered a three-month post on the Diptera floor, putting together a bibliography of research papers. I then went to Costa Rica for three months to explore possibilities for my PhD project, as back then NERC had a scheme where you could write your own PhD project proposal. I wanted to work in the tropics, so I went out with some ideas, came back and wrote an application, and received the funding for it. I had also applied for a job as a tour guide on a rain forest reserve in Peru, which catered for mostly American and German tourists. Travelling to the reserve was outrageously 

> Jane Memmott as PhD student in the Costa Rican rain forest. Many happy hours were spent looking for very small sandflies at the bases of very big trees.

exciting. We flew over the Amazon canopy for hour after hour, with a river meandering through the endless forest below us. This was followed by a couple of hours going upriver in a small boat, before finally arriving at a very splendid reserve with palm thatched huts. The tourists would come in for a two- or three-day adventure, so as guides we would walk them through the forest to a series of oxbow lakes, pointing out anything that we encountered on the way. There was lots to see, as there were seven species of primate on the reserve and many species of bird. I would talk about the numerous ants we met on the walk to the lake, and point out tarantula holes and social spider webs that teemed with small spiders. I often caught a grasshopper before the walk, and would throw it into the social spiders’ web so the spiders would rush out like hunting dogs to subdue this much larger prey. Once at the lake, we would load the tourists into canoes which had been lashed together into flotillas (to make it more difficult for them to capsize), and paddle out to fish for Piranhas. This was very simple, a piece of meat on a bent pin on a string and in thirty seconds you had a Piranha in the canoe. I would talk about their biology and their razor-sharp teeth, while trying not to lose a chunk of my finger. I would also point out the many birds around the edge of the lake. I remember the Hoatzins, which were stunning. They are very primitive birds that look a little like archaeopteryx. There were also the Horned screamers, and many others. The highlight was a family of four Giant river otters that would cruise by once we were out on the lake. These were huge, the size of basset hounds. We would then paddle around the lake for a couple of hours, before returning to the lodge for a rum and tonic. Working there was just heaven. Unfortunately, the reserve was owned by a wealthy individual who did not get 

Antenna 2021: 45 (2) 89 on with the local people. In fact, while I was there, the main lodge was burnt to the ground. A pointed lesson – if you want nature reserves to work from a conservation perspective, it’s important to work with the local community. But my time there was an astonishing experience. That same year I also walked a large chunk of the SW coastal path. I love Cornwall. Hiking the path was a big adventure. We had no money, so we wild-camped on the cliff path, but it was lots of fun. I also had a serious cycling accident that year, but I mended, and in that same year I met my partner, so overall it was a very good year.” 

PhD 

“My PhD had been written to work with Stephen Sutton, a tropical biologist who was then at the University of Leeds. I spent three years working on the aggregations of Sand flies on the buttresses of the large rainforest trees. In the day, I caught male and female flies and hand-sprinkled them with different coloured fluorescent dust, so when I inspected the buttresses at night, I could map their distributions. It transpired that these aggregations were static swarms which were male dominated, as you would expect, and the various species were vertically stratified on the buttresses. As I was a long way from my supervisor, I barked up a lot of wrong trees. Back then there was no email, so when I was stuck, I would write a letter asking for help, but by the time the answer arrived a month later I had usually solved the problem. I spent six months of each year in the forest staying at the La Selva field station. It was like living at a conference in the rain forest. There were usually talks at the end of each day as the great and the good passed through the station, people like E.O. Wilson and Joe Connell, who were amazing to meet. I spent the summers at the field station and returned to Leeds for the winter to process data and start writing up.” 

Post Doc 1 

“My first post doc was split between Imperial College and the NHM. Charles Godfray, who was then a new member of staff, was the lead investigator. He wanted to work on food webs, looking at the links between parasitoids, leaf miners and plants, and had decided to do it in the tropics just to make it really exciting and challenging. As I had been working in Costa Rica for the last three years I knew how to work in the tropics and had the right skill set, and I guess I must have been the right person at the right time to do the job. This was a very different experience from my PhD field work, as this time I was living in a tent under a giant Strangler fig tree. Travel was by bicycle, or I could rent one of the local horses. I was based in the deciduous dry forest, but if I went up the mountain I was in cloud forest, and going down to the coast there were beaches where thousands of turtles hauled out onto the sand to lay their eggs at the right phase of the moon. So, lots of adventures to be had. I am really just an old-fashioned natural historian at heart, and being able to live and work in those sorts of places was just the best thing ever. Most of the leaf miners I found were unknown, as were the parasitoids, but as I was part-based at the NHM I had access to all of their expertise. Life under the Strangler fig was not all good. I remember cycling nervously back to camp in an electric storm with my Wellingtons full of water. On arrival, I tried to have a conversation with an American ecologist who was camping on the other side of the tree, but the storm was so loud we could not hear each other talk. So, he handed me a piece of paper on which he had written, “ It’s a poorly lived life that knows no fear ”. Indeed, it is, as we often had visitors in our tents. Other than the regular mosquitos, the army ants would come through and clean out the cockroaches, but we also had racoons, amblypygids the size of a dinner plate, and vampire bats. Hence, keeping one’s toes tucked inside the mosquito net at night was doubly important.” 

Post Doc 2 

“This was also at Imperial College, but this time split with what was called then the International Institute for Biological Control. It was an interdisciplinary project on the ecology of biological control, which funded two post docs over five years. We had a huge amount of freedom to follow our own interests, and I worked mainly on the control of invasive plants. This took me to New Zealand for six months each year, where I worked with the weed biocontrol team. It was so different from Costa Rica. There were no snakes, no malaria, no dengue fever, and so it felt very safe. I was working on Broom and the two psyllid species that had the potential to control it. The psyllids were reared in the UK, and then shipped over to New Zealand and kept in quarantine. Once all the safety trials were complete, we released groups of them into fifty-five sites across South Island. The size of the released population varied, with the smallest being just two. Our field assistant gave all the couples names, and we had a Cathy and Heathcliff on a remote windswept Broom patch, and George and Mildred on a lowland farm site. The field seasons were spent driving around South Island, releasing and counting these insects, and it was a lot of fun. We monitored the psyllid populations for the next five years, and for three years after the post doc I would return to New Zealand every summer to continue the work.” 

Bristol 

“Towards the end of the post doc, I took a lecturing post at Bristol University, and three years after that I had children, and so overseas field work came to a halt. I had spent ten years living out of a rucksack by that time, and had become tired of travelling, and the idea of having a home, a dog and children was wonderful. I had to reinvent myself on the research front, and while I kept my interest in alien plants, I also started working on British agroecosystems. At that time, BBSRC were moving from looking at indicator species to looking at the interactions between species on farmland. Working with Bill Symondson at Cardiff, I applied for funding to look at ten organic and ten conventional farms using the same network approaches that I had used in Costa Rica. At that time, I also had a project on Hawaii, looking at the dark side of biocontrol, asking how safe it is, i.e., what happens when the biocontrol agents get into nature reserves. These two projects determined the direction of that stage of my career. They both worked out so well because I had a group of spectacularly talented and wonderful post docs and PhD students. Working with teams like these is one of the best aspects of my job.” 

Islands 

“I really like island systems. They are nature’s experimental arenas. Over the years, I have worked on a number of island 

90 Antenna 2021: 45 (2) chains, beginning with the Hawaii project. I then swapped, working in the Azores with some great students and collaborators. Both Hawaii and the Azores shared some of the same invasive plants, and it was possible to visit the Azores for few days while it was only worth visiting Hawaii if you were there for some weeks, which wasn’t very family friendly. I then worked on the Hebrides, and after a gap of five years without an archipelago, I am now working in the Channel Islands.” 

Pollination 

“There had been discussions about pollinator networks in the literature for some time. In fact, there was a comment in a paper by Nick Waser and colleagues, advocating surveys of entire local assemblages of plants and pollinators but describing it as “a daunting task”. I knew that it wasn’t as difficult as it looked, as I had worked on networks of species in the tropics with parasitoids, which were far more complex. So, funded with a small research grant from the British Ecological Society, I constructed the first quantitative plant pollinator network. It was just a single network which I published in Ecology Letters, but this paper led to several PhD students using this approach in a variety of different systems. I then received some grants, which culminated in the Urban Pollinator grant, which involved four cities and four universities, and some wonderful project staff and collaborators. We were asking about the effect of urban habitats on pollinators, and the problem was a lack of well-replicated comparative data, so we set out to collect this by systematically looking at these interactions at the community level at replicate sites in urban areas, farmland and nature reserves. The current large project I’m involved with is looking at the impact of climate change on pollinators, and the knock-on effects of this on micro-nutrients in the human diet in Nepal. Micro-nutrients such as Vitamin A and folic acid come in part from insect-pollinated crops, so if pollinators decline this can lead to deficiencies in these micro-nutrients. The research team comprises pollination biologists at Bristol University, climate change scientists at the University of Helsinki and human nutritionists at Harvard University, along with key collaborators in a number of other places. Working with an NGO in Nepal (HERD International) that works on developing evidence-based policy, especially in the health field, we have just appointed two project managers, and are about to appoint twenty field assistants to collect data on plant pollinator networks and on people’s diet in remote mountain villages. We are exploring whether restoring pollinators provides a more sustainable approach than dietary supplements.” 

Wellbeing and the environment 

“I have begun to take an interest in this area recently. The evidence used to be rather anecdotal regarding the beneficial effects of the natural world, but there are now really good data proving that both physical and mental health can be improved by spending time in green spaces. I always start my day with a dog walk in a local wood. It has been demonstrated that the benefits of a walk in a green space last for about seven hours. My morning dog walk lasts me until about three in the afternoon! At the moment I am just reading around the subject and including it in my teaching, but I think this could be an approach to use for conservation in urban habitats in particular. If we can manage to encourage both biodiversity and wellbeing at the same time, then it’s a win-win situation.” Our time was up. Introduction 

Like all universities, institutes, organisations and individuals with entomological leanings, the RES has always received enquiries about insects. As such, the Society will have responded to requests from a variety of sources and by a variety of means since its inception in 1833. More recently, the questions and answers strategy has become more formalised, firstly by taking an entomologist onto the staff in 2006 and, a decade later, as the Society became more outward looking, via the ‘National Insect Week’ website – including a specific query icon (Fig. 1). Clicking on the icon led to a form to complete with relevant details and an image upload of the insect. In the following year the Society’s main website was revised to include the same icon and form. Nevertheless, the Society still receives queries via email, telephone and Royal Mail – certainly the latter for actual specimens. When the post was established, insect queries came under the remit of the Director of Science, currently Jim Hardie, with advice from other Fellows and Members of the Society. Queries come in from all over the planet and where identification to species is essential, but not immediately possible, people are referred to relevant experts who may be able to assist. We recommend that all interesting UK finds are reported to iRecord (https://www.brc.ac.uk/irecord/) to feed into appropriate databases. Not surprisingly the numbers of queries and responses have risen over the years so last year we managed to recruit two volunteers to assist, particularly over the peak period – and to co-author this article. A couple of other offers had to be postponed when one headed off to survey Marlon Brando’s atoll, Teti’aroa, and the other was overtaken by more pressing tasks. Hopefully they’ll will be happy to oblige in the future. Should anyone else be interested please let us know! The reasons for questions are varied but include an interest in ‘What is this beautiful insect that I have never seen before’, ‘Will this kill my children and pets?’, ‘What is this extra protein in my sandwich?’ and the press often wishing to sensationalise high population densities/plagues. We are also approached by authors, TV shows and quiz programmes to ensure that their entomological content is correct. 

Responses over the last six years 

The volume of interest in the service is measured by the number of replies rather than the number of initial queries submitted, as many replies stimulate further questions. Over 

Antenna 2021: 45 (2) 93 the last six years the numbers have risen from just under 1000 to around 6000 in the last two years (Fig. 2). Numbers of replies vary with the seasons and, with the majority coming from UK, the responses peak in June -August (Fig. 3). During UK winters we get enquiries on household visitors, with some found dead or overwintering, from people looking through their photographs, and from the tropics and southern hemisphere.

In August Margaret Bowry sent pictures from Dorset of a male flame-shouldered blister beetle, Sitaris muralis . She initially found three specimens in her lounge, and another a few days later (which died after release), plus another dead one on the patio. The deceased specimens were sent to Max Barclay at the Natural History Museum London and posted on iRecord. Like other species in the family Meloidea, this blister beetle is a kleptoparasite in certain solitary bee nests. It is a poor traveller, flightless and with a bumbling gait as an adult, although the early-instar triungulin larvae will be transported by the bee host. This species is described as vulnerable and the UK Beetles’ website (https://www.ukbeetles.co.uk/ sitaris-muralis accessed 29/1/2021) reports that there was a population in Oxford between 1906 and the 1940s. It was rediscovered in the New Forest in 2010 (Brock, 2010) and seen in Wareham, Dorset in 2015 (Mellings and Piper, 2015). Brock (2019) also reports sightings in Wiltshire and Kent. Margaret’s finding of 4-5 specimens appears to be an impressive second sighting in Dorset.

Rosalia alpina is a charismatic beetle which is widespread in Europe, although populations are declining and it has legal protection in a number of countries. It is not a UK resident but is occasionally sighted, e.g. Halstead (1997). The larvae develop mainly in birch and a few other tree species so may be imported, only to later emerge from furniture manufactured in Europe. Adults do fly but mark-recapture studies have found flights with a maximum distance of 1.5 km, although this may underestimate true potential (Drag et al., 2011). Steve Fitton got in touch after spotting this female on a poppy leaf in his Suffolk garden on June 4. On June 16, Roger Leeke observed approximately 60 Villa cingulata in flight and resting among the meadow vegetation at Westonbirt Arboretum, Gloucestershire. The county recorder, John Phillips, informed us that a complete absence of any records in Britain since 1937 had been reversed in 2000 by the rediscovery of this species at Daneway Banks, Gloucestershire (see Thomas, 2017), where they have been seen regularly ever since. Small groups have now appeared over a wider geographical range, but encountering a group as large as 60 at one time is evidence of the efforts made by Andy Bryce and his team over many years working to improve habitats for a variety of flora and fauna at the Arboretum. While the solitary bee host remains unknown, it is reassuring to encounter a mass emergence such as this, since it suggests that the population is healthy and thriving. 

Household visitors 

We do, of course, see quite a few household insects throughout the year and for Jonathan Mitchell in Lancashire the sight of small brown beetles in a 19th Century house came on top of other problems common to older properties. Jonathan had done some research and we were able to confirm that these were not the woodworm he was dreading, 

but the Tribolium flour beetles he was hoping they were. Effusive thanks followed and we were delighted to learn what a positive impact a simple identification could have. 

Why should we offer this service? 

There are other avenues to facilitate insect identification, such as iSpot (https://www.ispotnature.org/) and the Natural History Museum London (https://www.nhm.ac.uk/take-part/identify-nature.html). The Royal Horticultural Society offers identifications of garden insects for members, the Amateur Entomologists’ Society also caters for members, and there are numerous online forums covering local interests and specialised insect groups. The RES Insect Identification service neatly fits into the public benefit requirements for charitable bodies and the Society’s objective for the ‘ diffusion of entomological science ’, as well as outreach ambitions. In addition, it provides data on national biodiversity. Anyone can request assistance and so it introduces the Society to thousands of people who may not otherwise come across it. Satisfyingly, we receive many messages of thanks for enlightenment, especially when it’s not bad news!

This is The Secret Life of Flies Vol. 2. Where Erica’s first book presented an overview of Dipteran diversity and ecology, her second book is a Haynes Manual that presents the inner workings of this order. Chapter one deals with pre-adulthood, and then subsequent chapters explore the various sections of the body, ranging through the head, antennae, mouth parts, thorax, wings, legs, abdomen and, finally, the terminalia. In these chapters, Erica outlines our understanding of the mechanics of each of these sections of the dipteran body. Using the most recent research as a starting point, she details the physiological and biochemical processes that have made this insect order one of the most successful groups in the biosphere. While the writing style of The Secret Life of Flies had an informal edge to it, this volume is pure McAlister. Anyone who has attended one of her talks will instantly recognise the irreverent informality. The text is densely informative, but her refusal to be entirely serious generates a very readable and entertaining text. Embedded within these chapters are snippets of the history of dipteran science, which offer a fascinating counterpoint to the recent advances that are detailed in each section. The book is indexed and also contains a list of references for further reading. While The Inside Out of Flies explores the mechanical and physiological solutions that the Diptera have evolved to solve the many problems that they face, it can also offer a broader appreciation of how these solutions apply to insects in general. If The Secret Life did not convince you that flies are truly amazing, then Inside Out certainly will. Scattered through the book is a collection of excellent photographs, which complement and enhance the text, adding a curious beauty to the narrative. 

Inside Out is a comprehensive overview of dipteran biology. It is a must for anyone who would like a better understanding of how flies in particular, and insects more generally, work. Peter Smithers

# Obituaries 

John Selborne (John Palmer, Lord Selborne) died on 12 th 

February 2021; he was 80 years old. John was a farmer, conservationist, science policy expert and parliamentarian. From 2007 he was Vice-Patron of the Royal Entomological Society. John’s family (he was a hereditary peer, the 4 th Earl of Selborne) live at Selborne in Hampshire, the village made famous by Gilbert White’s The Natural History of Selborne 

(1789). The family own an agricultural estate which is particularly famous for its apple production. Though John read history at Oxford, his background in farming and love of the Hampshire countryside strongly moulded his public career. After being a member, or chair, of a variety of different farming industry bodies, he became President of the British Crop Protection Council from 1977–80 and in 1983 Chairman of the Agricultural and Food Research Council (one of the forerunners of the BBSRC). He later served a term as President of the Royal Agricultural Society of England. John was passionate about the environment. In the 1990s he was a member of the Royal Commission on Environmental Pollution and in the same decade chaired the Joint Nature Conservation Committee. He was Chair of the Trustees of Kew Gardens, President of the Royal Geographical Society and Vice-President of the RSPB. Somehow, he also found time to be on the board of Lloyds TSB and Chancellor of Southampton University. His contributions to science policy led to his election to the Royal Society, and at the end of his career, he chaired the influential Foundation of Science and Technology (FST). John’s father was killed in the second world war and so he inherited his title and seat in the House of Lords when his grandfather died in 1971. When the number of hereditaries in the Lords was capped in 1999, he was elected by his peers to remain, and only retired in 2020 (sitting as a Conservative until 2019). He was a member of, or chaired, numerous select committees, and was a strong and vocal advocate of science and the environment at Westminster. A simple recitation of chairmanships and presidencies does little to explain why John was in so much demand, especially considering, as he frequently proclaimed, he was a generalist rather than someone with deep expert knowledge of a particular field (though apple growing was an exception). I had the great good fortune to be a Trustee of Kew when John was Chair, and later interacted with him at the Royal Society and FST, and so was able to see at first-hand how he operated. John had exceptional skills as a chair: he was always completely on top of his brief and his deep passion for the environment and science invariably shone through. He had the knack of ensuring everyone contributed to a topic, and was an activist chairman without ever seeming to be one. And we always finished on time. He was also wise, able to draw on his great experience of government and policy making to give hugely valuable advice, especially at times of crisis. Outside of the committee room John was fun. Quite short with a noticeably deep voice, he had a lively and self-deprecating sense of humour. He once told me with pride that his children teased him: “is there no subject on which you feel disbarred from having an opinion?”! He was always conscious and alive to the anachronisms of our parliamentary system and his position as a hereditary peer. He loved the outdoors and was a very keen and fit walker. John and his wife Joanna, a distinguished art historian, visited the Royal Society South-east Asian Rainforest Research Project in Sabah, Malaysia and amazed the local guides by climbing the very steep and muddy escarpment of the Maliau Basin in one go, John then in his early seventies. In 2016, he conceived the project of walking between all the cathedrals of England, which he completed on Easter Day 2018 when his extended family joined him at Exeter Cathedral (he describes the project in a newspaper article: https://www. independent. co.uk/news/long_reads/england-cathedrals-walking-routes-e a r l - s e l b o r n e - a r c h i t e c t u r e - b r e x i t - c o u n t r y s i d e -a8299431.html). John Selborne played a unique role in British public life for over 40 years. Many institutions, including the Royal Entomological Society, are the better for engaging with him. He is survived by his wife Joanna and children William, George, Luke & Emily.

Alan Clements dedicated his professional life to research on insect physiology, the development of novel pest control methods and advising international organisations, such as the World Health Organisation, but he will be best remembered by students and colleagues alike for his three volumes of The Biology of Mosquitoes , which elegantly summarise and integrate the research of over 5,000 published papers on mosquito biology. 

Early years 

Alan Clements was born in Beijing (Peking at the time), China, in 1927. His father was a missionary and later a salt tax collector for the Chinese government. From the ages of 7 to 11 he attended a boarding school in north China, a region at that time in the hands of the Japanese. In 1938, he and his elder brother, Colin, travelled to England, aged 11 and 13 years, to attend Taunton School in Somerset. Alan was fascinated by biology from an early age and as a boy enjoyed freely exploring the Somerset countryside. At the end of WWII Alan was posted to India with the British Army from 1946 to 1948, where he could continue to broaden his knowledge of insect-life, in spite of the political turmoil during which the subcontinent was separated into Pakistan and India. Alan’s interest in natural sciences led him to obtain a 1 st 

class BSc (Zoology) at Bristol University (1949-1951), and a PhD at Trinity College, Cambridge (1952-1955), supervised by Professor V.B. Wigglesworth, the ‘father of insect physiology.’ Given VBW’s well-known attitude to student supervision, Alan largely worked on his own to determine the hormonal control of ovary development in mosquitoes, which led to a lifelong fascination with physiology. 

Academic and Researcher 

Alan’s first academic appointment was at Birkbeck College in London (1954-1959), where students who were in employment during the day attended lectures during the evenings. His research was into metabolic activities in locust fat body using carbon-14 during a period of improved handling of that isotope. C14 –labelled proteins were converted to C 14 O2 by heating fuming sulphuric acid in glass equipment under high vacuum at a time when safety spectacles and security chambers were not yet available in biology departments; Alan once mentioned how fortunate he was to not have been harmed by an explosion! He met his wife to be, Giovanna (née Hambly) at Birkbeck College and they married on 6 August 1955. Four years later, Alan moved to a newly-formed Department of Biochemistry and Physiology in Southampton University (1959-1962) which, according to Alan, consisted of only four lecturers, leading to very heavy teaching loads. This was temporarily relieved when, at the request of WHO, Alan spent two periods in Australia (1963 & 1977), working at the government research organization CSIRO in Canberra, where the first insect cell culture had just been developed and biochemical support was needed. Following years of teaching and research in universities, Alan was offered the role of Insect Physiologist at Shell Research Ltd, as Senior Scientist undertaking research on insect biochemistry (1963-1965) and Woodstock Agricultural Research Centre, as Head of the Division of Entomology (1965-1971), responsible for evaluating candidate insecticides. He was appointed Principal Scientist, Shell Biosciences Laboratory (1971-1983), responsible for biochemical and pharmacological research to develop new insecticides, developing policy on integrated pest management and collaborations with the WHO to provide fundamental research in support of Shell’s agrochemical interests. These roles and responsibilities also provided opportunities to undertake basic research in highly equipped laboratories, with freedom to publish. Alan was also a consultant for the Overseas Development Administration, reporting on the activities of the Nepal Malaria Eradication Organisation, and adviser to the Trustees of the British Museum (Natural History) on the work of the Department of Entomology. In 1984, he was appointed head of the Department of Medical Entomology, renamed Department of Medical

Parasitology, at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine until his retirement in 1995, age 68 yrs. Alan’s research was largely biochemical, physiological or pharmacological, some of it devoted to mosquitoes. One long-term programme of research concerned the role of glutamic acid as a neuromuscular synaptic stimulant in the locust. Experiments undertaken on the retractor unguis muscle in the hind femur revealed glutamic acid to trigger neuromuscular synapses at low concentrations. Critics claimed that this could not be a functional system in living insects because the concentration of glutamic acid in locust haemolymph was 0.2 molar, well above the concentration that triggered the neuromuscular synapses. But those criticisms were discounted by his joint ultrastructural and neurophysiological investigations which showed the neuromuscular synapses to be deep within the bundles of muscle fibres and protected by the connective tissue sheath. 

Contributions to the Royal Entomological Society 

Honorary Fellow and stalwart of the Royal Entomological Society, Alan also supported academic journalism as amember of the Council of the Royal Entomological Society for a number of years, and chair of its Library Committee, overseeing an extensive holding of entomological books and some 750 journals. At present, 160 current journal titles are taken. Under his direction in 1987 the Society published the first volume of the journal Medical and Veterinary Entomology ,and in 1992 published the first volume of Insect Molecular Biology , both now flourishing journals. 

Scholarship 

Alan’s greatest contribution to our knowledge of mosquito biology and the accomplishment he will be best remembered for is his series of books that began in 1963, with the publication of ‘ The Physiology of Mosquitoes ’. Twenty-five years later it had not been superseded, so over the next 20 years, he extended the original to: ‘ The Biology of Mosquitoes ’Volume 1, ‘ Development, Nutrition and Reproduction ’ in 1992 (511 pp), Volume 2, ‘ Sensory Reception and Behaviour ’ in 1999 (740 pp), and Volume 3, ‘ Transmission of Viruses and Interactions with Bacteria ’ in 2012 (363 pp). This remarkable set of books integrates knowledge of essential aspects of mosquito biology, drawing on a comprehensive selection of peer-reviewed publications across disciplines related to mosquitoes and the biological relationships they have with associated vertebrates, invertebrates and micro-organisms. Alan is survived by his wife, Giovanna, along with their children, Zoe and Philippa, five grandchildren and one great-grandchild.

Charles Ragnar Buckingham Baker was born on 8 th July 1933 and died on 28 th December 2020. He became a Fellow of the Royal Entomological Society in 1962 and served on the Council between 1981 and 1983. Charles can be considered as a key pioneer in the development of Pest Risk Analysis (PRA), the process which is now so fundamental to plant biosecurity worldwide. Prior to the 1990s there was no such structured, evidence-based process that enabled clear decisions to be made on which non-native plant pests needed to be targeted for quarantine measures. Pest lists were drawn up by committees and any actions taken couldn’t readily be justified. After National Service, during which he qualified as a rear gunner in bomber aircraft, and a degree in zoology at Oxford, Charles worked for the UK Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food at Harpenden, north of London, for 36 years (1957 to 1993). Throughout his working life, his job was to enhance measures that enable the UK to be better forearmed and forewarned of the major non-native insect pests that threaten crops and the wider environment, identify the most appropriate methods to prevent their entry and eradicate any outbreaks. He was an extremely knowledgeable and gifted entomologist who applied his many talents in several areas of plant health, even designing experiments and writing models to enhance the assessment of pest risk. In addition to his research activities, he also visited key locations, such as ports and fields, to ensure that measures taken to ensure consignments were free from pests, e.g. gas fumigation against Potato Tuber Moth, Phthorimaea operculella, and to assist with the eradication of new outbreaks, such as the Colorado Beetle, Leptinotarsa decemlineata . He didn’t flinch from administrative roles and often had to set everything aside to focus on combatting the latest invasion, such as Western Flower Thrips, Frankliniella occidentalis and two American leafminers: Liriomyza trifolii and L. huidobrensis. 

He was also an excellent teacher, courteous, kind and very generous with his time, inspiring those around him to explore all avenues in the problems that needed to be tackled. In a key early contribution to the development of PRA (Baker, 1971), he identified “an objective solution to assess the ability of a species to survive and reproduce beyond the present limits of its geographical range” based on insect species’ responses to climate. The challenges to applying this approach and the influence of microclimate were explored by comparing development times of White Ermine moth (Spilosoma lubriceda ) eggs exposed to different constant temperatures and pupae placed outdoors on a north-south gradient in the UK (Baker, 1972). As a precursor of computer forecasting models such as CLIMEX, Baker and Bailey (1979) then mapped areas in the world with similar annual degree-days for development above a threshold of 10°C, a threshold considered to be representative for many warmth-loving pests. They divided the world diagrammatically into three zones based on their similarities with the climate in the UK. Zone 1 comprised the cool temperate areas of the world from which pests could be expected to survive outdoors, at least in southern areas of the UK. Organisms from Zone 2, the warm temperate areas with continental climates, might be expected to survive in a few localities and under glass, whereas those from Zone 3 could only be expected to survive in protected cultivation. He then extended this with a rule of thumb to assess the risk posed by poorly known species, taking into account the likelihood of a species establishing in glasshouses, a phenology model for those species with detailed developmental data and a cost: benefit analysis to assess potential impacts (Baker, 1981a). 

Recognising that such schemes depended on readily available information on the pests of economic importance worldwide that might pose a threat, he employed a team to write large numbers of pest datasheets which were set up in an extensive database so that it could be queried even to reveal, for example, the pest species recorded on roses in Japan. The database was later given to CABI to help populate the first version of the Crop Protection Compendium. He also collected temperature data from many locations worldwide to help identify parts of the world with analogous temperature accumulations to those in the UK where pests might be more likely to find a climate suitable for establishment. His analysis of pest populations worldwide was also used in a guide to importing invertebrates to help identify those insect families which are most and least likely to contain pests that might be damaging if released into the wider environment. 

Recognising the potential for phenology models not only to assess the potential distribution of non-native pests but 

# Charles Ragnar Buckingham Baker 

## a pioneer of Pest Risk Analysis 

Richard Baker 

Plant Health Consultant, York, UK Antenna 2021: 45 (2) 103 

also to time eradication measures that target vulnerable stages in a pest’s life cycle, he incorporated elements from the University of Michigan PETE modelling system, validated the refined model on the Colorado beetle and several Tortricidae using weather and soil temperature data he had collected nationwide (Baker & Cohen, 1985; Baker, 1991). In the process he identified and corrected a key problem with the calculation of accumulated temperatures (Baker, 1980) and explored how temperatures accumulate differently depending on slope and aspect by constructing a mound with temperature sensors outside the laboratory (Baker, 1981b). With his knowledge and experience of all the issues related to the assessment and management of pest risks he played a key role in the development of the first PRA scheme by the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organisation (EPPO) in 1990. After retirement, he was much involved in local Lepidoptera projects and co-authored the Butterflies and Moths of Bedfordshire (Arnold et al., 1997). He took a very active role in local nature conservation, helping set up and warden a reserve, planning and carrying out habitat restoration, particularly on Dunstable and Whipsnade Downs, and, with his wife Pat, on Studham Common near their home. 

In addition to Pat, he leaves behind his two daughters, Sue and Ros, and five grandchildren.

# Stephen David Wratten 

## (1947-2021) 

BSc PhD Glas. MA DSc FRSNZ 

Professor Nick Sotherton 

Game & Wildlife Conservation Trust Fordingbridge, UK 

Professor Stephen Goldson 

Bio-Protection Research Centre Lincoln University, New Zealand 

Distinguished Professor Steve Wratten, died in Christchurch on the 8 th of March 2021 aged 73. Steve was born in London, but the family moved to Essex where he was inspired by a Primary School teacher who took his class on nature walks. Steve dedicated his first research paper to that teacher. A summer job with Jack Dempster guided Steve down the science career path and a first degree at Reading University. There he met Claire and they were married for nearly 50 years. Steve graduated with a PhD on aphids on lime trees from Glasgow University and then worked at both Cambridge and Queen Mary, London Universities, where the theme of insects on trees continued on birch trees. Aphids were to become a lifelong interest. Early on in his career, Steve met up with the farmland ecology team at the Game Conservancy Trust, who were beginning to understand and appreciate the beneficial role of invertebrates in the British farmland ecosystem. Aprogramme of PhD studentships started. Studies on insect pest natural enemies, conservation biocontrol, the insect foods of farmland birds, insect/host plant interactions via chemical defences and economic threshold models for pests were key elements of over 20 studentships. Throughout, he had an eye for the practical use of research, best illustrated by the development of ‘Beetle Banks’. With Matt Thomas and a MAFF studentship, research on the overwintering habitat requirements of predators such as ground beetles and small spiders was converted into a recipe for strips of perennial, grassy banks planted across large arable fields to provide such cover in situ . These ‘Beetle Banks’ proved popular with farmers and are now eligible in England’s Agri-environment Scheme whereby farmers are paid to encourage wildlife. As an enthusiastic lecturer Steve organised field courses for undergraduates in southern Spain and Sussex. Insect taxonomy was taught in the warm sunny hills on the Spanish coast. Full days in the sun were followed by entertaining nights with a few beers. Steve’s supervision extended beyond the lab. With his wife Claire, dinner parties were numerous and great fun, always accompanied by fresh vegetables from the garden and late-night games of snooker. Steve went to New Zealand in 1993 where he was invited to join Lincoln University as a Reader in entomology. Steve’s enthusiasm coincided with a growing interest in the potential of biological control and how to deal with exotic pests that have frequently established in New Zealand. He found himself working in quite different farmland ecosystems from those in Britain. He therefore explored the natural history dimensions within New Zealand’s pastoral, crop and horticultural ecosystems and contributed major advances in understanding the nature and extent of these areas’ biodiversity. In all areas there was a profusion of novel and highly effective pest management research often using the value of deliberately sown non-crop plant species such as buckwheat (Fagopyrum esculentum ) and phacelia ( Phacelia tanacetifolia ). Such plants provided nectar and pollen-based food sources for the pests’ natural enemies, increasing their virulence and persistence. The size of this contribution is well-reflected in his successful supervision of almost 100 PhD students. Steve was always able to draw a crowd from a wide range of admirers. His talks within the local community were widely and enthusiastically attended; by way of demonstration, he grew many vegetables that he enjoyed turning into what he referred to as ‘pretentious culinary dishes’. Practicing what he preached, his presentation style was a refreshing antidote to the droning malaise that can settle-in from less accomplished speakers. This communication forte no doubt explains his perennial popularity with students; Steve was a firm believer that ‘professors must profess’. He was influential to many scientists around the world. He was also uniquely able to use humour and his informality to make people feel at ease in settings as diverse as a PhD oral exam to a conference dinner. In 2019 Lincoln University appointed Steve as a‘Distinguished Professor’. Steve taught in Britain, and in the USA at Oregon State University, in Australia at the University of Sydney, in Denmark at the University of Copenhagen and in China, at Zhejiang University. He was an elected Fellow of the Royal Society of New Zealand, a James Cook Scholar and the holder of a James Taylor Award from the Canterbury Horticultural Society for Communication in Horticulture. As well as his PhD supervision, Steve authored or co-authored eight books and over 400 refereed papers accepted for publication. In addition, through his supervisory skills, Steve won two Lincoln University Excellence Awards, one for Research and one for Teaching. The citation for the Royal Society Fellowship described him as an ‘outstandingly productive ecological entomologist and a gifted communicator’ who has made a ‘substantial impact on agricultural entomology and plant protection in New Zealand’. His Teaching Award citation described him as a ‘charismatic and inspirational teacher’. Speaking more personally, he had thoroughly developed his legendary hobby interest in ‘bird-spotting’. Indeed, he loathed being called a twitcher. During any trip away, there was always a surreptitious diversion into what birds, especially endemics, there were in the vicinity. Another passion, as well as Bob Dylan, was cricket. He was involved in hilarious games of cricket played at Southampton University in local Parks. This was an early format of T20, without the skill, and played in a great rush to catch the summer evening light and the pubs. Steve was well known for his humour often expressed in a self-deprecatory and understated way. Steve was generous with his time and caring of his students. He never rested in his use of science to solve ecological and agri-business problems and enhance productivity in an environmentally-friendly manner. Steve is survived by Claire, their two children and four grandchildren.
